hero.title: We turn public data into civic knowledge.
hero.lede: LoiClair exists to make French legislative work easier to consult and understand. We don't tell you what to think — we give you what you need to form your own opinion.

origin.title: Born from a need for clarity.
origin.sub: One Tuesday evening, staring at an unreadable bill.
origin.p1: I'd heard about a bill on the news. When I tried to read it to form my own opinion: dead end. Several versions, amendments everywhere, a language written for lawyers. Already passed? Why does the Senate have to vote on it again? In force when? Dozens of pages — and hours to barely scratch the surface.
origin.quote: "What if I gave the whole text to an AI, to ask it my questions directly?"
origin.p2: In five minutes, everything became clear: the status, the next steps, the concrete impact. And one thing was obvious: millions of French people go through the same thing. If that clarity had been enough for me, it could be useful to everyone.

stats.heading: Democratic disengagement isn't an opinion.
stats.sub: When three quarters of French people consider their elected officials and political leaders rather corrupt, and one registered voter in three did not vote in the second round of the 2024 legislative elections, it's no longer a political disagreement: it's a signal. Without accessible information, the democratic link frays. Without clarity, distrust sets in.

built.q: Who makes LoiClair, and with what means?
built.a: A non-profit association under the French law of 1901, founded by four volunteer citizens: no employees, no company, no sponsor or public subsidy. Its costs are currently covered by donations from its founders. On the technical side, the site runs on modern, proven building blocks, chosen to stay fast, reliable and cheap to run:

q2.q: Does LoiClair back a political side?
q2.a: No. Figures and summaries are produced from official institutional data, without partisan interpretation. The only bias is that this data should be accessible to everyone.

q3.a: Yes, and it will stay that way. No data is sold, no content is locked behind a paywall.

q4.q: Is there advertising on the site?
q4.a: None. No banners, no retargeting, no advertising cookies.

q5.q: What happens to my data if I subscribe to the newsletter?
q5.a: Your email address is kept in our database, hosted by OVHcloud in the United States until a server in Europe becomes available, and by Resend, the service that sends the newsletter, also in the United States. It is used only to send you the newsletter. You can unsubscribe at any time, or ask for it to be deleted at contact@loiclair.fr.

q6.a: No. The only cookies, none used for tracking, remember your language choice and serve the anti-bot check on the detail pages. Traffic is measured without cookies (pages viewed, country, device type) so we know what gets read: no profiles are built, there is no tracking across sites, and nothing is matched against your email if you are a subscriber. Your searches stay local to your device.

q7.q: Why GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5, and not other AI models?
q7.a: We choose the model task by task, through tests we run ourselves on real texts, graded blind by other AIs. For law summaries, we compared eight models on accuracy, neutrality, completeness, clarity and quality of examples: GPT-6 Luna (OpenAI, through Mammouth) writes summaries almost as reliable as the best ones, for a price at least 20 times lower. It also writes the summaries of debates and Constitutional Council decisions, and the newsletter. For the short dossier card and the sorting behind “What affects me”, a test specific to each task chose Anthropic's Claude Haiku 5.5, which also translates dossier titles into English. LoiClair does not depend on any of these models: they can be replaced at any time. Full method and results on the <prompts>AI model choice</prompts> page.

q8.a: What describes you stays in your browser. LoiClair sends everyone the same data, and your device does the sorting.

process.pageDesc: Understanding how laws are born: from the institutions involved to the full journey of a legislative text.

organes.heading: The Main Institutions and Their Roles
organes.intro: Five institutions share the power to draft, pass and enforce laws in France. Each has a specific role, a distinct method of appointment, and powers set by the Constitution — open a card to explore the details.

assemblee.role: Lower house of Parliament — {complet, select, oui {{an} sitting MPs} other {{an} sitting MPs ({siegesAn} seats)}}
assemblee.content: The National Assembly is the lower house of the French Parliament. Its primary role is to vote on laws, tabled either by the Government (government bills) or by MPs themselves (private members' bills). It scrutinises Government action through parliamentary questions, committees of inquiry and the examination of the State budget, and it can even remove the Government through a no-confidence motion. It is also the main forum for public debate on the major political orientations of the country. In the event of persistent disagreement with the Senate, the National Assembly can have the final say if the Government so requests — a power explicitly granted to it by the Constitution of the Fifth Republic.
assemblee.modeElection: Direct universal suffrage in two rounds. Each MP is elected in a constituency (a territorial district of roughly 125,000 inhabitants), but represents the whole Nation. The term is 5 years; the President of the Republic can, however, dissolve the Assembly: new elections then take place within 20 to 40 days, and no new dissolution is possible in the year following those elections (Article 12 of the Constitution).

senat.content: The Senate is the second chamber of Parliament. It represents the territorial authorities of the Republic — municipalities, departments, regions — and acts as a counterweight to the National Assembly. It reviews each bill after (or sometimes before) the Assembly, proposes amendments, and can delay the adoption of a text in case of disagreement. On constitutional laws and organic laws relating to the Senate itself, it holds equal power with the Assembly: no final say is possible. The Senate cannot be dissolved, which ensures institutional continuity even during political crises.
senat.modeElection: Indirect universal suffrage: senators are elected by a college of roughly 162,000 grand électeurs composed of MPs, senators, regional councillors, departmental councillors and — most importantly — delegates of municipal councils. The term is 6 years, with half of the Senate renewed every 3 years to ensure stability.

gouvernement.role: Executive power — led by the Prime Minister
gouvernement.content: The Government conducts the policy of the Nation. Led by the Prime Minister, it tables government bills. For a long time, about 80% of laws adopted (excluding international agreements) came from its bills; since the 2008 constitutional revision shared the agenda with the chambers, the share of private members' bills rose above 45% in the 15th legislature (2017-2022), according to the National Assembly. It also has powerful tools to push its texts through: the fast-track procedure, the blocked vote, or Article 49.3, which allows a text to be adopted without a vote unless a no-confidence motion is passed. Once laws are voted, it is still the Government that issues the implementing decrees required to put them into practice.
gouvernement.modeElection: The Prime Minister is appointed by the President of the Republic, usually chosen from the majority in the National Assembly. Other ministers are then appointed by the President on the Prime Minister's proposal. The Government is accountable to the Assembly, which can bring it down through a no-confidence motion.

president.role: Head of State — guardian of the institutions
president.content: The President of the Republic is the Head of State. In the legislative process their role is both symbolic and decisive: they promulgate the laws passed by Parliament within 15 days, which gives them binding force. Before promulgating, they can ask Parliament for a new reading or refer the law to the Constitutional Council. They also hold their own powers that weigh on the political balance: appointment of the Prime Minister, dissolution of the National Assembly, and recourse to a referendum on certain texts. They also chair the Council of Ministers.
president.modeElection: Direct universal suffrage in two rounds. The President is elected for a 5-year term (quinquennat) since the 2000 constitutional revision. Since 2008, the mandate can only be renewed once consecutively.

conseil.content: The Constitutional Council is the highest jurisdiction of the Republic in constitutional matters. It checks the conformity of laws with the Constitution before their promulgation (a priori review) when referred — by the President of the Republic, the Prime Minister, the Speaker of the National Assembly, the President of the Senate, or 60 MPs or 60 senators. It can declare a law, or some of its articles, contrary to the Constitution: those then cannot be promulgated. Since 2010, any party to a court case can also challenge a legislative provision that allegedly infringes the rights and freedoms guaranteed by the Constitution, through a priority preliminary ruling on constitutionality (QPC) referred by the Council of State or the Court of Cassation. Finally, the Council oversees the regularity of the presidential election and of referendums, and rules on disputes over legislative and senatorial elections.
conseil.modeElection: Established by the 1958 Constitution, the Constitutional Council has 9 members appointed for a single non-renewable 9-year term: 3 by the President of the Republic, 3 by the Speaker of the National Assembly, 3 by the President of the Senate. The Council is renewed by thirds every 3 years. Former Presidents of the Republic are ex officio members for life.

parcours.heading: A law's journey
parcours.intro: From the initial idea to entry into force, a text can go through up to eight distinct stages. Each stage involves different actors and can take several months — here is the typical journey of a French law.
parcours.step1Details: The text is tabled either by the Government (government bill) or by a member of Parliament (private member's bill).
parcours.step2Details: Detailed study, hearings, rapporteur appointed, proposed changes.
parcours.step3Desc: Debate and vote in the chamber
parcours.step3Details: Discussion article by article, then a vote on the whole text.
parcours.step4Desc: Harmonisation between the Assembly and the Senate
parcours.step4Details: Back-and-forth exchanges or compromise in the Joint Committee (Commission Mixte Paritaire).
parcours.step5Details: Both chambers adopt the same text; if disagreement persists, the Government can give the National Assembly the last word.
parcours.step6Desc: Mandatory for an organic law, possible for an ordinary law
parcours.step6Details: Verification of compliance with the Constitution.
parcours.step7Details: The President signs and publishes the law in the Official Journal.
parcours.step8Details: The Government publishes the implementing decrees needed for the law to be effectively applied. Where the law calls for them, the provisions concerned cannot be applied without them.

procedureRenforcee.label: Reinforced procedure:
procedureRenforcee.item1: A waiting period before the first debate in plenary: six weeks after tabling, fifteen days under the fast-track procedure
procedureRenforcee.item2: If the two chambers disagree, the National Assembly only has the last word by an absolute majority of its members (289 MPs)
procedureRenforcee.item3: An organic law concerning the Senate must be passed in identical terms by both chambers
procedureRenforcee.item4: Mandatory review by the Constitutional Council before promulgation
procedureRenforcee.examples: Examples: the framework of the State budget (LOLF), how the Constitutional Council works, the ban on holding several offices at once.

methode.chiffresLien: See all the facts and their method
methode.loisTexte: We link each bill to its official text, as published by the National Assembly, the Senate or Légifrance. activite.introText: LoiClair splits the work of a parliamentarian (MP or senator) into four core missions. The score (0–100) condenses 11 rankings into one. On each indicator (votes, amendments, floor speeches…), every member gets a mark based on their position among peers: 50 is the middle of the chamber, 100 the member ahead of everyone. When several members are on an exact tie, they all receive the mark at the middle of their group: a senator tied first with a hundred others therefore does not reach 100. The weighted average of those 11 marks gives the final score, according to the weight of each mission.

adopteAN.definition: The National Assembly adopted the text in the latest vote. A bill continues its journey, a resolution or a motion stops there.

adopteParlement.definition: Both chambers have voted on the text in identical terms. It now awaits promulgation by the President.

adopteSenat.definition: The Senate adopted the text in the latest vote. A bill continues its journey, a resolution stops there.

enCoursExamen.definition: The text has been tabled in Parliament but has not yet been voted on. It is awaiting examination or under discussion.

publie.definition: The text is finalised and made public. It is a report, fact-finding mission, committee of inquiry or petition — a document that is not meant to be put to a vote.

promulguee.definition: The text has been signed by the President and published in the Official Journal. It has the force of law.

rejete.definition: The text was rejected by both chambers, or by the only chamber examining it (a resolution, for example). A new tabling remains possible. For a no-confidence motion, it is the motion that is rejected: the Government stays in place and, after Article 49.3 has been used, the text is deemed adopted by the National Assembly.

allocutionPresident.term: Address by the Speaker of the National Assembly
allocutionPresident.definition: An official speech by the Speaker of the National Assembly, for example to open a session or mark a solemn occasion. This is not a legislative text.

commissionEnquete.definition: A group of members of Parliament set up to investigate a specific matter. It can summon witnesses and see confidential documents. It produces a report, not a law.

engagementResponsabilite.definition: Article 49 procedures: the Prime Minister stakes the Government's responsibility (for example under Article 49.3), or MPs table a no-confidence motion. They can get a text adopted without a vote, or bring the Government down.

missionInformation.definition: A parliamentary working group tasked with studying a topic and reporting on it. Lighter than a committee of inquiry, it has, in principle, no binding power.

petitions.definition: Requests addressed to Parliament by citizens. A committee may examine them, but they do not produce a law.

projetFinancementSecu.definition: The annual Social Security budget, tabled each autumn. It sets spending targets: health insurance, pensions, family benefits, workplace accidents, long-term care.

projetFinancesAnnee.definition: The annual State budget, tabled by the Government each autumn. It sets revenue (taxes, duties) and spending for the following year.

projetFinancesRectificative.definition: A mid-year change to the State budget, to adjust it to unforeseen events or to economic conditions.

projetLoiOrdinaire.definition: A text prepared and tabled by the Government to create or amend a law. It is the main route for major reforms, and it passes far more often than a private member's bill.

projetRatificationTraites.definition: Parliament authorises the ratification of a treaty signed by France (trade agreement, international convention, European treaty). It can accept or reject it, but not amend it.

projetLoiConstitutionnelle.definition: A text that amends the Constitution. The National Assembly and the Senate must pass it in identical terms. When it comes from the Government, it is then approved by referendum or by Congress (both chambers sitting together at Versailles) with a three-fifths majority. When it comes from members of Parliament, it must go to a referendum.

projetLoiOrganique.definition: A text that specifies how the Constitution is applied, for example the status of members of Parliament. It follows a reinforced procedure and must go before the Constitutional Council.

propositionLoiOrdinaire.definition: A text tabled by an MP or a senator, not by the Government. Most never pass, but some become major laws.

rapportInformation.definition: A report written on behalf of a committee to inform Parliament on a topic, without a mission being set up. It has no binding value.

resolution.definition: A text voted by a single chamber, to express a position (for example on a European proposal) or to decide on its own functioning (amending its rules of procedure, setting up a committee of inquiry). It is not a law.

resolutionArticle34.definition: A resolution through which the National Assembly or the Senate expresses a position on any subject, under article 34-1 of the Constitution. It has no force of law.

responsabilitePenale.term: Criminal liability of the President of the Republic
responsabilitePenale.definition: Despite this label, taken from National Assembly data, this is not a criminal trial: Parliament, sitting as the High Court, can remove the President of the Republic from office by a two-thirds majority, for a breach of duty manifestly incompatible with the mandate (article 68 of the Constitution).

premierDepot.definition: The first step: the author (government or MP) formally tables their text in Parliament. This marks the start of the legislative procedure.

premiereRecture1.term: First reading in the first chamber
premiereRecture1.definition: The first full examination of the text by the chamber that received it first. It includes committee work followed by a plenary debate.

premiereRecture2.term: First reading in the second chamber
premiereRecture2.definition: The first examination of the text by the second chamber, after adoption by the first. The parliamentary shuttle begins.

accordInternational.definition: A treaty or international convention linked to the dossier. Parliament authorises ratification but cannot amend the treaty text.

avisConseilEtat.definition: An advisory opinion on the legal quality of the text, issued by the Council of State on a government bill before it is tabled in Parliament. Requesting it is mandatory for government bills, but it does not bind the Government.

commissionMixteParity.definition: A meeting of 7 MPs and 7 senators tasked with finding a compromise text when both chambers disagree. If it agrees, the Government may put this text to a vote in both assemblies.

conclusionConseilConstitutionnel.definition: The final decision of the Constitutional Council on whether the text complies with the Constitution. It may validate, partially strike down, or fully strike down the text.

conseilConstitutionnel.definition: The stage where the text is reviewed for constitutional compliance. The Council verifies that the law respects the Constitution.

convocationCMP.definition: The Prime Minister (or the Speaker of the National Assembly and the President of the Senate for a private member's bill) requests the convening of a Joint Committee. This marks the start of the conciliation procedure.

creationCommissionEnquete.term: Creation of a committee of inquiry
creationCommissionEnquete.definition: The National Assembly's or the Senate's decision to launch a parliamentary inquiry. The committee has extensive investigative powers.

creationMissionInformation.definition: The decision to create a parliamentary working group on a given topic. The mission will produce a report at the end of its work.

debat.definition: A discussion in plenary session on the text or a related topic. MPs set out their positions and examine amendments.

decision.definition: The chamber's final vote on the text in plenary session. The text is adopted, rejected, or adopted with modifications.

decisionCMP.definition: The result of the Joint Committee's work. It can lead to an agreement (shared text) or a failure (deadlock).

decisionMotionCensure.definition: The National Assembly's vote on a no-confidence motion against the government. If passed, the government falls.

depotProjetLoi.definition: The government formally tables a text in Parliament. It is generally accompanied by an impact assessment; the opinion the Council of State gave on the text is usually published.

depotDeclarationGouvernement.definition: The government submits an official declaration to Parliament, which may give rise to a debate. It has no legislative value.

depotInitiativeNavette.term: Tabling of an initiative in the shuttle
depotInitiativeNavette.definition: Transmission of the text from one chamber to the other after a first vote. The shuttle continues until both chambers adopt identical text.

depotLettreRectificative.definition: The government amends its own bill before or during examination. This allows the text to be updated without withdrawing it.

depotRapport.definition: The rapporteur submits the committee report to the assembly. This document summarises the committee's work and recommendations.

depotRapportCMP.term: Tabling of a Joint Committee report
depotRapportCMP.definition: Publication of the compromise text produced by the Joint Committee. If it agrees, the Government may put it to a vote in both assemblies.

deuxiemeLecture.definition: A second examination of the text by a chamber, after the other chamber has made changes. The debate focuses only on the remaining points of disagreement.

discussionSeancePublique.definition: Examination of the text by all members of Parliament in the chamber. This is where amendments are debated and voted on.

etudeImpact.definition: A mandatory document accompanying government bills, assessing in particular the economic, social, legal, local-government, business, and gender-equality consequences of the text. It is published before examination begins.

procedureAcceleree.definition: The Government triggers this procedure so it can convene a joint committee after a single reading per chamber, instead of two. If the committee fails, each chamber reads the text again, then the Government can ask the National Assembly to make the final decision. This significantly shortens the examination of the text.

lectureDefinitive.definition: The National Assembly's last vote when the Joint Committee has failed and the government gives it the final say. The Senate can no longer oppose it.

lectureUnique.definition: The text is examined in a single reading by one chamber, with no possibility of a shuttle. This applies to certain resolutions or special texts.

miseEnApplication.definition: Publication of the decrees and orders needed for the law to take concrete effect. Without these texts, some provisions remain unenforceable.

motionCensure.definition: A procedure by which the National Assembly can bring down the Government. It requires the signature of at least one tenth of MPs to be tabled (at least 58 out of 577).

motionProcedure.definition: A request made during a session to change the course of a text's examination. It may aim to reject the text without debate or refer it back to committee.

nominationRapporteur.definition: The committee designates one of its members to study the text in detail and write a report. The rapporteur becomes the key reference for the text in committee and in plenary.

nominationRapporteurBudgetaire.definition: The committee designates a specialist rapporteur to examine a part of the budget. Each budget rapporteur covers a specific policy area (defence, education, health, etc.).

nouvelleLecture.definition: Resumption of the examination of the text by one chamber after the Joint Committee has failed. Both chambers try to agree on a common text.

promulgationLoi2.definition: The President of the Republic signs the law and orders its publication in the Official Journal. The law takes effect the day after publication, unless stated otherwise.

rapportApplicationLois.term: Report on the implementation of laws
rapportApplicationLois.definition: An assessment drawn up by Parliament on the effective implementation of a passed law. It checks whether the implementing decrees have been published.

renvoiCommissionFond.definition: The text is referred to the main committee responsible for examining it. This committee will write the report and propose amendments.

renvoiPrealable.definition: The text is first sent to a committee for a preliminary examination. In the National Assembly, this applies to European resolution proposals, examined by the European Affairs Committee before the lead committee.

renvoiPrealableCAE.term: Prior referral to the European Affairs Committee
renvoiPrealableCAE.definition: A European resolution proposal is first examined by the European Affairs Committee, before the lead committee.

retraitInitiative.definition: The author of the text (government or MP) withdraws their own bill or proposal. The dossier is closed.

reunionCommission.definition: A working session of the parliamentary committee tasked with examining the text. Amendments are debated and voted on before the plenary debate.

saisineConseilConstitutionnel.definition: The President of the Republic, the Prime Minister, the Speaker of the National Assembly, the President of the Senate, 60 MPs or 60 senators ask the Constitutional Council to check that the text complies with the Constitution. This referral, known as a priori review, always takes place before promulgation, and suspends the deadline for it until the decision. For an organic law, it is mandatory.

saisiePourAvisCommission.definition: A committee is consulted to give its opinion on a text that falls mainly within the remit of another committee. Its opinion is advisory.

travaux.definition: The set of activities related to the examination of a dossier. This generic term covers meetings, hearings and discussions.

travauxCommissionSaisieAvis.definition: Work carried out by a committee consulted for an advisory opinion on a text. It may propose amendments but the final decision rests with the lead committee.

travauxCommissionFond.definition: Work of the main committee responsible for examining the text. It writes the report and amendments submitted to the full assembly.

travauxCommissions.definition: The phase where the text is examined by parliamentary committees. Committee members hear experts, debate and propose changes.

texteDepose.definition: The initial version of the text, as tabled by its author (MP or government). This marks the start of the procedure.

commission.definition: The version of the text amended by the parliamentary committee responsible for examining it. It incorporates the amendments adopted in committee.

seance.definition: The version of the text adopted in plenary session, after debates and amendments in the chamber. This is the text as voted by the chamber.

legifrance.definition: The official version published in the Official Journal after promulgation. This is the definitive law text, as referenced on Légifrance.

appliquee.definition: The law has been promulgated, and the Government has taken every measure it called for. The law applies in full.

projetApprobationComptes.term: Bill on budget outturn and approval of the accounts
projetApprobationComptes.definition: Each year, the Government presents the final accounts of the past year. Parliament checks that money was spent as planned, then votes to approve or reject them.

propositionLoiReferendaire.term: Bill under Article 11 of the Constitution
propositionLoiReferendaire.definition: A text backed by at least one fifth of members of Parliament and supported by one tenth of voters. If Parliament does not examine it within six months, it is put to a referendum.

applicationComplete.definition: Every measure called for by the law has been taken: it applies in full.

decretsApplication.definition: Government texts that spell out how a law is applied in practice: who does what, from when, and under which rules.

loiApplicationDirecte.definition: A law that applies as soon as it is published, without waiting for a decree.

publicationDecretApplication.definition: A decree needed to apply the law has appeared in the Official Journal.

troisiemeLecture.definition: The text goes back before a chamber a third time, because the National Assembly and the Senate still disagree.

amendement.definition: A modification proposed by a member of Parliament or the Government on a text under discussion. A bill can receive hundreds of amendments before its final vote.

ordonnance.definition: A measure taken by the Government, with Parliament's authorisation (Article 38 of the Constitution), in a domain normally reserved for law. It must be ratified by Parliament to have permanent legal force. Example: labour code reform in 2017.

decret.definition: A regulatory text issued by the President of the Republic or the Prime Minister, for example to specify the implementation details of a law. It does not go through Parliament.

definitions.proceduresRenvoi: Government bill, private member's bill, committee of inquiry, resolution… These types of texts are explained on the legislative process page, grouped by who tables them.

rejeteAN.definition: The National Assembly rejected the text in its most recent vote on it. The text may continue to the Senate or to a new reading, or stop there.

rejeteSenat.definition: The Senate rejected the text in its most recent vote on it. The text may continue to the National Assembly or to a new reading, or stop there.

retire.definition: Its author withdrew the bill before it was adopted: it will no longer be examined.

answerCumulMandats.anomalieBadgeExecutif: Executive role, to be resolved according to the ministry's register
answerCumulMandats.anomaliesDesc: One row per person, both rules together. Passed deadlines first, then situations still within time.
answerCumulMandats.anomaliesAlerte: We cross-reference the lists of MPs and senators published by the National Assembly and the Senate, the national register of elected officials (edition published in {date}), the official websites of local authorities and courts, and the local press. Each situation is checked one by one, every month (last check: {verification}), and those settled since the register was published are removed. A situation listed here is not necessarily illegal: the law allows thirty days to choose, and a challenge to the election suspends that deadline.
answerCumulMandats.pageTitle: How many members of parliament also hold a local office?
answerCumulMandats.pageDescription: The share of MPs and senators who also sit on a municipal, departmental or regional council, what the law allows, and those who still run a local authority.
answerCumulMandats.shortAnswer: <hl>{part}%</hl> of members of parliament keep a local office: {total, number} MPs and senators who also sit on a municipal, departmental or regional council. The law allows it, on one condition: a single council seat (a seat in a municipality of fewer than 1,000 inhabitants does not count), and no executive role.
answerCumulMandats.heroDesc: Local offices recorded in {date}, matched against sitting members of parliament.
answerCumulMandats.heroAN: of MPs, or {cumulards, number} out of {effectif, number}
answerCumulMandats.heroSN: of senators, or {cumulards, number} out of {effectif, number}
answerCumulMandats.interditsDesc: {total, plural, one {# member of parliament} other {# members of parliament}} {total, plural, one {is} other {are}} in a situation the register records and case-by-case checking confirms. Of these:
answerCumulMandats.conceptsTitle: Worth knowing before reading the numbers
answerCumulMandats.concept1Body: It all starts with one distinction: a local official either runs the authority or sits on it. Running means being mayor, deputy mayor, chair or vice-chair of a council: you decide, you execute, you employ. Sitting means being a municipal, departmental or regional councillor: you deliberate and vote, without administering. <lo1411>Article LO 141-1</lo1411> bars a member of parliament from any executive role, with no exception and no population threshold. <lo141>Article LO 141</lo141> leaves them a single councillor's seat. The two rules are independent: a mayor breaks the first, an official sitting on two councils breaks the second, and one can fall under both.
answerCumulMandats.concept2Body: One councillor's seat, and only one, among those LO 141 lists: regional or departmental councillor, councillor of Paris, member of the Corsican, Guianese, Martinique or Mayotte assembly, or municipal councillor of a commune of at least 1,000 inhabitants. Below 1,000 inhabitants the municipal seat does not count: a member who sits on their village council may sit elsewhere as well.
answerCumulMandats.concept3Title: What happens if they do not choose
answerCumulMandats.concept3Body: Nothing happens, and that is precisely the mechanism: there is no fine and no penalty. <lo151>Article LO 151</lo151> allows thirty days to resign the mandate of one's choice; after that, the mandate acquired on the earliest date ends by operation of law, with no one having to rule on it. An MP who sits on a departmental council and is then elected to a regional council therefore loses the departmental seat if they do not decide themselves. The start of those thirty days, however, moves: it runs from the proclamation of the results of the election that creates the incompatibility and, if that election is challenged, from the judgment that finally confirms it. For a municipal election, the administrative court has three months to rule, an appeal to the Council of State extends that further, and the dual mandate stays lawful throughout.
answerCumulMandats.concept4Title: The inter-municipal seat does not count
answerCumulMandats.concept4Body: A municipal councillor often sits on the inter-municipal body as well, with no separate election. That seat follows from the municipal mandate and is not a second office under LO 141. It is shown here, but excluded from the count.
answerCumulMandats.concept5Title: Paris, Lyon and Marseille appear twice in the registers
answerCumulMandats.concept5Body: In those three cities an official is listed twice: on the city council and on the district council. It is one mandate seen at two levels, and it is counted once.
answerCumulMandats.concept6Title: Why small communes cannot be stacked
answerCumulMandats.concept6Body: Since the council of a commune under 1,000 inhabitants does not count, one might think a member of parliament could collect several of them. They cannot, for a reason unrelated to parliamentary cumulation: <l238>article L. 238 of the electoral code</l238> provides that no one may sit on more than one municipal council, whatever its size. Elected elsewhere, you automatically lose the first seat. The ceiling therefore stays at two deliberative offices: a village seat, plus a departmental, regional or territorial mandate.
answerCumulMandats.groupesChartTitleAN: Share holding a local office, by group, National Assembly
answerCumulMandats.groupesChartTitleSN: Share holding a local office, by group, Senate
answerCumulMandats.groupesChartDesc: Groups with at least {seuil, number} members. The figure after the name gives dual-mandate holders out of the total.
answerCumulMandats.groupesChartNote: Local roots are unevenly spread: they follow each group's history, the voting system that carried it, and the pool of local officials it recruits from.
answerCumulMandats.typesDesc: Number of local offices held by members of parliament, by type of authority.
answerCumulMandats.typesNote: The total exceeds the number of dual-mandate holders: inter-municipal seats add to the municipal mandates they follow from, without counting as another mandate.
answerCumulMandats.methodologySource: Local offices come from the national register of elected officials, published by the Ministry of the Interior under Open Licence 2.0, in its {date} edition. Six files are cross-referenced: municipal, district, inter-municipal, departmental and regional councillors, and members of special-status assemblies. The ministry announces an update every three months; LoiClair checks every week whether a new edition has been published. Each situation listed is also checked one by one every month.
answerCumulMandats.methodologyRapprochement: The register does not carry parliamentary identifiers: each official is matched on surname, first name and date of birth. All three must match, and the date of birth is essential: without it, namesakes merge. This matching is deliberately strict. A member of parliament whom the register lists under a different first name is not found, and their local office does not appear here. We would rather miss one instance of dual office-holding than wrongly attribute one to a namesake born on the same day.
answerCumulMandats.methodologyComptage: A member is counted as soon as they hold at least one local office, whatever the size of the commune: holding one is a fact, not a judgement. The 1,000-inhabitant threshold in LO 141 serves elsewhere, to say whether that office takes the single slot allowed; population comes from the government geo API, and every commune code in the register resolves. Inter-municipal seats and the district duplicates of Paris, Lyon and Marseille are not counted separately: the former follow from the municipal mandate, the latter are the same mandate seen at two levels. One reservation remains about deputy mayors of the districts of Paris, Lyon and Marseille: LO 141-1 names the district mayor and the deputy mayor, not the two combined. They are counted here as an executive role, on a reading nothing settles.
answerCumulMandats.methodologyLimite: The two datasets are not the same age: parliamentary status is refreshed daily, while the register of local officials follows the pace at which prefectures report changes to it. The lag falls mainly on offices that end and roles that are resigned: someone who has left a vice-chairmanship may still appear in it for several weeks. A local office gained since the last edition therefore does not show here, and one given up only drops out once the monthly check has picked it up.

answerPromulgation.pageTitle: How many laws are actually enacted?
answerPromulgation.conceptsTitle: What to understand before reading the numbers
answerPromulgation.conceptPerimetreTitle: What is the scope of this page?
answerPromulgation.conceptPerimetreDesc: This page only covers texts tabled in Parliament since the start of the 17th legislature (18 July 2024), and the laws that came from them. A law enacted since that date on a text tabled earlier is not counted: the rate compares laws to tabled texts, and a law whose text is not in the denominator would skew it. The Application page and the timeline of the Delays page, by contrast, count all laws enacted since 18 July 2024, whatever the tabling date of their text: their law totals are therefore higher.
answerPromulgation.concept1Title: Some texts are not meant to become law
answerPromulgation.concept1Desc: Not all texts tabled in Parliament are meant to become laws. Motions, resolutions, questions… cannot be enacted. Only <link>legislative texts</link> are counted in this rate.
answerPromulgation.concept2Desc: To become law, a text must first be voted in identical terms by both the National Assembly and the Senate or, if disagreement persists, passed by the National Assembly at a final reading — it is then said to be adopted. The President of the Republic then signs it: this is enactment, the moment the text officially becomes a law and receives its number (e.g., Law no. 2024-364). It is finally published in the Official Journal, making it binding and triggering its entry into force. <link>See the legislative process in detail →</link>
answerPromulgation.concept3Desc: An enacted law is not always immediately applied. About half of enacted texts are said to be 'directly applicable': they enter into force without any additional text. The others require implementing decrees published by the Government — without which some provisions remain without effect.
answerPromulgation.concept4Title: Government bills vs. private members' bills
answerPromulgation.concept4Desc: A government bill (projet de loi) is tabled by the Government; a private member's bill (proposition de loi) is tabled by a Member of Parliament. Both can become law, but their success rates differ significantly. <link>Compare success rates →</link>
answerPromulgation.concept5Desc: At the end of a legislature, texts still before the National Assembly lapse: to revive them, they must be tabled again, and their examination in the Assembly starts from scratch. A text then under examination in the Senate continues its course.
answerPromulgation.shortAnswer: Since the start of the 17th legislature, <hl>{totalDeposited}</hl> texts have been tabled in Parliament. Of the <hl>{total}</hl> legislative texts, <hl>{count}</hl> have been enacted into law so far — an enactment rate of <hl>{rate}%</hl>. The rate depends on where the text comes from: <hl>{rateProjets}%</hl> of ordinary government bills have become law, against <hl>{ratePropositions}%</hl> of ordinary private members' bills.
answerPromulgation.depositChartDescription: All types of texts tabled — last 24 months
answerPromulgation.source: Source: National Assembly open data — 17th legislature
answerPromulgation.typeChartNote: Population: every text tabled since the start of the 17th legislature, all types combined (bills, resolutions, reports, inquiry committees, petitions, etc.). Private members' bills (propositions de loi) dominate by a wide margin, but government bills (projets de loi) have far better chances of becoming law: the Government sets the agenda by priority for two sitting weeks out of four and has the resources to see a text through to enactment.
answerPromulgation.depositChartNote: Population: every text tabled (including resolutions, information reports, and other non-legislative texts). The pace of tabling follows the parliamentary calendar: peaks correspond to the resumption of parliamentary work (September, January), troughs to vacation periods.
answerPromulgation.promulgationChartNote: Population: laws that came from texts tabled since 18 July 2024, counted in the month of their enactment. The pace of enactments does not directly follow that of tabling: laws are often enacted at the end of the session (June) or before the year-end break (December), after several months — sometimes more than a year — of parliamentary back-and-forth.
answerPromulgation.groupeChartNote: Population: legislative laws enacted under the 17th legislature, grouped by the political group that tabled the text. Government bills produce by far the most laws, reflecting the priority it has over the parliamentary agenda (two sitting weeks out of four). Among parliamentary groups, results depend as much on group size as on political position and access to the sitting days set aside for opposition and minority groups.
answerPromulgation.whatIsPromulgationP1: Enactment (promulgation) is when the President of the Republic officially signs a law passed by Parliament. This signature makes the law enforceable: it is then published in the Official Journal and enters into force.
answerPromulgation.whatIsPromulgationP2: The President has 15 days to enact a law, counted from its transmission to the Government after final adoption. A referral to the Constitutional Council, by the President or by other authorities, suspends that period and so delays enactment.

Government bills are all grouped under 'Government', without ministry-level breakdown. Non-attached members, who do not form a political group, have their bar last, outside the ranking.

answerPromulgation.methodologyPerimeter: Scope — Texts tabled in Parliament since 18 July 2024, when the 17th legislature began, and the laws that came from them. A law enacted since that date on a text tabled earlier is not counted. Numerator: laws signed by the President and published in the Official Journal. Denominator: legislative texts — ordinary, organic and constitutional bills; finance and social security financing bills; treaty ratification bills. Resolutions, motions, committees of inquiry, information reports and other non-legislative texts are excluded from the denominator: counting them would skew the rate downward. Data: National Assembly open data, updated every day.
answerPromulgation.methodologyRate: Calculation — (Number of enacted texts ÷ number of legislative texts) × 100. Example: 120 enacted texts out of 400 legislative texts gives a rate of 30%, i.e. roughly 1 in 3 legislative texts that actually becomes a law.
answerPromulgation.methodologyCharts: Time charts — The tabling and enactment curves cover the last 24 rolling months, with one data point per month. Heads up: the tabling curve includes every text type, while the enactments curve only counts laws actually enacted. The two are not directly comparable.
answerPromulgation.methodologyGroups: Political groups — The ranking attributes each law to the group that tabled the text. Government bills are all grouped under 'Government', without ministry-level breakdown.
answerPromulgation.methodologyLimit: Limitations — This rate is provisional: texts still under review may pass later, so it will mechanically rise over the legislature. Conversely, many private members' bills are tabled as political signals with little real hope of passing — they inflate the denominator and pull the rate down. The rate says nothing about the quality or importance of the laws enacted: a high figure just means many texts reach the finish line, not that legislative activity is high-quality.
answerPromulgation.pageDescription: How many texts proposed in Parliament become law? Enactment rate for the 17th legislature — tabled texts that effectively become law. Open data, updated daily.

answerApplication.shortAnswer: Of the <hl>{totalLois}</hl> laws enacted more than 6 months ago, <hl>{appliquees}</hl> are fully implemented, or <hl>{tauxApplication}%</hl>: {applicationDirecte} are directly applicable and {totalementAppliquees} have received all their decrees. {enAttente, plural, one {# other is} other {# others are}} still awaiting some or all of {enAttente, plural, one {its} other {their}} decrees{sansEcheancier, plural, =0 {} one {, and # has no published decree schedule yet} other {, and # have no published decree schedule yet}}. {recentes, plural, =0 {} one {The law enacted less than 6 months ago appears in the charts below.} other {The # laws enacted less than 6 months ago appear in the charts below.}}
answerApplication.conceptsTitle: What to understand before reading the numbers
answerApplication.conceptPerimetreTitle: What is the scope of this page?
answerApplication.conceptPerimetreDesc: This page counts every law enacted since 18 July 2024, when the 17th legislature began, whatever the date its bill was tabled. The implementation rate also sets aside laws enacted less than 6 months ago, which have not yet had time to receive their decrees: this is the National Assembly barometer's convention. These recent laws remain in the charts.
answerApplication.concept1Title: What does it mean to implement a law?
answerApplication.concept1Desc: An enacted law does not always take effect immediately. About one law in two includes provisions that require implementing decrees published by the Government. Until these decrees are issued, some provisions remain without concrete effect for citizens.
answerApplication.concept2Desc: Some laws are 'directly applicable': they apply from their entry into force, without additional text. Others require one or more decrees. The application barometer lists all of them: directly applicable laws count as applied from the start, the others become so as their decrees are published.
answerApplication.concept3Desc: The implementation time measures the period between a law's enactment and the publication of its implementing decrees. This can range from a few days to several years. A long delay means citizens wait before benefiting concretely from the law.
answerApplication.concept4Desc: Enactment makes a law official, but implementation makes it effective. A law may have been enacted for months without any implementing decree being issued. To understand a text's full journey, see the <link>enactment rate page</link>.
answerApplication.concept5Desc: Each law may include several 'measures' (articles or provisions) requiring a decree. An individual law's implementation rate compares the number of measures actually taken to the total expected. The overall rate aggregates these figures across all laws.
answerApplication.donutTitle: Distribution of laws by implementation status
answerApplication.donutDesc: Of the laws enacted under the 17th legislature, how many are fully implemented?
answerApplication.donutNote: Population: laws enacted since 18 July 2024, whatever the tabling date of their text, and tracked by the application barometer. 'Fully implemented' groups directly applicable laws (applicable without a decree from their entry into force, usually the day after publication in the Official Journal) together with laws whose implementing decrees have all been published. 'Partially awaiting decrees': at least one decree published, others still pending. 'No decree issued': either no decree taken yet, or an implementation schedule not yet recorded by the barometer.
answerApplication.tauxCardDesc: Share of laws enacted more than 6 months ago that are fully implemented, either directly applicable or having received all their decrees.
answerApplication.tauxCardFormula: Calculation: ({directe} directly applicable laws + {appliquees} fully implemented laws) ÷ {total} laws enacted more than 6 months ago.
answerApplication.gaugeDesc: Each law contains measures (articles or provisions) that require a decree to take effect. A single decree can cover several measures at once.
answerApplication.monthlyAppliedNote: Population: laws enacted since 18 July 2024, whatever the tabling date of their text, that received an official 'direct application' or 'full application' act, an act LoiClair creates from the barometer. The date used is not the enactment date: for a directly applicable law it is the date of its publication in the Official Journal; for a law applied through decrees it is the date of the last decree published. A spike therefore reflects a wave of directly applicable laws or of recently published decrees.
answerApplication.decretsCardDesc: Number of enacted laws that are not directly applicable: they call for one or more Government decrees, already published or still awaited.
answerApplication.decretsCardNote: Total laws − directly applicable laws. Some may already have received part of their decrees.
answerApplication.topNonAppliedTitle: Top 15 laws with the most pending measures
answerApplication.topNonAppliedDesc: Laws with the largest absolute gap between expected and applied measures
answerApplication.topNonAppliedNote: Population: laws enacted since 18 July 2024, whatever the tabling date of their text, that had at least one expected measure and at least one measure still unpublished. Directly applicable and fully implemented laws are excluded. Sorting is by absolute volume: a law at 80/100 (20 missing measures) will appear before a law at 0/5, because it represents a larger regulatory backlog.
answerApplication.trimestreDesc: Older laws mechanically have a better rate, as the government has had more time to publish the decrees.
answerApplication.trimestreNote: Population: laws enacted since 18 July 2024, whatever the tabling date of their text, grouped by quarter of enactment. Directly applicable laws count as one applied measure, laws without a published schedule count as one unfulfilled expected measure — so every law contributes to the calculation. If older laws are well implemented but recent ones aren't, that's normal break-in time. If older laws remain poorly implemented, it's a sign of a real regulatory backlog.
answerApplication.methodologyPerimeter: Scope — Every law enacted since 18 July 2024, when the 17th legislature began, whatever the date its bill was tabled. Until 15 September 2026, only laws whose bill had been tabled since that date were counted, which left out 41 of the 144 laws at the time, often the slowest to pass. The implementation rate only keeps laws enacted more than 6 months ago; the breakdown by status, the measures, the ranking and the charts by period keep every law.
answerApplication.methodologyRate: Calculation — (Directly applicable laws + laws fully implemented by decrees) ÷ laws enacted more than 6 months ago × 100. A law counts as applied in two cases: direct application (no decree needed, the law applies from its entry into force, usually the day after publication in the Official Journal) or fully applied (all expected decrees published in the Official Journal). Every other law stays in the denominator as not applied: partially applied laws, laws with no decree issued, and laws for which the barometer has published no schedule ("not applicable" status), which the barometer also counts at 0%. Laws less than 6 months old have been set aside since 15 September 2026; before that, every law was counted. Sources: National Assembly Law Application Barometer, cross-referenced with Légifrance.
answerApplication.methodologyComparison: Comparison with the official barometer — The National Assembly's barometer publishes a higher rate. Like it, we set aside laws enacted less than 6 months ago and count laws whose implementation is unknown at 0%. But it averages each law's individual rate: a law with half its measures issued counts for 50%. Here, a law only counts as implemented if it is fully implemented, hence a lower rate.
answerApplication.methodologyMeasures: Measures — The measure ratio adds up every measure taken and divides by every measure expected, across all laws. A law with fifty measures therefore weighs fifty times more than a law with a single measure.
answerApplication.methodologyLimit: Limitations — The rate moves every month as laws pass the 6-month mark. More recent laws, which haven't had time to receive their decrees, remain visible in the breakdown by status and in the charts. The chart by enactment quarter uses virtual values so every law contributes: a directly applicable law counts 1/1, a law without a published schedule counts 0/1 — it is therefore not a strict ratio of measures. A law technically applied (decrees published) may still be poorly implemented in practice: this indicator measures official publication, not real-world effect.
answerApplication.pageTitle: How many laws are actually applied?
answerApplication.pageDescription: Law implementation rate for the 17th legislature: how many enacted laws are effectively put into force. Open data, updated daily.

answerDelais.shortAnswer: A law enacted since July 2024 took on average <hl>{depotPromulgation} days</hl> from the tabling of its bill to its enactment, across {nbDepotPromulgation, plural, one {# law} other {# laws}}: <hl>{adoption} days</hl> to be adopted by Parliament, then <hl>{promulgation} days</hl> until enactment by the President. Some laws apply directly at that point. Others require decrees: it took <hl>{application} days</hl> more on average to publish all of them, an average based on only {nbApplication, plural, one {# law} other {# laws}}, the only ones whose decrees have all been issued so far.
answerDelais.timelineDesc: Average delay at each stage of a law's journey
answerDelais.timelineStep2: Enactment, then publication: applicable from entry into force for directly applicable laws
answerDelais.timelineStep3: Decrees publication — the law becomes fully applicable
answerDelais.timelineSample3: average over {count} fully applied laws that required decrees
answerDelais.timelineNote: The first two stages cover laws enacted since 18 July 2024, whatever the date their bill was tabled. The third stage only covers laws that subsequently required decrees and are now fully applied: a much smaller population.
answerDelais.totalDecretsDesc: Average number of days between tabling and publication of the last implementing decree
answerDelais.totalDecretsSample: average over {count} laws fully applied by decrees
answerDelais.totalDirecteDesc: Average number of days between tabling and publication in the Official Journal, for laws that apply without any decree
answerDelais.conceptsTitle: What to understand before reading the numbers
answerDelais.conceptPerimetreTitle: What is the scope of the numbers?
answerDelais.conceptPerimetreDesc: The delays along a law's journey cover every law enacted since the start of the 17th legislature (18 July 2024), including laws whose bill was tabled under a previous legislature: leaving those out shortened the delays, since they are often the slowest to pass. Only the per-chamber delays cover bills tabled since 18 July 2024, enacted or not. The wait for decrees only rests on fully applied laws that needed decrees, still few in number: this figure will stabilise over time.
answerDelais.conceptDureeTitle: Why does it take so long?
answerDelais.conceptDureeDesc: A law doesn't become effective overnight. Between tabling and concrete application, there's the parliamentary shuttle (Assembly and Senate), sometimes a joint committee (CMP), a possible referral to the Constitutional Council, then the drafting and publication of implementing decrees by the government. Each step takes time.
answerDelais.conceptDepotAdoptionTitle: What is the tabling → adoption delay?
answerDelais.conceptDepotAdoptionDesc: It's the time between when a text is tabled at an assembly and when it is definitively adopted by Parliament (in identical terms by both chambers, or in a final reading at the Assembly). This delay depends on the number of readings, whether the fast-track procedure is used, and the political agenda.
answerDelais.concept15JoursTitle: What does the 15-day rule for enacting a law say?
answerDelais.concept15JoursDesc: Article 10 of the Constitution gives the President of the Republic at most 15 days to enact a law. But this deadline only starts running when the law is sent to the Government, not when Parliament adopts it. It is also suspended when the Constitutional Council is seized (by the President of the Republic, the Prime Minister, the Speaker of the National Assembly, the President of the Senate, 60 MPs or 60 senators), until the Council rules. The gap measured here starts at the final vote, so the average, {jours} days on this page, can exceed 15 days.
answerDelais.conceptDecretsDesc: Many laws refer to decrees to specify their concrete implementation (procedures, ceilings, schedules…). Until these decrees are published, some provisions remain inapplicable. See the <link>law implementation rate page</link> for details.
answerDelais.conceptMedianeDesc: Apart from the per-chamber chart, which also shows medians, the delays shown on this page are averages. Keep in mind that an average can be pulled upward by a few extreme cases: a single law stuck for two years can noticeably raise the overall mean. Medians (middle values) would generally be lower.
answerDelais.conceptAccelereeDesc: Under the ordinary procedure, a text goes through at least one full shuttle between the Assembly and the Senate. Under the fast-track procedure (initiated by the Government), there is only one reading per chamber before a CMP is directly convened in case of disagreement, which significantly reduces the overall delay.
answerDelais.chambreChartTitle: Distribution of examination delays by chamber
answerDelais.chambreChartDesc: Spread of delays between tabling and adopted decision in each chamber, in days
answerDelais.chambreChartNote: Population: every dossier tabled since the start of the 17th legislature that received at least one adopted decision in the relevant chamber — including texts not yet enacted (the two scopes are distinct and do not overlap exactly). The box represents the central 50% of dossiers (from Q1 to Q3), the vertical line is the median, the dot is the mean. These distributions do not reconstitute the timeline above, which relies on more restricted populations (enacted laws, then fully applicable laws).
answerDelais.typeChartTitle: Time to application by type of text
answerDelais.typeChartDesc: Average delay tabling → effective application, in days, by type of text
answerDelais.typeChartNote: Population: laws enacted since 18 July 2024, whatever the tabling date of their text, that are already fully applicable (directly applicable laws and laws whose implementing decrees have all been published). The number in parentheses shows how many laws are counted in each category. The delay covers the full parliamentary process, promulgation, and then the publication of decrees when required. The annual budget laws (State budget, social security budget) only appear here once fully applied; amending finance laws have short delays because they follow a tight calendar; other laws vary much more depending on their complexity and political weight.
answerDelais.trancheChartTitle: Distribution of applied laws by time since tabling
answerDelais.trancheChartDesc: How many laws became fully applicable within 6 months of their bill being tabled, between 6 months and 1 year, etc.
answerDelais.trancheChartNote: Population: laws enacted since 18 July 2024, whatever the tabling date of their text, that are already fully applicable (directly applicable or with all their decrees published). Some laws become applicable in a few months, while others wait years for their implementing decrees.
answerDelais.topLentesDesc: Laws that took the most days between enactment and publication of their last implementing decree
answerDelais.topLentesNote: Population: laws enacted since 18 July 2024, whatever the tabling date of their text, that required implementing decrees and whose decrees have all now been published. The displayed delay is the number of days between the law's enactment and the publication of its last implementing decree — it only measures the implementation lag, not the parliamentary process upstream.
answerDelais.methodologyPerimeter: Scope — Laws enacted since 18 July 2024, when the 17th legislature began, whatever the date their bill was tabled. Until 15 September 2026, only laws whose bill had been tabled since that date were counted, which left out 41 of the 144 laws at the time, often the slowest to pass. Four delays are computed on distinct populations: (1) tabling → enactment delay on all these laws, (2) enactment → application delay on those that required decrees and whose decrees are now all published, (3) National Assembly delay = date of the last adoption decision at the NA − first tabling date at the NA, on bills tabled since 18 July 2024, enacted or not, (4) Senate delay = same logic for the upper chamber. When a text goes back and forth between chambers, the last adoption in the chamber is used: the delay covers every reading, including the joint committee and the final reading.
answerDelais.methodologyMediane: Calculation — Apart from the per-chamber chart, delays are arithmetic means (sum of delays ÷ number of texts). Example: a law tabled on 1 January and enacted on 1 July has a 181-day delay. The application delay uses the date of the latest decree published (not the first), since that's what marks full application. A handful of extreme cases — a bill stuck in shuttle for three years — is enough to pull means upward; medians, which are more representative, only appear in the per-chamber chart.
answerDelais.methodologyExclusions: Exclusions — Non-enacted texts: excluded from the tabling → enactment delay. Directly applicable laws: excluded from the application delay (zero delay by definition, which would pull the average down). Partially applied laws: excluded from application metrics. Dossiers with no adoption decision in a chamber: excluded from that chamber's delay.
answerDelais.methodologyLimit: Limitations — The enactment → application delay for a given law is the delay of its latest decree, not an average of decrees. The legislative timeline adds three averages computed on different populations: it's a teaching estimate, not the journey of a single text. A very short delay at the NA or Senate may reflect the fast-track procedure rather than more efficient scrutiny — this indicator does not measure the depth of debate or the number of amendments examined.
answerDelais.pageTitle: How long does it take for a law to be applied?
answerDelais.pageDescription: Legislative delays of the 17th legislature: how many days elapse between a text being tabled in Parliament, its adoption, its enactment and the effective application of its implementing decrees.

answerAgeRepresentants.shortAnswer: The average age is <hl>{an} years</hl> in the National Assembly and <hl>{sn} years</hl> in the Senate. For comparison, the average age of the whole French population, children included, is <hl>{insee} years</hl> as of 1 January 2026 (INSEE). Both chambers are older than the population they represent — the Senate notably more than the Assembly. Part of the gap is mechanical: you must be at least 18 to be elected to the Assembly, and 24 to be elected to the Senate.
answerAgeRepresentants.heroDesc: The two chambers that represent the French, plus two benchmarks for comparison
answerAgeRepresentants.conceptsTitle: What to understand before reading the numbers
answerAgeRepresentants.conceptPerimetreDesc: This chapter covers those who are elected to represent the French people: the {an} sitting MPs and the {sn} senators. This is the population on which democratic representativeness can be judged — they were chosen to speak on behalf of a constituency or a territory.
answerAgeRepresentants.conceptGouvDesc: Ministers are not elected: they are appointed by the President of the Republic. So we do not treat them as “representatives” in the strict sense. We still show them as context — small figures next to the two chambers, and in some charts — because they take part in political decisions and their age is a useful benchmark. But they are not part of the central population of this chapter.
answerAgeRepresentants.conceptMoyenneTitle: Mean vs. median: what's the difference?
answerAgeRepresentants.conceptMoyenneDesc: The mean adds every age together and divides by the count. The median indicates the middle age in the sorted list: half the elected officials are younger, the other half older. Both are useful. We mainly show the mean in the headline numbers, and the median in the box plot to highlight when they tell slightly different stories.
answerAgeRepresentants.conceptTranchesTitle: How are the age brackets defined?
answerAgeRepresentants.conceptTranchesDesc: The brackets follow decades, with a single bracket for those under 40 and a final one for those 70 and over. This makes the generational spread readable at a glance without multiplying categories.
answerAgeRepresentants.conceptBoxplotTitle: How do I read the box plot?
answerAgeRepresentants.conceptBoxplotDesc: The box represents the central 50% of individuals: its left edge is the age below which a quarter of them fall (Q1), its right edge the age above which another quarter fall (Q3). The vertical line inside is the median, and the dot is the mean. The wider the box, the greater the age spread.
answerAgeRepresentants.conceptDateTitle: On what date is age calculated?
answerAgeRepresentants.conceptDateDesc: Age is calculated from the date of birth and the current date. It is refreshed at each daily data update, so at the latest the day after a birthday.
answerAgeRepresentants.boxChartDesc: Spread of ages in the Assembly and Senate, in years. Government shown as context.
answerAgeRepresentants.boxChartNote: Population: sitting MPs, senators and ministers whose date of birth is available in the open data. The box represents the central 50% (from Q1 to Q3), the vertical line is the median, the dot is the mean. Government figures rely on a very small headcount (a few dozen people): they are shown as a benchmark, not as the main population of this chapter.
answerAgeRepresentants.trancheChartDesc: Number of MPs and senators in each decade
answerAgeRepresentants.trancheChartNote: Population: sitting MPs and senators whose date of birth is available. Ministers are excluded from this distribution — we focus on the age spread of elected representatives. Brackets follow decades, with the extremes (under 40, 70 and over) grouped.
answerAgeRepresentants.groupeANChartTitle: Average age by group in the Assembly
answerAgeRepresentants.groupeANChartDesc: Average age of MPs in each political group, from youngest to oldest
answerAgeRepresentants.groupeANChartNote: Population: sitting MPs whose age is available. The number in parentheses indicates the number of MPs in each group — a group of 10 produces a more volatile average than a group of 100. Groups are shown from the youngest at the top to the oldest at the bottom.
answerAgeRepresentants.groupeSNChartTitle: Average age by group in the Senate
answerAgeRepresentants.groupeSNChartDesc: Average age of senators in each political group, from youngest to oldest
answerAgeRepresentants.groupeSNChartNote: Population: sitting senators whose age is available. The number in parentheses indicates the number of senators in each group. Groups are shown from the youngest at the top to the oldest at the bottom. Because the Senate is renewed by half every three years and elected by indirect suffrage, its generational profile differs structurally from the Assembly's.
answerAgeRepresentants.genreChartTitle: Average age of women and men
answerAgeRepresentants.genreChartDesc: Comparison by institution of the average age of sitting women and men
answerAgeRepresentants.genreChartNote: Population: sitting parliamentarians and ministers whose age and gender are available.
answerAgeRepresentants.topDesc: The 5 youngest and 5 oldest, across all three institutions
answerAgeRepresentants.topNote: Population: sitting MPs, senators and ministers whose date of birth is available in the open data. This ranking includes the Government out of curiosity: it lists the most extreme individuals across the three institutions, without implying that a minister “represents” anyone.
answerAgeRepresentants.methodologyPerimeter: Scope — This chapter covers sitting MPs and senators, because they are the ones who “represent” the French in the constitutional sense. The Government is added as context (small figure at the top of the page, present in the distribution chart and top 5) but excluded from the main age-bracket distribution.
answerAgeRepresentants.methodologyCalcul: Calculation — Age is computed in whole years between date of birth and today. It is refreshed at each daily data update, so at the latest the day after a birthday.
answerAgeRepresentants.methodologyExclusions: Exclusions — We drop individuals whose date of birth is missing from the open data ({count} currently). No other exclusion: even a minister just appointed is counted.
answerAgeRepresentants.methodologyComparaison: Comparison with the French population — INSEE publishes an average age of 43.1 years as of 1 January 2026 for the whole population, children included (provisional data, Demographic Balance). That is the benchmark used, because elected officials represent the entire population, minors included. Part of the gap is therefore mechanical: you can only be elected to the Assembly from age 18, and to the Senate from age 24. This gap is an indicator of demographic representativeness: it says nothing about the quality of parliamentary work, but it shows that elected officials do not share the age pyramid of those they represent.
answerAgeRepresentants.methodologyLimit: Limitations — These figures are a snapshot, which will shift with renewals. Age is only one dimension of representativeness: this chapter says nothing about gender, occupation, geographic origin or education level. The following chapters cover occupation, gender and the weight of territories.
