answerMetiersRepresentants.pageTitle: What jobs did our elected officials do before being elected?
answerMetiersRepresentants.shortAnswer: Out of the <hl>{total} elected officials</hl> whose occupation is known, about <hl>{pctCadres}%</hl> held a job classed as “managers and higher intellectual professions” before being elected, compared with only <hl>{pctCadresFrance}%</hl> among French people aged 15 and over. Workers and clerical employees, who make up nearly <hl>{pctOuvriersEmpFrance}%</hl> of the population, hold only <hl>{pctOuvriersEmp}%</hl> of the seats. The gap remains when comparing only the economically active, leaving out retirees and people with no professional activity: <hl>{pctCadresActifs}%</hl> managers and higher intellectual professions against <hl>{pctCadresActifsFrance}%</hl>, <hl>{pctOuvriersEmpActifs}%</hl> workers and clerical employees against <hl>{pctOuvriersEmpActifsFrance}%</hl>.
answerMetiersRepresentants.heroChartTitle: Parliament versus French people aged 15 and over
answerMetiersRepresentants.heroChartDesc: Share of each major socio-professional category in Parliament, compared with its share of the French population aged 15 and over
answerMetiersRepresentants.heroChartNote: Population: {avecFam} sitting MPs and senators whose socio-professional family is available in the open data ({sansFam} elected officials without usable data are excluded from the percentages). French reference: INSEE, 2023 Population Census, structure of people aged 15 and over by socio-professional group (current or former occupation, PCS classification, eight-family level). This base includes retirees and people without a professional activity, so all eight major families can be compared side by side.
answerMetiersRepresentants.conceptsTitle: What to know before reading the numbers
answerMetiersRepresentants.concept1Desc: This page covers every MP and senator sitting today. Ministers, former members and standby substitutes are not included. The source is the occupation each elected official declared on taking office, as recorded in the parliamentary open data.
answerMetiersRepresentants.concept2Desc: On taking office, every parliamentarian declares the job they held just before being elected, or that they continue to hold alongside their mandate. It is a self-declaration, not an administrative check. Some officials keep declaring their former job long after moving to politics full-time.
answerMetiersRepresentants.concept3Desc: INSEE classifies every French occupation through a nomenclature called PCS (socio-professional categories). Its broadest level groups the whole population into eight families: senior executives and professionals, intermediate occupations, clerical employees, workers, self-employed and shopkeepers, farmers, retirees, and people with no professional activity. The same nomenclature underlies every official statistic on the French population, which makes comparison possible.
answerMetiersRepresentants.concept4Desc: In the INSEE nomenclature, the senior-executive family covers doctors, lawyers, teachers, engineers, senior civil servants and more broadly any job requiring a long degree. It is not a statement about income; it is a statistical category. It bundles together very different situations.
answerMetiersRepresentants.concept5Title: Why compare with people aged 15 and over?
answerMetiersRepresentants.concept5Desc: We compare with the share of each family among French people aged 15 and over, which is the official statistical base for the PCS nomenclature. It includes retirees and people with no professional activity, who alone make up more than four French adults in ten. Comparing against that population lets us place the eight families side by side in Parliament and in France, without having to exclude any of the elected officials from the comparison.
answerMetiersRepresentants.concept6Title: What are the limitations of this data?
answerMetiersRepresentants.concept6Desc: The data is self-declared and frozen at the moment of entry into office. An official in post for fifteen years still declares their former job, even if they no longer hold it. Some parliamentarians have never had any activity other than politics and declare labels such as “parliamentary assistant” that inflate the senior-executive category. The officials with no socio-professional family in the open data, or with no usable job title, are excluded from the percentages.
answerMetiersRepresentants.donutChartTitle: Breakdown by major family in Parliament
answerMetiersRepresentants.donutChartDesc: The major socio-professional families declared by sitting MPs and senators
answerMetiersRepresentants.donutChartNote: Population: {avecFam} sitting MPs and senators whose socio-professional family is available in the open data. {sansFam} officials without usable data are excluded. This view shows the raw distribution inside Parliament, without comparison with the French population.
answerMetiersRepresentants.topLibChartDesc: Number of elected officials who declared each of these jobs, across both chambers
answerMetiersRepresentants.topLibChartNote: Population: sitting MPs and senators whose specific job title is available. Masculine and feminine forms are grouped together (for instance, lawyers of either gender are counted together). The number in parentheses shows how many officials declared that job.
answerMetiersRepresentants.chambreChartTitle: Assembly and Senate: two different profiles
answerMetiersRepresentants.chambreChartDesc: Share of each major socio-professional family in the National Assembly and in the Senate
answerMetiersRepresentants.chambreChartNote: Population: {an} sitting MPs and {sn} sitting senators whose socio-professional family is available. The comparison covers all eight major families, including retirees and people with no professional activity. Because the Senate is elected through indirect suffrage by local officials, its social recruitment does not mirror the Assembly's.
answerMetiersRepresentants.groupesChartDesc: Breakdown of the eight main socio-professional families in each parliamentary group (groups of at least five members with a declared profession)
answerMetiersRepresentants.groupesChartNote: Population: sitting MPs and senators whose socio-professional family is available, grouped by political group (Assembly and Senate combined). The number in parentheses shows the group size taken into account. Each bar is normalised to 100% and groups are sorted by descending share of senior executives. The first row (“France”) reflects the INSEE distribution for people aged 15+, as a benchmark.
answerMetiersRepresentants.methodologyPerimeter: Scope — We count every MP and senator sitting today, based on the parliamentary open data. Ministers, former officials and standby substitutes are excluded.
answerMetiersRepresentants.methodologyData: Data used — Every parliamentarian declares an occupation on taking office. The National Assembly or the Senate sorts that declaration, using INSEE's nomenclature, into one of eight major socio-professional families: senior executives, intermediate occupations, clerical employees, workers, self-employed and shopkeepers, farmers, retirees, and people with no professional activity. We display that distribution as declared. For officials the open data files under “no declared occupation” while giving a job title, the family is inferred from that title.
answerMetiersRepresentants.methodologyComparison: Comparison with France — We compare with the distribution of French people aged 15 and over across the major socio-professional families, published by INSEE based on the 2023 Population Census. This base covers every adult, including retirees and people with no professional activity, which lets us align the eight families exactly as they are coded for parliamentarians.
answerMetiersRepresentants.methodologyExclusions: Exclusions — Parliamentarians for whom the open data gives no socio-professional family are not counted in the percentages, nor are those whose family is “no declared occupation” and who have no usable job title ({count} officials in total). When the open data says “no declared occupation” but gives a job title, the official is filed according to that title: “former…” or “retired…” among retirees, “no activity” or “student” among other people with no professional activity, a few recognised jobs (manager, engineer, farmer…) in their own family. Each chart displays the number of elected officials actually kept in the count.
answerMetiersRepresentants.methodologyLimit: Limitations — The data is self-declared. An official sitting for twenty years still declares their former job. Some parliamentarians have never had any activity other than politics: they inflate the senior-executive category through labels such as “parliamentary assistant”.

The two chambers remain <hl>{ecartAN} and {ecartSN} points</hl> below women's share of the population.
answerGenreRepresentants.heroTitle: Share of women among our representatives
answerGenreRepresentants.heroDesc: The two chambers that represent the French, plus two benchmarks for comparison
answerGenreRepresentants.conceptsTitle: What to understand before reading the numbers
answerGenreRepresentants.concept1Desc: This chapter covers the {an} sitting MPs and the {sn} senators — {total} parliamentarians in total. Ministers are shown as a secondary benchmark because they are not elected but appointed by the President of the Republic: they fall outside the strict definition of “representatives”.
answerGenreRepresentants.concept2Desc: Parliamentary open data records a title, “M.” (Mr) or “Mme” (Mrs), for every elected official. That is the data used here. The approach is binary and acknowledged as such: the official data does not include any non-binary self-declaration — a topic that goes beyond this chapter.
answerGenreRepresentants.concept3Title: Why not exactly 50% despite the parity laws?
answerGenreRepresentants.concept3Desc: France's first parity law dates back to 2000. In list elections, such as the Senate elections in departments electing three or more senators, it requires candidates to alternate between women and men. In legislative elections, which are single-member, it only provides for a financial penalty on parties that do not field as many female as male candidates. It therefore does not guarantee a parity-elected chamber: a party can accept the penalty, or place women in unwinnable constituencies. Legal parity therefore does not automatically translate into 50% of elected officials.
answerGenreRepresentants.concept4Title: Why is the gap between Assembly and Senate so narrow?
answerGenreRepresentants.concept4Desc: The Assembly is elected by single-member majority vote, where each party picks one candidate per constituency: parity then depends on each party's voluntary choice. The Senate is partly elected through proportional list representation, where alternating women and men is mandatory — mechanically pushing the share of women up at every triennial renewal. Today, women make up {an}% of MPs and {sn}% of senators.
answerGenreRepresentants.concept5Title: Why is the Government above both chambers?
answerGenreRepresentants.concept5Desc: Ministers are appointed, not elected. The President and the Prime Minister pick their team directly, and no law requires a gender-balanced Government: where parity exists, it is hand-crafted parity, much easier to achieve than parity through the ballot box.

answerGenreRepresentants.donutChartNote: Population: {total} sitting parliamentarians (MPs + senators), of whom {f} women and {h} men. The Government is excluded from this total. Binary Mr/Mrs title as recorded in parliamentary open data.
answerGenreRepresentants.groupeANChartTitle: Share of women by group in the Assembly
answerGenreRepresentants.groupeANChartDesc: Percentage of women MPs in each political group, from the most to the least feminised
answerGenreRepresentants.groupeANChartNote: Population: sitting MPs. The number in parentheses indicates the total size of the group. Groups with fewer than three members are not shown. Visual reference at 50% in the middle of the scale (axis 0–100%).
answerGenreRepresentants.groupeSNChartTitle: Share of women by group in the Senate
answerGenreRepresentants.groupeSNChartDesc: Percentage of women senators in each political group, from the most to the least feminised
answerGenreRepresentants.groupeSNChartNote: Population: sitting senators. The number in parentheses indicates the total size of the group. Groups with fewer than three members are not shown. Because the Senate is renewed by half every three years and partly elected by proportional list, its feminisation progresses more steadily at each renewal.
answerGenreRepresentants.methodologyPerimeter: Scope — {an} sitting MPs and {sn} senators, i.e. {total} parliamentarians. The Government ({gouv} members) is shown as a secondary benchmark, excluded from the two big figures at the top of the page and from the ring chart.
answerGenreRepresentants.methodologyCalcul: Calculation — Share of women in each chamber: count of “Mme” (Mrs) titles divided by the total. Same formula by political group for the detailed charts. 100% coverage: no elected official is missing the title field.
answerGenreRepresentants.methodologyExclusions: Exclusions — Standby substitutes, former parliamentarians, MEPs and local elected officials are excluded. The Government is excluded from the main figures but shown as a benchmark.
answerGenreRepresentants.methodologyComparaison: Comparison with France — INSEE, population estimates as of 1 January 2026 (provisional data): 51.4% women, i.e. 35,531 thousand out of 69,082 thousand. This is the official demographic reference for comparing the share of women in Parliament with the French population.
answerGenreRepresentants.methodologyLimit: Limitations — The Mr/Mrs title is binary: official data does not allow for non-binary self-declaration. The figures are a snapshot for today and will shift at the next renewals. This chapter says nothing about parity in parliamentary executive positions (committee chairs, bureau seats).

answerGeographieRepresentants.shortAnswer: A parliamentarian does not weigh the same number of inhabitants depending on the department. Among the departments of mainland France and overseas, the most over-represented is <hl>{deptMin}</hl> with <hl>{minRatio}</hl> inhabitants per elected official. The most under-represented is <hl>{deptMax}</hl> with <hl>{maxRatio}</hl> inhabitants per elected official. The gap reaches <hl>1 to {ratioExtremes}</hl> between these two extremes.
answerGeographieRepresentants.heroChartDesc: Each department is coloured by the average number of inhabitants an MP or senator represents.
answerGeographieRepresentants.heroChartNote: Population: INSEE, official populations, {millesime} vintage, effective 1 January {vigueur}. Parliamentary data: {total} elected officials attached to a territory. The “French citizens abroad” circle represents {etranger} elected officials with no territory in France; coloured using an estimated population of 1.7 million consular registrants (MAE).
answerGeographieRepresentants.concept1Desc: This chapter covers the {an} MPs of the National Assembly and the {sn} sitting senators, i.e. {total} parliamentarians. Each MP is attached to a constituency, and each senator to a department. Ministers are excluded: they are not tied to a territory.
answerGeographieRepresentants.concept2Desc: The figures are set by law. The National Assembly has {an} MPs, elected by direct universal suffrage in single-member constituencies for five years. The Senate has {sn} senators, elected by indirect suffrage via a college of grand electors mostly made up of municipal councillors, for six years and renewed by half every three years.
answerGeographieRepresentants.concept3Desc: Boundaries are revised periodically to track demographic change. The law of 13 January 2009 (art. 2), within the framework set by Constitutional Council decision 2008-573 DC, requires that a constituency deviate by no more than ± 20% from the average population of the constituencies in its department. This rule applies inside a department: it limits the gaps between neighbouring constituencies, not between departments. A small department keeps at least one MP even if its population is far below the national average.
answerGeographieRepresentants.concept4Title: Why does the Senate over-represent rural areas?
answerGeographieRepresentants.concept4Desc: The number of senators for each department is set by law, and even the least populated one has at least one: rural departments therefore obtain proportionally more seats than their strict demographic weight would suggest. The college of grand electors, more than 95% composed of delegates from municipal councils, weighs on who gets elected, not on the number of seats: small towns count for more in it than their actual population.
answerGeographieRepresentants.concept5Title: Why is the Government not included?
answerGeographieRepresentants.concept5Desc: Ministers are appointed by the President of the Republic, not elected on a territory. They represent no constituency in their own name: “inhabitants per minister” would therefore make no sense. The Government is excluded from both the calculation and the map.
answerGeographieRepresentants.concept6Title: How is “inhabitants per elected official” calculated?
answerGeographieRepresentants.concept6Desc: For each department, we add together the sitting MPs and senators attached to that department, then divide the legal population by that total. Simple example: a department of 600,000 inhabitants with 6 MPs and 2 senators gives 600,000 ÷ 8 = 75,000 inhabitants per elected official. Population data come from INSEE, {millesime} vintage, effective 1 January {vigueur}.
answerGeographieRepresentants.topOverDesc: The ten territories where a parliamentarian represents the fewest inhabitants.
answerGeographieRepresentants.topOverNote: Population: inhabitants per elected official — the shorter the bar, the more over-represented the territory. The ranking covers all territories, overseas collectivities, New Caledonia and French citizens abroad included. Calculation: INSEE legal population divided by the number of MPs and senators attached to the territory.
answerGeographieRepresentants.topUnderDesc: The ten territories where a parliamentarian represents the most inhabitants.
answerGeographieRepresentants.topUnderNote: Population: inhabitants per elected official — the longer the bar, the more under-represented the territory. The ranking covers all territories, overseas collectivities, New Caledonia and French citizens abroad included.

answerGeographieRepresentants.idfCardVerdictOver: → Île-de-France is slightly over-represented: its share of elected officials exceeds its demographic weight by {diff} point(s).

answerGeographieRepresentants.zonesChartDesc: How the {total} sitting MPs and senators split between mainland France, Île-de-France, overseas, and French citizens abroad.
answerGeographieRepresentants.zonesChartNote: Population: {total} sitting parliamentarians (MPs + senators). The “French citizens abroad and others” zone covers the eleven constituencies of the French established outside France and the senators representing French citizens abroad. The “Overseas” zone covers the overseas departments, the overseas collectivities (Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon, Saint-Barthélemy, Saint-Martin, Wallis and Futuna, French Polynesia) and New Caledonia, all drawn on the map.
answerGeographieRepresentants.methodologyPerimeter: Scope — {anTotal} sitting MPs and {snTotal} senators. Of these, {territoires} are attached to a department, an overseas collectivity or New Caledonia, and {etranger} represent French citizens living abroad. The Government is excluded.
answerGeographieRepresentants.methodologyCalcul: Calculation — For each department, we divide the legal population by the number of MPs and senators attached. Population data come from INSEE, {millesime} vintage, effective 1 January {vigueur}. Results are rounded to the nearest integer.
answerGeographieRepresentants.methodologyExclusions: Exclusions — MPs for French citizens abroad and senators representing French citizens abroad have no territory in France: they are counted in the zone aggregates and shown on the map as a symbolic circle ({etranger} elected officials). The overseas collectivities (Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon, Saint-Barthélemy, Saint-Martin, Wallis and Futuna, French Polynesia) and New Caledonia are counted in the “Overseas” zone and drawn on the map, but left out of the colour scale, which their atypical ratios would distort.
answerGeographieRepresentants.methodologyComparison: Comparison — The ± 20% rule around the average population of a department's constituencies bounds the drawing of National Assembly constituencies (law of 13 January 2009, art. 2, and decision 2008-573 DC). It does not apply between departments. The Senate escapes this rule because its members represent local authorities, not inhabitants directly.
answerGeographieRepresentants.methodologyLimit: Limitations — This chapter measures an arithmetic ratio, not a democratic deficit. A small department keeps at least one MP to remain represented, which mechanically lowers its ratio. The map shows gaps; it does not judge whether they are legitimate — that judgement belongs to the citizen.

answerParticipation.shortAnswer: An MP takes part on average in <hl>{an}%</hl> of the National Assembly's final votes. In the Senate, this average rate is <hl>{sn}%</hl>. For solemn ballots at the Assembly, the public votes announced in advance, it rises to <hl>{solennel}%</hl>.
answerParticipation.caveatBody: In the Senate, at an ordinary public ballot, a single member of a group can drop the ballot papers of all their colleagues into the urn, even when nobody else from the group is in the chamber. So the {sn}% says a ballot was cast in the senator's name, not that they were there.{contraste, select, oui { When a senator has no group on the day of the ballot, and so nobody to drop theirs in, they vote {tauxSansGroupe}% of the time, against {tauxAvecGroupe}% when they have one.} other {}}
answerParticipation.heroDesc: Average participation rate per parliamentarian, at the Assembly since July 2024 and at the Senate since October 2023
answerParticipation.conceptsTitle: Key concepts before reading the figures
answerParticipation.concept1Desc: This page covers the {an} MPs and {sn} senators in office. MPs' votes count since the start of the 17th legislature (18 July 2024), senators' votes since 2 October 2023, when the senators elected in September 2023 took office, whatever year they were elected. Only parliamentarians with at least one recorded vote are included — a few newly elected members or those who arrived mid-term may be absent. Ministers, former parliamentarians, and substitutes are excluded. The count may vary slightly between metrics: an MP with no solemn ballot recorded yet (e.g. a very recent arrival) will appear in final votes but not in solemn ballots. Note: only votes recorded digitally in official databases are counted. Some votes take place by a show of hands or other non-digitised methods — those are not included in these statistics.
answerParticipation.sourceAN: National Assembly, fact sheet no. 56 on votes
answerParticipation.sourceLoi: Ordinance of 7 November 1958 on vote delegation
answerParticipation.concept2Desc: A final vote is the ballot that settles the fate of a text. At the National Assembly it takes three forms: the vote on the text as a whole (or on its single article, or on the first part of a budget), the adoption of a procedural motion that rejects the text without examining it, and the vote on a resolution. In the Senate, the final votes counted are the vote on the text as a whole and the adoption of a preliminary question or a plea of inadmissibility, the two motions that reject it without examination. This is the type of ballot measured here, in both chambers, to allow a direct comparison. No-confidence motions are excluded: they target the Government, not a text. The Senate also holds solemn public ballots, but its open data does not tell them apart from the others, so this page cannot single them out.
answerParticipation.concept3Title: Solemn ballot: the vote announced in advance (NA)
answerParticipation.concept3Desc: A solemn ballot is a solemn public vote (SPS) at the National Assembly, used for significant texts such as the budget. What sets it apart from an ordinary ballot? It is announced in advance, giving every MP the chance to organise their vote regardless of other commitments, in person or by proxy. As a result, its participation rate is mechanically far higher: {solennel}% on average. Most solemn ballots are also final votes, but not all: some concern a statement by the Government, which settles the fate of no text. No-confidence motions count towards no rate at all: the Constitution has only the votes in favour recorded, so an MP who opposes one is indistinguishable from one who was away.
answerParticipation.concept4Desc: Ministers and the Speaker of the National Assembly do not vote in ballots — their institutional role keeps them out of it. In the Senate, the session chair, senators who are members of the Government and those who recuse themselves (who refrain from voting to avoid a conflict of interest) are in the same position. All of them are therefore excluded from the denominator in our calculations. Without this exclusion, the participation rate would appear artificially lower, since these individuals would be counted as absent when they did not have to take part in the vote.

answerParticipation.methodologyPerimetre: What is counted: the MPs and senators in office, with MPs' votes since the start of the 17th legislature (18 July 2024) and senators' votes since 2 October 2023. Group rates also include the votes of members who have since left, each in the group it was cast in. Two things are measured. First, final votes, the ones that settle the fate of a text, in both chambers. At the Assembly these are the vote on the whole text, the adoption of a procedural motion rejecting it without examination and the vote on a resolution; in the Senate, the vote on the whole text and the adoption of a preliminary question or a plea of inadmissibility, which reject it in the same way. Second, solemn ballots, at the Assembly only, announced in advance so that everyone can plan for them. LoiClair does not count votes on amendments. No-confidence motions do not count either, because the Constitution has only the votes in favour recorded: being against one and being absent look exactly the same. Finally, only votes recorded by machine are visible. A show of hands leaves nothing usable behind.
answerParticipation.methodologyFormule: The calculation: for each member, the number of times they took a position, whether for, against or abstention, divided by the number of ballots held while they were in office. The counter starts on the day they actually took office, not on the official date. Months spent in government drop out of the calculation, since a minister does not vote. If a member has their vote corrected afterwards, what is called a mise au point, the correction is taken into account. A group's rate divides its members' votes by all the votes they could have cast, ballot by ballot: each vote counts in the group the member belonged to that day, including members who have since left or changed group.
answerParticipation.methodologyExclusions: Who drops out of the calculation: some members are not allowed to vote because of the role they hold. The Speaker of the National Assembly, whoever is chairing the sitting, and members of the Government. Counting them as absent would hold a rule against them that they cannot escape, so they drop out of both sides of the division. In the Senate this also covers senators who recuse themselves, meaning they abstain to avoid a conflict of interest. Finally, a member with fewer than {min} ballots during their term does not appear in the rankings: their rate would rest on too few votes to mean anything. The Senate comparison with or without a group is counted differently: vote by vote, by the group held on the day of the ballot, and it only shows when at least {minSenateurs} senators each have {min} possible votes with no group.
answerParticipation.methodologySenat: The Senate's case: the Senate holds solemn public ballots (at the rostrum), but its open data does not tell them apart from the others, so there is nothing to show for it in this variant. More importantly, its rate does not say who was in the chamber, but whose ballot was cast: at each ordinary public ballot a single senator per group can drop in the ballot papers of all their colleagues, absentees included. The Senate thus records a position for almost all of its members, and publishes no count of those actually present. All groups therefore vote at a rate close to 100%, and the gap between them ranks nobody: when the gap is measurable, a chart on this page sets the senators who have a group against those who do not, the only contrast that says anything. For the same reason, this page publishes no list of the senators with the highest and lowest rates: a single senator per group can cast everyone's ballots, so the gap between two senators ranks nobody.

answerActivite.caveatBody: A very active member can produce a great deal that leads nowhere: here, a rejected amendment counts as much as one that passes. The score is also incomplete, because official sources do not publish everything: constituency work, for one, appears in no counter. What it does measure, it measures by public rules, and every error found is <corrections>corrected in public</corrections>. On the criteria listed below, it places each member against colleagues in the same chamber.
answerActivite.conceptsTitle: What to understand before reading the data
answerActivite.concept1Desc: The {an} MPs and {sn} senators currently in office (17th legislature). Ministers are excluded: their executive role prevents them from engaging in normal parliamentary activity. The Speaker of the National Assembly and the President of the Senate, political group leaders and members with less than six months (180 days) in office are shown, but not ranked. Former ministers back as MPs or senators stay in the ranking, with their ministerial period deducted from their active days. What they did as ministers does not count: neither their government's bills nor their speeches from the Government bench.
answerActivite.concept2Desc: Four steps lead from raw data to a score out of 100.
answerActivite.concept2Etape1Desc: Each counter — bills, amendments, questions, speeches, attendance — is divided by the member's number of active days in office. That is what makes a substitute who arrived in 2026 comparable to a member sitting since July 2024.
answerActivite.concept2Etape2Desc: MPs' rates are ranked against MPs, senators' against senators. Each member receives the share of colleagues they beat: percentile 80 means better than 80% of their peers. Members on an exact tie, everyone who produced no oversight report for instance, share the percentile at the middle of their group: neither the top, which would reward doing nothing, nor the bottom, which would punish it twice.
answerActivite.concept2Etape3Desc: The percentiles are averaged across the four functions of the mandate, which do not carry equal weight: Legislate 25%, Deliberate 20%, Scrutinise 25%, Examine bills 30%.
answerActivite.concept2Etape4Titre: Measures dropped when they do not apply
answerActivite.concept2Etape4Desc: Vote participation for members whose rate cannot be established, committee attendance for those who sit on no committee. The measure leaves the calculation together with its weight, and the member leaves the ranking that produces it so as not to shift everyone else's. The score therefore rests on 9, 10 or 11 measures depending on the profile.
answerActivite.concept2Note: Members with fewer than 180 active days in office are not ranked. That threshold is the one used by NosDéputés.fr.
answerActivite.tableDesc: Sorted by descending composite score — select a column header to re-sort
answerActivite.tableNote: Score 0–100: weighted average of the percentiles across 11 metrics (4 functions, 10 points in total), normalised by active days. Rank recalculated according to the active chamber filter. Members with fewer than 180 active days appear at the bottom, without a score, followed by the presiding officers of the chambers and the leaders of political groups.
answerActivite.tableCountWithMinisters: {count} parliamentarians shown ({excluded} minister{plural} currently in government not counted)
answerActivite.colRangTooltip: Rank among classified parliamentarians in the chamber (mandate ≥ 180 days, excluding serving ministers, presiding officers of a chamber and group leaders). Members with equal scores share the same rank.
answerActivite.badgeMandatRecentTooltip: Less than 180 active mandate days — score unavailable. Raw counts remain shown.
answerActivite.badgeNonClasseTooltip: Less than 180 active mandate days — the member cannot be fairly compared to others. Raw counts remain visible.
answerActivite.badgePresidentChambreTooltip: Speaker of the National Assembly or President of the Senate: the office rules out tabling amendments, asking questions and co-signing bills, and chairing a sitting does not count as speaking in it. The member is left out of the ranking and of the comparisons; their raw figures remain visible.
answerActivite.joursActifsTooltip: Number of days since the member's effective start of office, or since the start of the time window when that is later (excluding ministerial periods), used to normalise the score.
answerActivite.methodologyPerimetre: Scope — {an} MPs and {sn} senators in office, 17th legislature. Three different headcounts therefore coexist on this page, and the gap between them is deliberate. Serving ministers leave the table: holding a government position suspends normal parliamentary activity. Members with fewer than 180 effective mandate days then stay in the table but without a score, for lack of being comparable. So do the presiding officers of both chambers: chairing rules out most of what is measured, and the score read that as inactivity. So do the leaders of political groups: organising the group and aligning its positions appears in no counter. A rank is therefore read against ranked members only, not against the chamber's full membership: {an} MPs in office, {anTableau} in the table, {anClasses} ranked; {sn} senators, {snTableau} in the table, {snClasses} ranked. Former ministers back as MPs or senators stay in the ranking, but their ministerial period is deducted from their active days (see Normalisation). What they did as ministers does not count: their government's bills are neither initiated bills nor co-signed texts, and their speeches from the Government bench are not floor speeches. Data covers the current mandate, since 18 July 2024 for MPs and since 2 October 2023 for senators, with two caveats, both on the Assembly side: NA session records released as open data start on 9 October 2024, and its questions on 1 October 2024.
answerActivite.methodologyCentile: Percentiles — For each metric, each member's value is converted to a percentile (0–100) relative to other members of the same chamber (NA and Senate calculated separately). A percentile of 80 means "top 20% of MPs" or "top 20% of senators" — never a cross-chamber mix. This avoids structurally penalising a chamber whose legislative calendar or culture differs from the other. When many members share exactly the same value, they all receive the percentile at the middle of their group: on a metric where half the chamber sits at zero, that zero is worth about 25, not 50. Intended consequence: a chamber's average score sits around 50, as a percentile-based score should. Two consequences are worth knowing. The percentile caps the effect of volume: in the Senate, a member who asked several hundred written questions receives the top percentile on that measure and still ranks among the very last. However high the volume, the percentile cannot exceed 100, and this measure weighs only 0.25 points out of 10. Conversely, when nearly all members have close values, a tiny gap weighs heavily: in the Senate, where participation rates are almost all close to 100%, a single missed vote can cost dozens of places.
answerActivite.methodologyScore: Weighted composite score — Weighted average of the available percentiles (9 to 11 depending on the member), themselves computed on daily rates (counter ÷ active days). Each measure carries the weight of the effort it demands, for a total of 10 pts: Legislate (25%) — bill initiated 1.25; amendment author 0.75; co-signed text 0.3; amendment co-signer 0.2; Deliberate (20%) — final votes (all ballots) 1.25; floor speeches 0.75; Scrutinise (25%) — oversight report 1.75; oral questions 0.5; written questions 0.25; Examine bills (30%) — bill rapporteur 1.75; committee attendance 1.25. Voting and committee attendance carry the same weight: the first can be delegated but decides, the second costs hours every week, where bills are actually written. A metric that cannot be computed for a member is dropped along with its weight, and the denominator becomes the sum of the weights actually available: vote participation when it is not established, committee attendance for a member who sits on none.
answerActivite.methodologyFenetre: Time window — Every metric is computed over each member's current mandate, never over their pre-mandate history. For MPs, the window starts on 18 July 2024 (start of the 17th legislature), except on two measures the Assembly does not publish that far back: questions start on 1 October 2024 and speeches on 9 October 2024. For senators, it starts on 2 October 2023 (2023 senatorial election) and holds for all eleven measures, the Senate publishing its full history. A senator re-elected in September 2026 keeps that cut-off: their mandate carries on without a break, and their activity since 2023 still counts. That is the only reason the cut-offs differ from one measure to the next on the Assembly side: they follow what each source makes available, never a rule of the score's own. Concretely: a dossier, a co-signed text, a report or an amendment is credited to a member only if its tabling date is later than the cut-off for their mandate. A senator re-elected in 2023 does not regain the activity of their previous mandates, even on dossiers still in shuttle today — comparison remains fair to members who entered office at the same date. A member who changes chamber starts from zero: an MP elected senator in 2026 takes neither their activity nor their days as an MP with them, and neither does a senator who becomes an MP.
answerActivite.methodologyNormalisation: Normalisation by active days — Each counter (initiated bills, amendments, questions, speeches, committee attendance…) is divided by the number of active days since the member's effective start of office, or since the start of the time window when that is later (ministerial periods are excluded from the denominator). The result is a daily rate, compared between members of the same chamber. Raw counts remain shown everywhere — the number of active days is exposed alongside the score for transparency. Members with fewer than 180 active days: excluded from the ranking (score unavailable) with an “Unranked — mandate shorter than 6 months” badge, but their raw counts remain visible. The presiding officers of both chambers carry an “Unranked: presides over the chamber” badge, under the same rule. Leaders of political groups carry an “Unranked: leads a political group” badge. This threshold aligns LoiClair with NosDéputés.fr's practice (6 months for their summary).
answerActivite.methodologyLimites: Limitations — The score is descriptive, not normative. A low score on co-signatures may reflect deep committee work rather than inactivity. Some measures reward a way of working as much as the amount of work: co-signing bills and amendments as a group, being appointed rapporteur on a bill, producing an oversight report. Being appointed rapporteur, moreover, does not depend on the member alone: the committee decides. Measured against their share of seats, the share of reports obtained sets groups several times apart, while their committee attendance falls within a far narrower spread. So this is not a difference in effort: the groups most often appointed rapporteur are not the most present ones, nor the other way round. A group kept away from positions of responsibility starts at a disadvantage on a measure that carries 17.5% of the score. The ranking should be read as an exploration tool, not a verdict. Participation, not attendance — the figure measures whether a position was recorded for the member, not whether they were physically in the chamber. Proxy votes count, and there are many: a third of the votes cast in a solemn ballot at the NA. In the Senate, only solemn public ballots publish named proxies. On the others, nothing separates those present from those represented. That is also what explains the gap between the two chambers, which comes down to the type of ballot far more than to diligence: a solemn ballot at the NA gathers far more MPs than an ordinary one, and a vote on a whole text in the Senate records almost every senator. Final votes, not solemn ballots: the score's measure counts every final vote, ordinary ballots included, rather than solemn ballots alone, whose rate an MP's page also shows. Most solemn ballots are also final votes, but participation in them tightens between 85% and 100% for most MPs: one or two absences would cost dozens of places, the flaw seen in the Senate. Untracked absences — parental leave, sick leave and official missions are not published in open data. A member on three months' maternity leave will mechanically see her daily rate drop without that reflecting her engagement. Ministerial periods, on the other hand, are properly excluded from the active-days count. Volume without quality weighting — an adopted amendment counts as much as a rejected one; a bill enacted into law counts as much as one that never reached the floor. This is a deliberate choice: weighting by success would mechanically advantage the current majority and penalise the principled positions of the opposition.

cpPart.quoi: The share of ballots the member took part in, among those deciding whether a text passes. Formula: votes for, against and abstentions, divided by the ballots held during their term.
cpPart.source: Public ballots of the National Assembly and of the Senate.
cpPart.fenetre: MPs since 18 July 2024, senators since 2 October 2023, including those re-elected in 2026.
cpPart.compte: Every final vote, the ones that settle the fate of a text, ordinary ballots included in the Assembly and the votes “on the whole” in the Senate, along with the adopted motions that reject a text there. A proxy vote counts as a vote. The Assembly publishes which votes were cast by proxy, and an MP's page shows that share of their final and solemn votes. In the Senate, only solemn public ballots publish named proxies. On the others, senators delegate their vote to their group, and nothing tells the present from the represented.
cpPart.exclut: No-confidence motions, where the Constitution has only the votes in favour recorded. Shows of hands, which leave no record of who voted what. And ballots where the member could not vote because of their office, or because of a recusal for conflict of interest in the Senate, the only chamber to record it in the ballot result: those leave both sides of the calculation, never counted as an absence. In the Assembly, the recusal is kept in a separate register, not in the ballot: it therefore weighs as an absence.

cpDoss.quoi: The texts the member wrote and tabled: a bill or a resolution they authored. Legislative initiative in the strict sense.
cpDoss.source: Legislative files of the National Assembly, texts tabled in the Senate.
cpDoss.fenetre: MPs since 18 July 2024, senators since 2 October 2023, including those re-elected in 2026.
cpDoss.compte: One file per tabled text, credited to every author: the Senate often declares several on equal footing, commonly up to five.
cpDoss.exclut: Co-signatories, counted separately. On resolutions convening the High Court, only the first signatory counts: the organic law of 24 November 2014, which implements article 68 of the Constitution, requires one tenth of the members to sign, which is an admissibility condition, not a team of authors. Government bills and statements: a former minister back in Parliament is not credited with them.

cpCosign.quoi: A colleague's texts the member signed in support, without writing them. A way to weigh in without originating.
cpCosign.source: Co-signatories published by the National Assembly, signatures published by the Senate.
cpCosign.fenetre: MPs since 18 July 2024, senators since 2 October 2023, including those re-elected in 2026.
cpCosign.compte: One co-signature per supported text. Two successive versions of the same file remain two co-signatures.
cpCosign.exclut: Withdrawn co-signatures, texts the member already authored, and no-confidence motions: co-signing one is a political act rather than work on a text, and the Senate has none. Government texts signed as a minister.

cpRapp.quoi: To report on a text is to be in charge of it before one's committee: analysing it article by article, hearing those it affects, proposing changes, then defending it on the floor.
cpRapp.source: Rapporteurs of reports and opinions, in both chambers.
cpRapp.fenetre: MPs since 18 July 2024, senators since 2 October 2023, including those re-elected in 2026.
cpRapp.compte: One unit per file reported on, however many volumes it runs to. These capacities count: rapporteur, rapporteur for opinion, general rapporteur, and special rapporteur in the Senate only (the Assembly publishes its special reports as annexes, which the site does not import). Each co-rapporteur receives a full unit.
cpRapp.exclut: Oversight reports, counted in their own measure, and the annexes to a report.

cpRappCtrl.quoi: An oversight report accompanies no law: a committee picks a subject, holds hearings for months, then publishes its findings and recommendations. This is Parliament's other mission, to watch and to assess.
cpRappCtrl.source: Information reports published by the National Assembly and by the Senate.
cpRappCtrl.fenetre: MPs since 18 July 2024, senators since 2 October 2023, including those re-elected in 2026.
cpRappCtrl.compte: Information reports, committee of inquiry reports, parliamentary office reports and reports on a petition. A report in several volumes counts as one unit, and each co-rapporteur receives a full unit.
cpRappCtrl.exclut: The Senate's comparative law studies, produced by its staff with no parliamentary author, and the chairing of a committee of inquiry, which the Assembly never lists among rapporteurs.

cpAmendAuteur.quoi: An amendment is a change proposed to a text under examination. Here, those the member wrote themselves.
cpAmendAuteur.source: Amendments published by the National Assembly and by the Senate.
cpAmendAuteur.fenetre: MPs since 18 July 2024, senators since 2 October 2023, including those re-elected in 2026.
cpAmendAuteur.compte: Amendments the member authored, tabled on a file the site tracks.
cpAmendAuteur.exclut: Government amendments, and those tabled on a file absent from the database.

cpAmendCosign.quoi: A colleague's amendments the member signed in support: engagement in the line-by-line work.
cpAmendCosign.source: Amendments published by the National Assembly and by the Senate.
cpAmendCosign.fenetre: MPs since 18 July 2024, senators since 2 October 2023, including those re-elected in 2026.
cpAmendCosign.compte: Amendments the member co-signed without being their author.
cpAmendCosign.exclut: Government amendments, and those tabled on a file absent from the database.

cpQuestO.quoi: A question put aloud to a minister, in the chamber. Questions to the Government, on Tuesday and Wednesday in the National Assembly and on Wednesday in the Senate, are its best-known form.
cpQuestO.source: Questions to the Government and oral questions of both chambers.
cpQuestO.fenetre: MPs since 1 October 2024, the source publishing nothing before. Senators since 2 October 2023, including those re-elected in 2026.
cpQuestO.compte: Questions to the Government and oral questions without debate in the Assembly; the Senate adds oral questions with debate, European oral questions and topical questions.
cpQuestO.exclut: The text of the questions is not reproduced: only the link to the Official Journal is kept.

cpQuestE.quoi: A written question sent to a ministry, which has one month, extendable by one month, to answer in the Official Journal. The most common oversight tool, and the most unevenly used: from none to several hundred per term.
cpQuestE.fenetre: MPs since 1 October 2024, the source publishing nothing before. Senators since 2 October 2023, including those re-elected in 2026.
cpQuestE.compte: Written questions published in the Official Journal, excluding reminders of an unanswered question.
cpQuestE.exclut: The text of the questions and the ministries' answers, which stay with the Assembly and the Senate. An unanswered question counts as much as one that got a reply: the reply does not depend on its author.

cpPrisesParole.quoi: What the member said on the floor, as the official record captures it. A “Thank you, Mr President” does not count: more than twenty words are needed.
cpPrisesParole.source: Full records of sittings, published by both chambers.
cpPrisesParole.fenetre: MPs since 9 October 2024, the source publishing nothing before. Senators since 2 October 2023, including those re-elected in 2026.
cpPrisesParole.compte: Contributions of more than twenty words made in the debate on a text.
cpPrisesParole.exclut: Everything not tied to a text, which cannot be attached to one: questions to the Government, tributes, points of order, motions, debates without a vote. That is six contributions out of ten. Also excluded: the chair's conduct of the sitting and stage directions (“Applause”). Nor contributions made as a member of the Government.

cpCommPres.quoi: Attendance at committee meetings, where work on texts happens before the floor. A member sitting on no committee is not penalised: the measure is dropped from their score, along with its weight.
cpCommPres.source: Meeting agenda of the National Assembly, senators' activity published by the Senate.
cpCommPres.fenetre: MPs since 18 July 2024, senators since 2 October 2023, including those re-elected in 2026.
cpCommPres.compte: Recorded attendance at meetings of standing, special, inquiry and European committees, missions, joint committees, delegations, friendship groups and study groups. Standing in for a colleague counts as attendance.
cpCommPres.exclut: Rapporteur hearings and field visits, which the two chambers do not document the same way. Plenary sittings too: the Assembly publishes no attendance sheet for the chamber floor, unlike the Senate.

answerSuccesLegislatif.conceptsTitle: What to know before reading the numbers
answerSuccesLegislatif.concept1Title: Scope: only texts that can become laws
answerSuccesLegislatif.concept1Desc: We only count texts tabled since 18 July 2024 that can be enacted: government bills and private member's bills, State and social security budgets, constitutional and organic laws, treaty ratifications. Resolutions, information reports, fact-finding missions, petitions and committees of inquiry are excluded — they can be voted on by a chamber, but never become laws. Example: the RN resolution denouncing the Franco-Algerian agreements was adopted by the Assembly, but does not appear here — it is not a legislative text.
answerSuccesLegislatif.concept2Title: Adopted vs. enacted — what's the difference?
answerSuccesLegislatif.concept2Desc: An adopted text has been voted on by at least one chamber (Assembly or Senate). An enacted text has been signed by the president and published in the Official Journal — meaning it has become law. Between the two, there can be multiple back-and-forths between chambers, then potentially a joint committee, before signature.
answerSuccesLegislatif.concept3Desc: A large group mechanically tables more texts than a small one, simply because it has more elected officials. Dividing the total by the group's number of members gives the per-member value — example: 10 enacted laws for 46 MPs = 0.22 law per MP. This is the column that lets you see whether a small group punches above its weight.
answerSuccesLegislatif.concept4Title: Why is the Government set apart?
answerSuccesLegislatif.concept4Desc: The Government is not a parliamentary group: it has no reference seat count. We can count its bills in absolute terms, but not 'per member'. Successive governments of the legislature (Attal, Barnier, Bayrou, Lecornu…) are merged into a single line, because it's the same executive continuity.
answerSuccesLegislatif.concept5Desc: It's the majority that passes laws. A majority group therefore naturally sees more of its texts succeed than an opposition one — this is arithmetic. A low rate for the opposition says nothing about the quality of work done; it reflects the parliamentary mechanics.
answerSuccesLegislatif.concept6Desc: Each group's size is today's (sitting MPs and senators), not an average over the legislature. A member who switches groups mid-term is only counted in their current group. Within a single legislature, this effect stays limited.
answerSuccesLegislatif.howToReadLead: Each chart shows the same measure from two angles: raw count on the left, divided by group size on the right. A large group can lead in absolute terms but fall behind per member.
answerSuccesLegislatif.howToReadExampleBoth: Example — laws enacted. <hl>{bigName}</hl> ({bigSize} members) leads in absolute terms with {bigAbs} laws, i.e. {bigPer} per member. But relative to size, <hl>{topName}</hl> ({topSize} members) reaches {topPer} per member — the highest ratio ({topAbs} laws in total).
answerSuccesLegislatif.howToReadExampleSingle: Example — laws enacted. <hl>{name}</hl> ({size} members) has enacted {abs} laws, i.e. {per} per member — the highest ratio.
answerSuccesLegislatif.butterflyDepotDesc: On the left, raw number of texts tabled. On the right, per member. Resolutions, reports and petitions are excluded.
answerSuccesLegislatif.butterflyDepotNote: Population: legislative texts (bills and proposed laws, budgets, constitutional and organic laws, treaty ratifications) tabled by each group since 18 July 2024. Resolutions and other non-enactable texts are not counted. Only groups that have initiated at least 10 texts appear. The Government appears in raw counts only — it has no parliamentary size.
answerSuccesLegislatif.butterflyAdoptionTitle: Legislative texts adopted by a chamber
answerSuccesLegislatif.butterflyAdoptionDesc: On the left, raw count adopted by the Assembly or the Senate. On the right, per member.
answerSuccesLegislatif.butterflyAdoptionNote: Population: same texts as the Tabling card — legislative texts only. A text is counted as 'adopted' as soon as it has been voted on by at least one chamber, whether subsequently enacted or still shuttling between chambers. Adopted resolutions (such as symbolic chamber positions) are not counted — they are not legislative texts.
answerSuccesLegislatif.butterflyPromulgDesc: On the left, raw number of laws stemming from the group's texts. On the right, per member — the final efficiency measure.
answerSuccesLegislatif.butterflyPromulgNote: Population: laws stemming from legislative texts tabled since 18 July 2024. Texts still shuttling between chambers or stuck in committee mechanically drag the numbers down — this is a snapshot, not a final tally. The dashboard tile counts all laws enacted since that date, including those whose text was tabled earlier: its figures are therefore higher.
answerSuccesLegislatif.methodologyPerimeter: Scope — Legislative texts tabled since 18 July 2024, and the laws that came from them. A law enacted since that date on a text tabled earlier is not counted: the tabled, adopted, enacted path only reads on the same texts. The dashboard tile 'Who writes the laws that pass?' counts, by contrast, all laws enacted since 18 July 2024. We compare groups that have initiated at least 10 texts over that period. Successive governments are merged into a single 'Government' line. Each bill is placed in its author's group on the day it was tabled, even if the author has changed groups since. Bills whose author had no known group that day (between two groups, or a group not yet published by the National Assembly) count in the totals but appear in no per-group chart: each chart's caption says how many are missing.
answerSuccesLegislatif.methodologyRate: Calculation — For each group: texts initiated, texts adopted by at least one chamber, laws enacted. Each figure is also divided by group size to get the per-member value — example: 10 laws for 46 MPs = 0.22 law per MP. The Government is hidden from this column: it has no parliamentary seat count.
answerSuccesLegislatif.methodologyTaille: Group sizes — Number of parliamentarians currently in office, counted directly from the open data. An MP who switches groups mid-legislature is no longer counted in their former group. Within a single legislature, this effect stays limited.
answerSuccesLegislatif.methodologyExclusions: Exclusions — Groups that have initiated fewer than 10 texts are set aside: with so few cases, a single success or a single failure would swing the rate. The Government is hidden from the 'per member' columns — it has no parliamentary seat of reference.
answerSuccesLegislatif.methodologyLimit: Limitations — It's the majority that passes laws: an opposition group arithmetically sees fewer of its texts succeed, regardless of their quality. Recent texts still shuttling between chambers drag the rates down — the picture shifts week by week. Finally, group size is measured today, not averaged over the legislature.

answerSuccesLegislatifEfficacite.shortAnswer: Under the 17th legislature, a typical parliamentary group (Government and non-attached members excluded) gets on average <hl>{tauxAN}</hl> of its texts adopted at the National Assembly, <hl>{tauxSN}</hl> at the Senate, and <hl>{tauxPromulg}</hl> are ultimately enacted. <hl>{topGroupe}</hl> is the group that best converts proposals into laws (<hl>{topTaux}</hl>).
answerSuccesLegislatifEfficacite.concept1Desc: We only count texts tabled since 18 July 2024 — the start of the 17th legislature. Older texts still in the parliamentary pipeline are not included, nor is a law enacted since that date on a text tabled earlier. This is a snapshot of the current mandate, not a historical view.
answerSuccesLegislatifEfficacite.concept2Desc: Each rate is calculated on a different population. The NA adoption rate covers all texts except those that cannot be voted by a chamber (petitions, information reports, missions, inquiry commissions, speeches). The Senate adoption rate also removes government confidence procedures (Article 49) and texts classed as “Résolution”; those classed “Résolution Article 34-1” stay counted. The enactment rate only covers texts that can become a law (bills, budgets, constitutional or organic laws, treaty ratifications). Comparing the same group across all three gives three distinct pictures.
answerSuccesLegislatifEfficacite.concept3Title: Adopted by a chamber ≠ definitively adopted
answerSuccesLegislatifEfficacite.concept3Desc: A text is counted as 'adopted' as soon as it has received a favourable vote in the relevant chamber, even if it was later rejected or buried elsewhere. This measure reflects the support received, not the final outcome. A text adopted by the NA but rejected by the Senate therefore appears in the NA denominator (as adopted) and in the Senate denominator (as rejected).
answerSuccesLegislatifEfficacite.concept4Title: Chamber of origin and shuttle effect
answerSuccesLegislatifEfficacite.concept4Desc: A text is first examined by the chamber where it was tabled, then sent to the other. A group can get its texts adopted in the chamber where it is strong and see them stall in the one where it carries less weight. That's why the 'chamber of origin' filter at the top lets you compare on equal footing: NA groups among themselves, Senate groups among themselves.
answerSuccesLegislatifEfficacite.concept5Desc: Below that, a rate based on 3 proposals is not interpretable: a single success or failure swings the number. Groups that have initiated fewer than 10 texts that a chamber can vote on since July 2024 are not shown.
answerSuccesLegislatifEfficacite.concept6Desc: This page measures success rates, not raw number of texts. A group can table many and get few passed, or vice versa. To see who tables and who gets things adopted in absolute terms, see Chapter 1 — Volume.
answerSuccesLegislatifEfficacite.heroAdoptionANLabel: Adoption at the Assembly — average per group
answerSuccesLegislatifEfficacite.heroAdoptionSNLabel: Adoption at the Senate — average per group
answerSuccesLegislatifEfficacite.heroCaption: Average across parliamentary groups, Government and non-attached members excluded (non-attached members do not form a political group). For the overall rate of the legislature (all texts combined, Government included), see the Enactment rate page.
answerSuccesLegislatifEfficacite.combinedChartDesc: For each group: share of its texts adopted at the National Assembly, at the Senate, and finally enacted. Sorted by NA adoption rate.
answerSuccesLegislatifEfficacite.combinedChartNote: Each bar is read against its own denominator (hover to see the numerator/denominator). A missing bar means the group has fewer than 10 texts in that category — the rate is not computable. Only groups that have initiated at least 10 texts eligible for a chamber vote since 18 July 2024 are shown.
answerSuccesLegislatifEfficacite.methodologyPerimeter: Scope — Texts tabled since 18 July 2024 (start of the 17th legislature), and the laws that came from them: a law enacted since that date on a text tabled earlier is not counted. Successive governments of the legislature are merged into a single 'Government' line. Each bill is placed in its author's group on the day it was tabled, even if the author has changed groups since. Only groups that have initiated at least 10 texts are shown. Texts without a known group (no identified author, or an author without a group that day) enter no rate: the chart caption says how many there are.
answerSuccesLegislatifEfficacite.methodologyDenominateurs: Three rates, three denominators — The NA adoption rate excludes texts without a chamber vote (petitions, information reports, missions, inquiry commissions, speeches). The Senate adoption rate also excludes government confidence procedures (Article 49) and texts classed as “Résolution”; those classed “Résolution Article 34-1” stay counted. The enactment rate only covers texts that can become a law.
answerSuccesLegislatifEfficacite.methodologyAdoption: Chamber adoption — A text is counted as 'adopted' by a chamber as soon as it has received a favourable vote from it (first reading, new reading, final reading or joint committee), regardless of whether the text is subsequently enacted. Official sources: legislative acts from the NA and Senate with a status containing 'adopted', 'modified' or 'definitively adopted'.
answerSuccesLegislatifEfficacite.methodologyExclusions: Exclusions — Petitions, information reports, missions, inquiry commissions, and speeches are not counted in the NA and SN denominators. Government confidence procedures (Article 49) and texts classed as “Résolution” are further removed from the SN denominator; those classed “Résolution Article 34-1” are not. Non-attached members, who do not form a political group, are left out of the per-group averages and of the choice of the top group, but their rate appears in the charts.
answerSuccesLegislatifEfficacite.methodologyLimit: Limitations — It's the majority that passes laws. A low rate for an opposition group often reflects its parliamentary position, not the quality of its texts. Recent texts still shuttling between chambers pull rates down — the picture shifts week by week.

The group most often aligned with the final outcome is <hl>{topGroupeAN}</hl> at the National Assembly (<hl>{topTauxAN}</hl>) and <hl>{topGroupeSN}</hl> at the Senate (<hl>{topTauxSN}</hl>).
answerSuccesLegislatifVictoires.concept1Desc: This page covers final votes of the 17th legislature at the National Assembly (since 18 July 2024) and final votes published by the Senate since 2 October 2023, when the senators elected in September 2023 took office. A final vote is the one that settles a text's fate at a given reading: the vote on the text as a whole (or on its single article, or on the first part of a budget), the adoption of a procedural motion that rejects it without examination, or the vote on a draft resolution. In the Senate, the vote on the text as a whole is included, along with the adoption of a preliminary question or a plea of inadmissibility, the two motions that reject it without examination. Technical votes (amendments, articles) are excluded, as are no-confidence motions, which record only the votes in favour.
answerSuccesLegislatifVictoires.concept2Title: The winning side of a vote
answerSuccesLegislatifVictoires.concept2Desc: This is the official result of the vote — 'adopted' or 'rejected' — as published by the National Assembly or the Senate. An adopted text means the 'for' side won; a rejected text means the 'against' side won. This result already accounts for qualified-majority rules where relevant — we never recompute it from a raw vote count.
answerSuccesLegislatifVictoires.concept3Desc: For each vote, we use the position held by the largest share of the group's voting members ('for', 'against', or 'abstain'). At the NA, it is computed from the group's vote count published by the Assembly, rather than taken from the position the Assembly publishes alongside it, which contradicts that count in about 3% of cases; at the Senate, which publishes no group position, from individual votes in the official export. A group has no position when none of its members voted, or when the two leading options are tied. A group's position is aligned with the outcome when it matches the winning side, whether or not the group authored the text.
answerSuccesLegislatifVictoires.concept4Title: Abstention is excluded from the calculation
answerSuccesLegislatifVictoires.concept4Desc: When a group's majority position is 'abstain', that vote is excluded from the calculation: the group didn't take a side for or against the winning outcome, so we can't say whether it was aligned with the outcome or not. Only votes where the group took a for/against position count toward the rate.
answerSuccesLegislatifVictoires.concept5Desc: Below that, a rate based on 3 or 4 votes is not interpretable: a single outcome swings the number. Groups with fewer than 10 usable votes (for/against position plus a known winning side) are not shown. 'Unaffiliated' members are also excluded: this isn't a coherent political group but an administrative catch-all for members with no shared label, so its 'majority position' doesn't reflect any shared voting strategy.
answerSuccesLegislatifVictoires.concept6Desc: This page measures whether a group ends up on the right side of the final outcome — whether it authored the text or simply supported or blocked someone else's. To see who gets their own texts passed, see Chapter 2 — Efficiency.

answerSuccesLegislatifVictoires.heroVictoiresSNLabel: Alignment rate — average per group, Senate

answerSuccesLegislatifVictoires.groupeANDesc: Share of final votes where the group's position matches the winning side, sorted from highest to lowest
answerSuccesLegislatifVictoires.groupeANNote: Population: groups with at least 10 usable votes. Official group colours.
answerSuccesLegislatifVictoires.groupeSNDesc: Share of final votes where the group's position matches the winning side, sorted from highest to lowest
answerSuccesLegislatifVictoires.groupeSNNote: Population: groups with at least 10 usable votes. Official group colours, taken from senat.fr.
answerSuccesLegislatifVictoires.methodologyPerimeter: Scope — Final votes of the 17th legislature at the National Assembly (since 18 July 2024) and final votes published by the Senate since 2 October 2023, when the senators elected in September 2023 took office. No-confidence motions are removed: they record only the votes in favour, so a rejected motion would count as a defeat for its signatories alone and as nothing at all for those who brought it down. Only groups with at least 10 usable votes are shown.
answerSuccesLegislatifVictoires.methodologyCalcul: Calculation — For each group, alignment rate = number of votes where its majority position (for/against) matches the winning side (adopted→for, rejected→against) ÷ number of votes where the group took a for/against position × 100.
answerSuccesLegislatifVictoires.methodologyPositionMajoritaire: A group's majority position — For each vote, this is the option (for / against / abstain) with the most votes among the group's members who voted. At the NA, LoiClair computes it from the vote count published by the Assembly, rather than using the position the Assembly publishes alongside it: that position contradicts its own count in about 3% of cases, almost always naming the option that came second, and reads 'for' when no member voted. At the Senate, which publishes no group position, it is reconstructed from individual votes. Absent members do not affect the majority position.
answerSuccesLegislatifVictoires.methodologyExclusions: Exclusions — Votes with no identifiable winning side, votes where the group has no position (no member voting, or a tie between the two leading options), votes where the group's majority position is 'abstain', groups with fewer than 10 usable votes, technical votes (amendments, articles and, in the National Assembly, procedural motions that were not adopted). 'Unaffiliated' members (NA and Senate) are excluded: not being an organised political group, their 'majority position' doesn't measure any shared voting strategy.
answerSuccesLegislatifVictoires.methodologyLimit: Limitations — This rate mostly reflects membership in the governing coalition: an opposition group will structurally score lower, regardless of the quality of its positions. A high rate doesn't mean the group authored the texts that pass — it may simply support or block others' texts (see Chapter 2 — Efficiency to tell the two apart).

answerAlliances.concept1Desc: This page covers the final ballots of the 17th legislature at the National Assembly (since 18 July 2024) and the final ballots published by the Senate since 2 October 2023, when the senators elected in September 2023 took office. A final vote is the ballot that settles a text's fate at a given reading: the vote on the text as a whole (or on its single article, or on the first part of a budget), the adoption of a procedural motion that rejects it without examination, or the vote on a draft resolution. In the Senate, the vote on the text as a whole is included, along with the adoption of a preliminary question or a plea of inadmissibility, the two motions that reject it without examination. Technical ballots (amendments, articles) are excluded; they're less readable and often driven by tactical logic rather than political stance. So are no-confidence motions, which record only the votes in favour and would therefore hand every group present a 100% agreement score.
answerAlliances.concept2Desc: Two groups are said to "agree" on a ballot if their majority positions are strictly identical — both "for", both "against", or both "abstention". An abstention versus a "for" counts as disagreement. This choice deliberately tightens the measure: only clear alignments count, not a shared reluctance to oppose.
answerAlliances.concept3Desc: On each ballot, we keep the position (for / against / abstention) held by the largest share of voters within the group. At the NA, it is computed from the group's vote count published by the Assembly, rather than taken from the position the Assembly publishes alongside it, which contradicts that count in about 3% of cases; at the Senate, which publishes no group position, from individual votes in the official export. A group has no position when none of its members voted, or when the two leading options are tied. A divided group still has a majority position: so this is not a measure of internal cohesion, but of the group's stance.
answerAlliances.concept4Desc: A cell of the matrix is only coloured if the two groups have voted on at least 10 shared final ballots. Below that, an agreement or disagreement wouldn't be statistically interpretable — the cell is greyed out. This mostly concerns groups created or dissolved mid-legislature, whose overlap with others may be very small.
answerAlliances.concept5Desc: Two groups can show a high agreement rate without sharing ideas: they may oppose the same texts for opposite reasons (e.g. a finance bill rejected by both far-left and far-right). Agreement only measures one thing: the coincidence of final positions. Pair it with the actual content of the texts to judge real political proximity.
answerAlliances.matrixANDesc: Share of shared final votes where both groups hold the same majority position
answerAlliances.matrixANNote: Each cell gives the share of shared final votes where both groups took the same position, in %. Colour: pink = high agreement, blue = strong disagreement, white = average. Greyed cells: fewer than 10 shared ballots.
answerAlliances.matrixSNDesc: Share of shared final votes where both groups hold the same majority position
answerAlliances.matrixSNNote: Each cell gives the share of shared final votes where both groups took the same position, in %. Colour: pink = high agreement, blue = strong disagreement, white = average. Greyed cells: fewer than 10 shared ballots.

answerAlliances.methodologyPerimeter: Scope — Final ballots of the 17th legislature at the National Assembly (since 18 July 2024) and final ballots published by the Senate since 2 October 2023, when the senators elected in September 2023 took office. In the National Assembly, a ballot is treated as "final" if it is referenced by a legislative act in our data, that is, if it settles the text's fate at a given reading; in the Senate, these are the votes on the text as a whole and the adopted preliminary questions or pleas of inadmissibility, which reject it. No-confidence motions are then removed: they record only the votes in favour, so every group appearing on one agrees with every other, and those opposing it do not appear at all.
answerAlliances.methodologyCalcul: Calculation — For each pair of groups (A, B), we identify the final ballots on which both groups expressed a majority position. Agreement rate = number of ballots where A and B share the same position ÷ number of shared ballots × 100. Strict agreement: "for"="for", "against"="against", "abstention"="abstention" — any other combination counts as disagreement.
answerAlliances.methodologyPositionMajoritaire: A group's majority position — On each ballot, it's the option (for / against / abstention) with the most votes among the group's members who voted. At the NA, LoiClair computes it from the vote count published by the Assembly, rather than using the position the Assembly publishes alongside it: that position contradicts its own count in about 3% of cases, almost always naming the option that came second, and reads 'for' when no member voted. At the Senate, which publishes no group position, it's reconstructed from individual votes. Absent members don't influence the majority position.
answerAlliances.methodologyExclusions: Exclusions — Ballots where a group has no position: group absent, or a tie between the two leading options. Pairs with fewer than 10 shared ballots, technical ballots (amendments, articles and, in the National Assembly, procedural motions that were not adopted). Ministers and presiding officers, who do not vote, do not alter their group's majority position.
answerAlliances.methodologyLimit: Limitations — Cross-group agreement is a descriptive measure, not a political compass. Two groups can converge on a vote for opposite reasons. The measure ignores the content of the texts: a high agreement rate may reflect ideological proximity, a tactical alliance, or shared opposition to the government. Read these rates in the legislative context of the period covered.
