answerLoyaute.shortAnswer: When a parliamentarian casts a vote, they follow their group's majority position <hl>{an}%</hl> of the time at the National Assembly and <hl>{sn}%</hl> at the Senate. Overall, <hl>{shareHigh}%</hl> of elected members cross the 95% loyalty threshold — meaning individual dissent is rare.
answerLoyaute.heroDesc: Share of votes where a parliamentarian aligns with their group's majority position
answerLoyaute.conceptsTitle: Key concepts before reading the figures
answerLoyaute.concept1Body: This page covers MPs of the 17th legislature (serving since 18 July 2024) and senators in office, whose votes count since 2 October 2023, whatever year they were elected. Only parliamentarians whose loyalty could be computed are included — they must have voted on at least one ballot where their group itself expressed a majority position. Ministers do not vote and are excluded. The Speaker of the National Assembly and the President of the Senate, whose institutional role limits their voting, do not appear in the rankings.
answerLoyaute.concept2Title: "Voting with your group" = following the majority position
answerLoyaute.concept2Body: For each final vote, we look at how the majority of the group voted — “for”, “against” or “abstention”. A member who votes with that majority counts as loyal on that vote. Voting differently is a dissent. The majority position is reconstructed from the group's individual votes, ballot by ballot.
answerLoyaute.concept3Body: Ballots a parliamentarian did not take part in are not counted in their loyalty. A low participation rate therefore does not mechanically lower loyalty: the two measures are independent. Loyalty is assessed only on votes actually cast.
answerLoyaute.concept4Body: Only public ballots — those where every individual vote is digitally recorded and published — enter the calculation. Show-of-hands votes and ballots not released in electronic form are out of scope. Of those ballots, loyalty keeps only the final votes, the ones that settle a bill's fate. In the National Assembly, they take three forms: the vote on the text as a whole (or on its single article, or on the first part of a budget), the adoption of a procedural motion that rejects it without examination, and the vote on a draft resolution. In the Senate, the vote on the text as a whole is included, along with the adoption of a preliminary question or a plea of inadmissibility, the two motions that reject it without examination. No-confidence motions are set aside: a motion records only the votes in favour, so any member appearing on one agrees with their group's position by construction, and counting it would inflate the loyalty of the groups that vote them.
answerLoyaute.concept5Body: Low loyalty does not reduce a parliamentarian to being a "bad soldier" of the group. It may reveal intentional dissent, disagreement on matters of conscience (bioethics, social questions), an atypical political path, or a group with heterogeneous positions. Read this rate as a descriptive indicator, not a judgment.

answerLoyaute.methodologyPerimeter: Scope — Final votes of public ballots, at the National Assembly since 18 July 2024 (17th legislature) and at the Senate since 2 October 2023, for all senators in office. Loyalty per group also includes the votes of members who have since left. Only individual votes recorded digitally enter the calculation. Ballots that do not settle a bill's fate are set aside, as they are for the turnout rate. So are no-confidence motions: only the votes in favour are recorded, which makes agreement with one's group automatic.
answerLoyaute.methodologyCalcul: Calculation — Individual loyalty = number of final votes where the member voted with the group's majority ÷ number of final votes where both the member and the group expressed a position × 100. Average loyalty per chamber is the arithmetic mean of individual rates. Loyalty per group is the share of its members' votes that match the group's position, on the same final votes. Each vote counts in the group the member belonged to on the day of the ballot, including members who have since left or changed group. The ballot count shown next to each member in the rankings and search is the total number of final votes held during their term: it is indeed the upper bound of the denominator, which drops the ballots where either side expressed no position.
answerLoyaute.methodologyExclusions: Exclusions — Ministers do not vote and are excluded from the denominator. The Speaker of the National Assembly and the President of the Senate, whose institutional role shapes their voting, do not appear in the rankings. Ballots where the group has no identifiable majority position (tie) are removed from the calculation. For rankings and search, a minimum threshold of {min} final votes held during the term is applied to avoid noisy rates. Non-attached members belong to no group: with no group position to follow, they have no loyalty rate and appear in neither the averages nor the rankings.
answerLoyaute.methodologySource: NA / Senate comparison — Both chambers are measured on the votes that settle a bill's fate: in the National Assembly, the three forms of final vote; in the Senate, the vote on the text as a whole and the adopted motions that reject it. Each also publishes its other public votes. The sources remain distinct, each chamber's own open data, and their calendars differ: the figures should not be read down to a tenth of a point.
answerLoyaute.methodologyLimit: Limitations — Loyalty measures alignment with the group's majority position, nothing more. It does not distinguish strict voting discipline from natural agreement. It does not measure positions on amendments, floor speeches, or committee work. Read these rates as an indicator of visible cohesion, not as a measure of political commitment.

answerAmendements.conceptsTitle: WHAT TO KNOW BEFORE READING THE NUMBERS
answerAmendements.conceptPerimetreBody: Only enacted laws whose bill was tabled since 18 July 2024 and that received at least one recorded amendment are counted. Laws enacted since then on an older bill are set aside: amendments tabled at the National Assembly under the previous legislature are not in our data. Bills still under examination are excluded, as their figures are provisional.
answerAmendements.conceptAmendementBody: A proposed change to a bill during its parliamentary journey. It may add, delete, or rewrite one or more articles.
answerAmendements.conceptQuiDeposeBody: Any MP or senator, as well as the Government. Government amendments are included in the totals per text.
answerAmendements.conceptAdopteBody: The vast majority of amendments are not adopted: many are rejected at the vote, others are withdrawn, ruled inadmissible or fall without being examined.
answerAmendements.conceptNavetteBody: A bill may go back and forth between the National Assembly and the Senate (navette). The figures here cumulate amendments from all readings.
answerAmendements.heroDesc: Scope: {count} enacted laws whose bill was tabled since the start of the 17th legislature (July 2024), with at least one recorded amendment
answerAmendements.heroNote: All three metrics include every enacted law whose bill was tabled since July 2024 and that received at least one recorded amendment — including finance laws (State budget, social security budget, amending budget). Amendments tabled at the National Assembly and Senate are counted together per law, without distinguishing the chamber.
answerAmendements.barDescDepose: Total amendments tabled, by type of enacted law (excluding finance laws)
answerAmendements.barNote: Population: enacted laws whose bill was tabled since 18 July 2024, with at least one amendment, grouped by procedure type, excluding finance laws (State budget, social security budget, amending budget).
answerAmendements.barFinancieresDesc: Budget texts alone account for {pctFinancieres}% of all amendments in scope
answerAmendements.barFinancieresNote: These laws are excluded from the charts above: their amendment volume is structurally incomparable to ordinary laws. Only the State budgets exceed ten thousand amendments per text; the social security budgets draw several thousand, and end-of-year amending finance laws a few hundred. Finance laws follow a procedure under calendar constraints that mechanically generates a massive influx of amendments.
answerAmendements.boxDesc: Spread between the most and least amended texts, by procedure type (excluding finance laws)
answerAmendements.boxNote: Population: enacted laws whose bill was tabled since 18 July 2024, with at least one amendment, grouped by procedure type (types with at least 5 laws). Finance laws (State budget, social security budget, amending budget) are excluded — their exceptional volume (over ten thousand amendments for a State budget) would crush the scale and hide variation among ordinary laws. The box represents the central 50% of laws (Q1 to Q3), the vertical line the median, the dot the mean.
answerAmendements.groupeTotalDesc: Total amendments tabled on these enacted laws, by the group of their author on the day of tabling
answerAmendements.groupeTotalNote: Data: amendments on the laws in the scope above, placed in the group their author belonged to on the day of tabling, even if they have since changed group. Those from the Government, from committees, those whose author is not published and those whose author had no group that day are not shown. NA = National Assembly · Senate = Senate · NA+S = group present in both chambers. Non-attached members, who do not form a political group, appear as a grey bar placed after the groups, outside any ranking.
answerAmendements.groupeMoyTitle: Average amendments tabled per member, by political group
answerAmendements.groupeMoyDesc: Amendments tabled on these laws by each group, divided by its number of serving members today (groups of at least 5 members): removes the size effect to compare individual activity
answerAmendements.groupeMoyNote: Example: a GDR MP tables on average {gdrMoy} amendments on these laws, vs {lrMoy} for an LR senator. The calculation divides by the group's current headcount, so a member who joined or left since tabling skews it slightly. Opposition groups structurally table more amendments per head: it is their main lever to influence a bill without the votes to pass it. Non-attached members, who do not form a political group, appear as a grey bar placed after the groups, outside any ranking.
answerAmendements.top10Desc: Enacted laws that received the most amendments, among those whose bill was tabled since 18 July 2024
answerAmendements.top10Note: Population: enacted laws whose bill was tabled since 18 July 2024, with at least one amendment. The rate per text is the ratio of adopted to tabled amendments for that law.
answerAmendements.methodologyPerimeter: Scope — Only enacted laws whose bill was tabled since 18 July 2024 and that received at least one recorded amendment are retained. This is a caveat: since 15 September 2026, the other pages about laws count every law enacted since 18 July 2024, whatever the date its bill was tabled. This page cannot, because amendments tabled at the National Assembly under the 16th legislature are not in our data: a law whose bill predates July 2024 would be undercounted. Bills still under examination are excluded: their figures are provisional and skew averages.
answerAmendements.methodologyCalcul: Calculation — The overall adoption rate is the ratio of total adopted amendments to total tabled amendments across the full scope. The median per law is the number of amendments tabled on the middle law, once laws are ranked from least to most amended: unlike an average, it is not moved by an outlier.
answerAmendements.methodologyChambres: Chambers — Amendments tabled at the National Assembly and Senate are combined into a single total per law: this page does not show a breakdown by chamber.
answerAmendements.methodologyLimit: Limitation — A three-word amendment and an amendment that restructures an entire article are counted the same way. The count measures volume of changes, not their scope.
answerAmendements.methodologyNavette: Shuttle — For a law that went through the shuttle procedure, amendments from all readings are cumulated. A heavily debated law may therefore show high figures reflecting multiple back-and-forth exchanges between the two chambers.

promptsIA.pageMetaDesc: The seven uses of AI on LoiClair, from bill summaries to the newsletter: their exact instructions, settings and models.
promptsIA.introBody: An AI writes part of the texts on LoiClair, such as bill and debate summaries or the newsletter. It does not compute any figures. Here is what we ask of it, word for word, and how it works.
promptsIA.introNote: Nothing is hidden: this page reflects the actual code, which you can browse directly on <github>GitHub</github>.

resumeLoi.title: Legislative text summary
resumeLoi.usedOn: When a visitor opens a text's page (the “AI Summary” tab), the AI writes — if it hasn't already — a clear four-part summary: the text's objective, its main measures, concrete examples, and the key takeaway. The summary is then cached, and is only rewritten if the instructions or the model change. The goal: to understand a law without reading the full official document, which is often long and technical.

debatsReduce.title: Debate synthesis
debatsReduce.usedOn: From the official transcripts of floor debates, the AI distils a three-part synthesis: an overview, the arguments in favour of the text, and the arguments against. This gives a quick view of where political groups disagree, without reading hours of debate. The synthesis appears on each dossier page, in the “The debate” section of the “AI Summary” tab.

promptsIA.usedInSearch: These instructions produce the short card of a dossier: a summary and one to three themes, written only once, based primarily on the text as tabled by its authors. The summary appears as is in the newsletter's “Dossier spotlight” section, whose AI it also guides, and the site's search finds a dossier from the words in its title, its themes and this summary. meta.title: AI Act compliance — LoiClair
meta.description: LoiClair's compliance with the EU AI Act: role, risk level, obligations and timeline.

card1.label: Deployer
card1.desc: LoiClair deploys third-party AI systems to generate summaries.

card2.label: Limited risk
card2.desc: Our AI system does not fall under the high-risk categories defined in Annex III.

card3.label: Transparency
card3.desc: Our transparency obligations (Article 50) have applied since 2 August 2026.

aiact.title: What is the AI Act?
aiact.p1: The EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689) is the first horizontal regulatory framework for artificial intelligence in the European Union. It entered into force on 1 August 2024 and applies in stages, on a timeline amended in 2026 by the Digital Omnibus on AI (see the timeline below).
aiact.p2: It applies to all organisations — whether providers (those who develop AI systems) or deployers (those who integrate them into their products) — that use AI in a context affecting EU users.

role.title: LoiClair's role
role.intro: LoiClair uses AI in two distinct capacities:

provider.title: Provider role
provider.desc: LoiClair designs and publishes instructions, parameters and formatting rules that determine the structure and content of generated summaries. In this respect, LoiClair can be considered a provider of an AI system.

deployer.title: Deployer role
deployer.desc: LoiClair integrates and calls the APIs of two third-party AI providers, Mammouth and Anthropic, to generate summaries displayed to users. In this respect, LoiClair acts as a deployer of third-party AI systems.

risque.title: Risk level
risque.intro: The AI Act classifies AI systems into four risk levels. LoiClair falls under:
risque.desc: Our system generates informational summaries of public legislative texts. It does not make decisions about individuals, does not handle sensitive data, and does not fall under any high-risk category defined in Annex III of the AI Act (biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, essential services, law enforcement, migration, justice).
risque.tableIntro: The AI Act classifies AI systems into four risk levels:

rows.desc: Behavioural manipulation, social scoring, mass facial recognition. Not applicable to LoiClair.
AI influencing elections, criminal justice, employment. Not applicable: LoiClair informs without influencing votes.
AI generating text to inform the public. This is LoiClair's category.

risque.quizSansIa: The political affinity quiz's calculation does not use AI: it compares the user's answers with the groups' positions in the votes. AI plays a part upstream: it sorts dossiers by theme, and the quiz relies on these themes to offer votes on a range of topics, and shows these themes on each question.

obligations.title: Our obligations
obligations.intro: As a deployer of a limited-risk AI system, LoiClair must:
obligations.articleIntro: Article 50 of the AI Act concerns transparency. It applies to any deployer of an AI system that generates text intended to inform the public on matters of general interest — which includes LoiClair's legislative summaries.

items.title: Visible disclosure
items.desc: Clearly indicate to the user that content was generated by AI (human-readable).

items.title: Machine-readable marking
items.desc: Mark generated content in a format detectable by other systems. LoiClair implements <meta> tags in the <head> of each summary page (ai-generated, ai-model, ai-provider).

items.title: Clear and immediate information
items.desc: The information must be given clearly and distinctly, at the latest when the reader is first exposed to the content.

obligations.warning: These obligations have applied since 2 August 2026.

conformite.title: Our compliance measures
conformite.etiquetteDesc: Every summary carries the notice “Generated by AI”, clickable, leading to the page that details the instructions and parameters used. Dossier themes, picked by AI from a closed list of {nbThemes}, do not carry this notice: they are a classification, not written text.
conformite.promptsDesc: The exact instructions given to the AI are published on a dedicated page. Any citizen can read how the AI was guided.
conformite.parametresDesc: The model used, temperature, maximum token count, and input character limit are displayed publicly and update automatically.
conformite.neutraliteDesc: The law summary instructions say “You are direct, concrete, and neutral.” and impose four parts: objective, main measures, concrete examples, key takeaway.
conformite.temperatureDesc: Temperature sets how much randomness the model uses: the lower it is, the fewer liberties it takes with the source text. It is {resumeLoi, number} for law summaries, {cc, number} for Constitutional Council decisions and {debats, number} for the debate synthesis. The weekly newsletter, which is more written, uses {newsletter, number}. The short dossier card keeps the default value of its model, Claude Haiku 5.5, which accepts no other.
conformite.sourceDesc: Every summary includes a direct link to the official text published on institutional websites (National Assembly, Senate, Government).

timeline.title: Regulatory timeline
timeline.entreeVigueurDetail: Regulation 2024/1689 enters into force. Its obligations then apply in stages.
timeline.interdictionsDetail: Prohibited AI practices (social scoring, manipulation, certain uses of biometrics) are banned.
timeline.gpaiDetail: Obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models, such as those LoiClair uses, and the governance rules apply.
timeline.transparenceDetail: The regulation applies as a whole, including Article 50 on transparency, which concerns LoiClair. The rules for high-risk systems, however, are postponed.
timeline.hautRisqueDetail: Originally due on 2 August 2026, the rules for Annex III high-risk systems were postponed to 2 December 2027 by the Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation 2026/1744), in force since 27 July 2026. Those for regulated products under Annex I will apply on 2 August 2028.

confidentialite.pageDescription: How LoiClair collects, uses and protects your personal data.
confidentialite.section1Body: LoiClair is published by the LoiClair association, a non-profit registered under the French law of 1901 (RNA W751286466), headquartered at 104 rue de Richelieu, 75002 Paris, France, whose mission is to make the French legislative process accessible to everyone. The association acts as data controller within the meaning of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR).
confidentialite.section2NewsletterBody: When you subscribe to the newsletter, we collect only your email address. It is used solely to send the LoiClair newsletter. The legal basis is explicit consent, obtained through a double opt-in mechanism.
confidentialite.section2NavigationCookie: No tracking cookies and no advertising tools are used. The only cookies set are strictly necessary and enable no tracking. NEXT_LOCALE, set when you switch language, remembers that choice for one year at most. cf_clearance, set by Cloudflare when you open the page of an elected official or a bill, remembers for a limited time (one day at most) that the anti-bot check succeeded, so you are not asked again on every page. During that check, Cloudflare may also set technical cookies (cf_chl_rc_i, cf_chl_rc_ni, cf_chl_rc_m) that help it spot its own incidents.
confidentialite.section2NavigationAudience: Analytics and performance monitoring (Cloudflare Web Analytics), with no cookies and no storage in your browser, count pages viewed, referring site, country, device type, browser, its operating system and page load speed, in order to gauge traffic. No profile is built, no cross-site tracking takes place, and these measurements are never cross-referenced with the newsletter subscriber list. The legal basis is the legitimate interest (article 6.1.f GDPR) in measuring the audience and performance of a free service.
confidentialite.section2NavigationLogs: In addition, Cloudflare processes your IP address in the technical logs needed to deliver pages and protect the site against abuse. The site's server, hosted by OVHcloud, also receives it with each request, as does Upstash, to cap the number of requests a single address can send (see section 4).
confidentialite.section3Body: A newsletter subscriber's address is kept until they unsubscribe, then deleted from the database at once. It disappears from backups when they expire, after about thirty days. A subscription that is never confirmed is deleted within three days: the confirmation link is only valid for 48 hours. If Resend ever refuses to delete an address, the deletion is retried automatically before the next newsletter is sent.
confidentialite.section4Intro: Data is never sold, transferred or shared for commercial purposes. The following processors are involved, strictly within the scope of their duties:
confidentialite.section4ResendDetail: Your email address is passed to Resend to deliver the newsletter, as are the email address and message of a report, and the content of a membership request, so that they reach us. Once a subscription is confirmed, the email address is also stored as a contact at Resend, which sends the newsletter, and stays there until you unsubscribe. Hosted in the United States, covered by the Standard Contractual Clauses (SCC) approved by the European Commission.
confidentialite.section4CloudflareDetail: All site traffic passes through the Cloudflare network, which processes the IP address and request metadata to deliver pages and block attacks. Before showing the page of an elected official or a bill, Cloudflare may also check that the visitor is not an automated scraper, and then sets the cf_clearance cookie (see section 2). Turnstile, used on the forms (newsletter, unsubscribe, problem report, membership) to tell a human from a bot, also receives the IP address. Cloudflare also provides analytics and performance monitoring (Cloudflare Web Analytics), with no cookie, through a small script it adds to the pages (see section 2). Cloudflare also stores the daily database backups, including the subscriber list (R2 service). Cloudflare also forwards emails sent to the loiclair.fr domain to our mailbox (see Proton Mail). Cloudflare is a US company; transfers are covered by the Standard Contractual Clauses (SCC).
confidentialite.section4GithubDetail: The LoiClair source code is hosted on GitHub. The automation pipelines (GitHub Actions) use database access secrets to synchronise legislative data. GitHub can therefore access subscriber data indirectly through those credentials. Reports and suggestions sent from the site are published there as public issues, without the email address.
confidentialite.section5Body: The site's server and its database are hosted in the United States by OVH US LLC, which participates in the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework. This transfer relies on the adequacy decision adopted by the European Commission on 10 July 2023, pursuant to article 45 GDPR. This choice reflects what was available when the service went live: OVHcloud's servers in Europe were out of stock. We plan to move the server and its database to the European Union as soon as an equivalent offer becomes available there. Other providers (notably Resend, Cloudflare, GitHub, Upstash, OpenAI, OpenRouter and Anthropic) are US companies and may process data outside the European Union. These transfers are covered by Standard Contractual Clauses (SCC) adopted by the European Commission, pursuant to article 46 GDPR.
confidentialite.section6Intro: Under the GDPR, you have the following rights:
confidentialite.section6AccesDesc: obtain a copy of the data concerning you
confidentialite.section6RectificationDesc: have inaccurate or incomplete data corrected
confidentialite.section6EffacementDesc: request deletion of your data (or use the unsubscribe link in every email)
confidentialite.section6PortabiliteDesc: receive your data in a structured, interoperable format
confidentialite.section6OppositionDesc: object to the processing of your data
confidentialite.section6RetraitDesc: withdraw your consent at any time, without retroactive effect
confidentialite.section6Exercer: To exercise your rights, send your request to <mail>contact@loiclair.fr</mail>. We undertake to reply within one month.
confidentialite.section6Portabilite: To exercise your right to portability, email contact@loiclair.fr with the subject “Data export request”. Within one month we will send you the data concerning you (email, subscription date) in a readable format (JSON).
confidentialite.section7Body: You have the right to lodge a complaint with the competent supervisory authority: the Commission nationale de l'informatique et des libertés (CNIL), 3 place de Fontenoy — TSA 80715 — 75334 Paris Cedex 07 — cnil.fr.
confidentialite.section8Body: Appropriate technical and organisational measures are in place to protect data against unauthorised access, loss or alteration. Access to the systems is restricted and providers are selected for their security guarantees.
confidentialite.section9Body: This policy may be updated to reflect legal or technical developments. The date of the last update appears at the top of the document. Any substantial change will be notified to subscribers through the newsletter.
confidentialite.section2ElusBody: LoiClair publishes information under their own names about three groups of people: sitting members of parliament, members of the Government, and former members of the National Assembly and the Senate whom the National Assembly's archives still publish. For each: identity, date and place of birth (only the age is displayed), declared occupation, mandates and political groups, along with the contact details published by the chambers (email address, telephone, social media). For the period in which they sat: votes, floor speeches, questions, committee attendance. For sitting members of parliament, this also includes their declared interests, the gifts and trips they have declared, the bills they step away from over a conflict of interest, and their local mandates. For members of the National Assembly who left their seat during the legislature, the gifts, trips and recusals that the Assembly's register still publishes remain displayed. This information is made public by the institutions themselves, on account of the exercise of an elected mandate or a government office. Items in a declaration that concern a member's relatives are never reproduced, including a spouse's occupation: the law requires it to be declared, but the High Authority for Transparency in Public Life masks it in what it publishes, and LoiClair does not reproduce it.
confidentialite.section2ElusSources: It is not collected from the representatives themselves but taken from public sources: the open data of the National Assembly and the Senate, the Ministry of the Interior's national register of elected officials, the High Authority for Transparency in Public Life, the ethics registers of both chambers, and Wikidata to find each representative's Wikipedia article. Every page of the site names the source it relies on.
confidentialite.section2ElusBase: The legal basis for this processing is the performance of a task carried out in the public interest (Article 6(1)(e) GDPR): making legislative activity understandable to citizens. As the data is not collected from the data subjects, this section serves as the information required by Article 14 GDPR.
confidentialite.section3Elus: Public information about elected representatives follows a different rhythm: it is refreshed every day from the official sources. Anything a source stops publishing is removed on the next pass, with one exception: a former representative's page stays online (see section 2).
confidentialite.section6Elus: These rights also apply to information published about elected representatives, with one limit: data whose publication is required by law cannot be erased on request. An error should first be corrected with the institution that published it, as LoiClair picks up the correction automatically. Write to us if any information looks inaccurate.
confidentialite.section2SignalementBody: The report form publishes your message, the report type and, if you provide it, the page concerned in a public GitHub issue. The address of the page you are on is not sent. Your email address, which is optional, is never published: Resend passes it to contact@loiclair.fr solely so we can reply to you. The legal basis is your consent, given by filling in this optional field.
confidentialite.section3Signalement: An email address left with a report is kept for the duration of the exchange, and deleted no later than 12 months after the last message.
confidentialite.section4UpstashDetail: To prevent abuse, the number of requests a single IP address sends to the forms and to several site features (AI summaries, view counters, feedback on the site) is recorded at Upstash. The IP address is the key of that counter, which deletes itself at the end of the rate-limiting window, no later than 48 hours after the request. Upstash is a US company.
confidentialite.section4MammouthDetail: Official legislative texts and public debate transcripts are sent to Mammouth AI, a French company, which has them summarized by OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna model, sometimes through OpenRouter, a routing service. Those transcripts carry the names of the members of parliament who spoke, as their chamber publishes them; no data about site visitors is passed on. According to Mammouth, these texts are not used to train any model and are not kept more than 30 days by the model provider. OpenAI is a US company: the texts may be processed outside the European Union.
confidentialite.section2AdhesionBody: A membership request, made through the site's form, reaches us by email at contact@loiclair.fr without being kept on the site. It contains your name, your email address, what you would like to do for the association and your answer about any elected office, role in a political party or representation of interests. That last answer may reveal a political opinion: it is only processed with your explicit consent, given by ticking the box provided, and used solely to preserve the neutrality of the association, which carries out its activity on a non-partisan basis (article 2 of the articles of association). This information is used to review the request and, if you are admitted, to keep the register of members and invite you to general meetings. Only members of the board can access it.
confidentialite.section3Adhesion: A rejected membership request is deleted three months after the decision. A member's data is kept for as long as they remain a member, then deleted.
confidentialite.section4ProtonDetail: Emails sent to contact@loiclair.fr and admin@loiclair.fr, including membership requests, reports that leave an address and messages written to us, are forwarded by Cloudflare to a Proton Mail mailbox, which stores them encrypted. Proton is a Swiss company; Switzerland benefits from an adequacy decision of the European Commission.
confidentialite.section2ElusDuree: A representative's page stays online after their term ends, with no time limit: their public activity is part of the history of the bills they voted on or championed, and the chambers keep it themselves. Only representatives currently in office appear in the site's directory and search. Declarations of interests, on the other hand, are removed as soon as the parliamentary term ends, and local mandates at the next weekly update. Gifts, trips and recusals follow the register of the chamber that publishes them: the Senate's keeps only sitting senators, while the National Assembly's keeps every member of the current legislature, including those who have left their seat.
confidentialite.section4AnthropicRole: AI-written short dossier cards and “What affects me”
confidentialite.section4AnthropicDetail: The official legislative texts of dossiers, their articles and their adopted amendments are sent to Anthropic, whose Claude Haiku 5.5 model writes each dossier's short card (summary and themes), translates its title, those of published laws and those of votes into English and says which reader situations each article affects. What you tick on “What affects me” stays in your browser and is never sent. No data about site visitors is passed on. According to Anthropic, data sent through its API is not used to train its models and is deleted within 30 days. Anthropic is a US company: the texts may be processed outside the European Union.
confidentialite.section2NavigationPortraits: Portraits of members of Parliament are not copied onto LoiClair: your browser loads them directly from the National Assembly and Senate websites, which then receive your IP address and the portrait requested, as on a visit to their own sites. This also applies to the “Write to my elected officials about this bill” band on a bill page, which shows the officials found from the postcode or country you entered. That postcode, that country and those officials stay in your browser: LoiClair never receives them.
confidentialite.section2NavigationLogos: Likewise, on a bill page, the small logos of cited news outlets are loaded from a Google service (gstatic.com), which then receives your IP address and the name of the outlet's website.
confidentialite.section2NavigationStockage: Some settings and markers stay in your browser: LoiClair does not receive them and does not use them to track you. In its local storage: the light or dark theme, the representatives found through “My representatives”, the situations ticked on “What affects me”, your quiz results, the fact that you have already given feedback on the site (the feedback itself reaches us, stored with nothing that identifies you), and the sections you collapsed on detail pages. For the duration of the visit only, the site also keeps your position in lists, the “My representatives” filter and the pages already counted as viewed, so that each page is counted only once per visit. Finally, the search index is stored in your browser (IndexedDB) so that search answers instantly. All of this is erased when you clear the site's data in your browser.
confidentialite.section4OvhDetail: The site and its PostgreSQL database, which holds the newsletter subscriber list, are hosted on a server rented from OVH US LLC (OVHcloud), in a data centre in Virginia, United States. The association administers this server itself; OVHcloud provides the machine and the network. The email address of confirmed subscribers is also copied to Resend (see above). The transfer to the United States is covered by the Data Privacy Framework (see section 5).

quiz.methodBody: Each month, 20 National Assembly votes are picked using fixed rules. Seven major votes are always included, chosen by hand so that the country's main debates are there: assisted dying, security and administrative detention, repealing the pension reform, the 2026 state budget and social security budget, the fight against drug trafficking, and the emergency farming law. A program fills in the rest: it leaves out votes where every group voted the same way, first covers twelve major topics among the dossiers' themes (police and security, employment, budget, economy and finance, social affairs and health, environment, energy, justice, education, agriculture, housing, defence), prefers solemn votes, scheduled in advance, then those that best tell the groups apart. The same text never appears twice.

answerBudgetAssemblee.pageTitle: How much did the National Assembly cost in 2025, and where did the money go?
answerBudgetAssemblee.pageDescription: The National Assembly's 2025 budget explained simply: where the money comes from, what it pays for, how MPs use their expenses, who audits them and what remains out of sight.
answerBudgetAssemblee.shortAnswer: In {annee}, the National Assembly spent <hl>{depense}</hl>, about <hl>{parHabitant}</hl> per inhabitant over the year, or <hl>{parMois}</hl> a month. Its staff take up <hl>{personnel}</hl> of that spending, MPs' assistants <hl>{collaborateurs}</hl> and pensions <hl>{retraites}</hl>. MPs' allowances alone account for <hl>{indemnites}</hl>. Its TV channel, LCP-Assemblée nationale, is not counted: the State funds it through a separate line of its budget, <hl>{chaine}</hl> in 2025, bringing the full cost to <hl>{complet}</hl>.
answerBudgetAssemblee.heroDesc: Expenditure actually paid during the year, according to the Assembly's accounts as certified by the Court of Audit.
answerBudgetAssemblee.heroDeficit: deficit: the Assembly spent more than it received
answerBudgetAssemblee.conceptsTitle: Worth knowing before reading the numbers
answerBudgetAssemblee.conceptPerimetreTitle: Which budget are we talking about?
answerBudgetAssemblee.conceptPerimetreBody: The institution's own budget: what it takes to run the Assembly, pay MPs, their teams and the staff, and maintain the buildings. Not the State budget MPs vote on every autumn, which runs into hundreds of billions. Not counted here: public funding for political parties, paid by the State (the political groups funded by this budget are the groups of MPs within the Assembly), the Senate, which has its own budget, and the LCP-Assemblée nationale channel, which receives its own State funding: {lcp} in 2025, according to the <plf2026>Senate finance committee report</plf2026>. The figures come from the <comptes>Assembly's official accounts</comptes>.
answerBudgetAssemblee.conceptCircuitTitle: Voted, paid, spent: three different figures
answerBudgetAssemblee.conceptCircuitBody: Every year, three amounts coexist. The voted budget is a forecast: {vote} for 2025. The allocation is what the State actually pays: {verse}. The Assembly first asked for {demande}, then gave up that increase to contribute to the budget effort. Expenditure is what was actually paid: {depense}. To compare two years, always compare the same one of the three.
answerBudgetAssemblee.conceptCollaborateursTitle: Assistants and staff: two different worlds
answerBudgetAssemblee.conceptCollaborateursBody: Assistants work for an MP, who hires and dismisses them personally; the Assembly only pays their salary. Staff, civil servants and contract staff, work for the institution itself. Each group's numbers are set out in "Who works at the Assembly".
answerBudgetAssemblee.conceptDissolutionBody: The June 2024 dissolution forced the dismissal of every MP's assistants, including those of re-elected MPs, and meant paying both outgoing and incoming MPs for a month. Its final cost was {cout}. Any comparison between 2024 and 2025 is skewed as a result: a drop in 2025 may simply mean a return to normal.
answerBudgetAssemblee.resourcesDesc: Almost all of it comes from the State; the rest comes from some own revenue and a deficit.
answerBudgetAssemblee.ressourcePropres: Own revenue: insurance payouts, social security reimbursements, sums returned by MPs, rentals and sales
answerBudgetAssemblee.resourcesDeficitNote: How was this {deficit} deficit paid for? Not by dipping into the Assembly's savings. First, the State allocation is invested until it is spent, and these investments earned {placements} in interest in 2025: this interest is not counted as budget revenue, but it adds to the Assembly's cash. Second, according to the <commission>special committee's report</commission>, the Quaestors said that payment of some end-of-year expenses could be pushed back to the following year.
answerBudgetAssemblee.sectionPostes: Where the money goes, item by item
answerBudgetAssemblee.postesIntro: The official report sorts spending by accounting category, which scatters a single topic across several lines. For example, IT appears there twice: {invest} of investment in one chapter, {prestations} of services in another. Recounted line by line, with small equipment, telephony and website hosting, it costs {total}. Here, each budget line is sorted by what it pays for. Open an item to see its breakdown.

personnel.desc: The {fonctionnaires} civil servants and {contractuels} contract staff who run the institution, presented below in "Who works at the Assembly". This item is not the report's "staff" chapter. What the Assembly pays into its civil servants' pension fund, its employer share and a balancing grant ({caisse}), is taken out: it is the "Staff pension fund" line of the "Pensions" item. The canteen, temporary staff and payroll taxes, filed elsewhere in the report, are added in. Pension contributions for contract staff, who are not covered by that fund, stay here.

collaborateurs.desc: Each MP's envelope 2 ({credit} a month in 2025, with unused sums carried over from month to month), plus what the Assembly pays on top. In 2025, {surCredit} of salaries and bonuses were paid from that allowance, and {enPlus} on top: employer contributions, payroll tax, seniority bonus, end-of-term dismissals and travel. {contrats} contracts were running at the end of 2025.

retraites.desc: What the budget pays into the Assembly's own two pension funds, for former MPs and for its former civil servants: its employer share and a balancing grant, because contributions are not enough to cover the pensions. Historical pensions go to former members of the Assembly of the French Union, abolished in 1958, and to former temporary employees.

fraisMandat.desc: Each MP's envelopes 1 and 3, explained in the expenses section. Envelope 1: the office expense allowance paid to the MP and the material allowance, whose invoices the Assembly paid. Envelope 3: air and rail tickets, and accommodation in Paris, with {loyers} MPs having their rent reimbursed and {nuits} hotel nights.

deputes.desc: MPs' parliamentary allowances, their social security, and back-to-work support, the equivalent of unemployment benefit for former MPs. An MP who is not re-elected and is looking for work receives {allocation} gross a month, 57% of the allowance, cut by 30% from the seventh month for those under 55, for 18 months at most, and up to 27 months from age 57. A fund pays it from a contribution by sitting MPs, {cotisation} a month, and the Assembly covers the shortfall: that is the "Back-to-work support" line below. {allocataires} former MPs were receiving it at the end of 2025.

batiments.desc: The Palais Bourbon and the neighbouring buildings: renovation works, routine maintenance, rent and energy. The largest project in 2025 is the renovation of the Colbert wing of the Palais Bourbon.

groupes.desc: A monthly grant to each of the eleven groups, which employ their own staff, and an allowance for their IT equipment.

informatique.desc: Maintenance, computers, licences and cloud, including the sovereign cloud "Bleu" launched in 2025. Not counted here: the salaries of the Assembly's IT staff, included under staff, and the equipment MPs buy out of their own expenses.

fonctionnement.desc: Vehicles, supplies, furniture, insurance and printing, as well as meals for the Republican Guard officers who provide security at the Palace.

activite.desc: Travel and receptions linked to MPs' work: delegations to international assemblies, friendship groups, committee missions and inquiry committees.

communication.desc: Filming and broadcasting the sittings, and informing the public.

patrimoine.desc: Documentation, subscriptions and the upkeep of the collections: artworks, books and antiques.

sousPostes.retourEmploi: Back-to-work support for former MPs (unemployment equivalent)
sousPostes.salairesCredit: Salaries and bonuses paid from the assistants' allowance
sousPostes.dotationMaterielle: Material allowance: mail, taxis, printing, equipment

answerBudgetAssemblee.controleDesc: From voting the budget to auditing each MP's expenses.
answerBudgetAssemblee.controleDeputes: outgoing MPs audited after the dissolution
answerBudgetAssemblee.controleRestitues: returned by MPs because it was not spent
answerBudgetAssemblee.controleReversements: claimed back from {deputes} MPs for wrongly charged expenses
answerBudgetAssemblee.controleMotifs: After the audit, {demandes} MPs had to provide explanations. Two thirds of the repayments claimed correct accounting mistakes about which parliamentary term an item belonged to; about 10% concern spending unrelated to the mandate, mostly legal fees.
answerBudgetAssemblee.controleExemple: Serious abuse has been found. In 2025, one MP repaid about {montant} of taxis, clothing, restaurant meals for their children or manicures, and {exclusions} MPs were temporarily suspended for misusing their allowance between 2022 and 2024.
answerBudgetAssemblee.retraitesCouverture: MPs' contributions cover only {couvDeputes} of former MPs' pensions ({pensions} for {beneficiaires} beneficiaries). Adding the contribution the Assembly pays as an employer, coverage reaches about {couvTotale}, the rate the reports quote. The budget pays the rest.
answerBudgetAssemblee.retraitesEngagements: No savings are set aside for these pensions. Rights already earned amount to {deputes} for former MPs and {personnel} for former civil servants, according to the <etatsFinanciers>financial statements</etatsFinanciers>, or about {annees} years of the Assembly's spending: what it will have to pay over the coming decades, out of future budgets.
answerBudgetAssemblee.historiqueDesc: Actual spending, and surplus or deficit, for each year. {deficits} of the {annees} years ended in deficit: over the six years, spending exceeded revenue by {cumul} in total. This pace is what raises fears that reserves will run out around {epuisement} (see "What lies ahead for the Assembly").
answerBudgetAssemblee.methodologyPerimetre: Scope: the spending actually paid by the National Assembly in 2025. The figures come from the four documents published on the 2025 accounts: the <questeurs>Quaestors' report</questeurs> on budget execution, the <commission>special committee's report</commission>, the <etatsFinanciers>financial statements</etatsFinanciers> and the <certification>Court of Audit's certification report</certification>, supplemented by the <deontologue>ethics officer's report</deontologue> for office expenses. The pension and social security funds keep their own accounts: only what the budget pays into them is counted. The cost per inhabitant divides spending by the population on 1 January 2026, 69.1 million people according to <insee>INSEE's demographic report</insee>.
answerBudgetAssemblee.methodologyDecoupage: Breakdown: each item of the execution table is assigned to a single category, according to what it pays for. Three items mix several topics and are split using the detailed tables of the Quaestors' report: MPs' social contributions (former MPs' pensions, sitting MPs' social security), secretarial costs (what is paid from the assistants' allowance, what the Assembly pays on top) and material costs (material allowance, accounting fees). The full item-by-item mapping can be <csv>downloaded as CSV</csv>.
answerBudgetAssemblee.methodologyArrondis: Rounding: the items of the execution table add up to {articles}, {ecart} less than the official total of {officiel}, a rounding gap present in the report itself. Each item's share is calculated on the sum of the items and rounded to one decimal place.
answerBudgetAssemblee.methodologyLimites: Limits: salaries are not broken down by department, so the real cost of IT or buildings exceeds their category, which does not count the staff working on them.
answerBudgetAssemblee.conceptComptesTitle: Budget and accounts: two ways of counting
answerBudgetAssemblee.conceptComptesBody: The budget counts the money coming in and going out during the year: it shows a deficit of {deficit}. The accounts spread the cost of building works over several years and include investment income: they show a surplus of {resultat}. Both are correct. This page follows the budget, because it shows what was actually paid.
answerBudgetAssemblee.resourcesPlacementsNote: The Assembly also holds {reserves} in reserves, invested in a long-term fund and in bank accounts. They pay for major building works.
answerBudgetAssemblee.retraitesContractuels: The staff pension fund is less and less self-financing: excluding the subsidy, its revenue covered {couv2019} of pensions in 2019 and {couv2025} in 2025. Retiring civil servants are partly replaced by contract staff, who do not pay into this fund: they went from {part2021} of staff in 2021 to {part2025} in 2025. The balancing grant paid by the Assembly reached {subvention} in 2025, up {hausse} in a year.
answerBudgetAssemblee.groupesNote: Monthly grant multiplied by twelve, excluding payroll and accounting support and the IT equipment allowance. The amount rises with the number of MPs in the group.
answerBudgetAssemblee.dotationTitle: What each MP receives, and what the Assembly pays on their behalf
answerBudgetAssemblee.dotationDesc: Monthly amounts in 2025. The resources that come with the office fund the MP's work and do not go into their pocket. They do not all have a fixed amount: the page gives the average for the material allowance, the cost of assistants and travel, 2025 spending divided by {sieges} seats and by 12 months.
answerBudgetAssemblee.reglesTitle: Allowed or refused: what the rules say
answerBudgetAssemblee.reglesDesc: Cases settled by the ethics officer, anonymised as in his report.
answerBudgetAssemblee.regleSansJustificatif: {plafond} a week without receipts. From their office expense allowance, an MP can spend up to {plafond} a week without providing any receipt. The ethics officer proposes lowering this to {propose}; his two predecessors already proposed {avant}, in 2022 and again in 2023.
answerBudgetAssemblee.regleChant: Refused: singing lessons. An MP wanted to take them to strengthen their voice. The ethics officer sees them as a leisure activity and recommends public-speaking training instead.
answerBudgetAssemblee.regleBaguettes: Allowed: printed baguette bags. Handed out in the constituency's bakeries to announce a cycling tour, provided the operation stays one-off and limited in quantity.
answerBudgetAssemblee.regleAvocat: Refused: personal legal fees. An MP used their expenses to pay a lawyer in a dispute linked to their pre-election job, although they had been told back in 2021 that this dispute had no connection with the mandate.
answerBudgetAssemblee.regleAmitie: Mandate and private business. The ethics officer reminded an MP that a friendship-group mission paid for by the Assembly cannot be used to look after one of their companies in the country visited. In that case, the MP must at least pay part of the costs.
answerBudgetAssemblee.regleProches: Paying a relative: tolerated until now. An MP could fund a contract with themselves or a relative if they proved the link with the mandate, a market price and competing quotes. Only renting property owned by close family was banned. The ethics officer is calling for an outright ban, as for local elected officials.
answerBudgetAssemblee.reglesNote: Based on the <deontologue>ethics officer's report</deontologue> published in May 2026.
answerBudgetAssemblee.sectionControle: Who audits, and where the gaps are
answerBudgetAssemblee.controleDecision: Who decides. The budget is prepared by the three Quaestors, MPs elected by their colleagues, then adopted by the Assembly's Bureau. A committee shared by both chambers sets what the State pays them.
answerBudgetAssemblee.controleCommission: The special committee. MPs check the accounts once the year is closed and approve the Quaestors' management, in a public report.
answerBudgetAssemblee.controleCour: The Court of Audit. It has certified the accounts every year since an agreement signed in 2013. For 2025, it found them regular and fair, with {nb} recommendations.
answerBudgetAssemblee.controleDeontologue: The ethics officer. He audits how office expenses are used: every MP each year from their bank statements, and each one in detail once per parliamentary term, chosen by lot.
answerBudgetAssemblee.faillesTitle: Gaps in the audit, in examples
answerBudgetAssemblee.faillesDesc: Identified by the ethics officer, the Court of Audit and the special committee themselves.
answerBudgetAssemblee.faillePayer: An audit that can be avoided by repaying. In the past, an MP selected by lot preferred to repay the entire expense allowance received for the audited period rather than hand over their file. Ignoring a formal notice from the ethics officer has no consequence.
answerBudgetAssemblee.failleRembourser: Repaying without referral to the Speaker. The ethics officer can only refer a case to the Speaker, and open the way to a sanction, if the MP disputes it. An MP guilty of a serious and deliberate breach can therefore close the matter by repaying. The ethics officer is asking to be able to refer cases in all circumstances.
answerBudgetAssemblee.failleTirage: No selection by lot in 2025. The dissolution made it void. The ethics officer checked the balances and bank statements of every MP, but no detailed report on 2024 spending could be passed on to the Court of Audit.
answerBudgetAssemblee.failleCour: The Court certifies expenses without seeing the files. On office expenses, it can carry out "only part of the work required by auditing standards". It relies on what the ethics officer and a Quaestor declare, in a signed letter.
answerBudgetAssemblee.failleConvention: The scope of the Court's audit under discussion. The Court wants to revise the 2013 agreement. The Quaestors want to keep "the limits placed on access to certain information" and a flexible timetable, and refuse to open MPs' individual data to it. Their argument: "The Court has no business auditing MPs on how they use their expense envelope; that is the Ethics Officer's job." The special committee partly agrees, but asks for the agreement to set out each body's role more clearly.
answerBudgetAssemblee.failleAnonymisation: Too long to anonymise. The Court was able to check about a hundred anonymised expense slips. Processing all of them, {releves} slips a year, would take {jours} days of work according to the Assembly's departments, an argument put forward for not extending the practice.
answerBudgetAssemblee.failleConges: Undeclared leave. Only {part} of the leave earned by assistants shows up as taken. According to the Court, some MP-employers do not declare leave, with the risk of wrongly paying out untaken leave when assistants are dismissed.
answerBudgetAssemblee.failleAudit: Unfinished internal control. According to the Court, the Assembly's internal audit unit does not receive evidence of the checks carried out by departments, and does not run any of its own.
answerBudgetAssemblee.faillesNote: Based on the <deontologue>ethics officer's report</deontologue>, the <commission>special committee's report</commission> and the <certification>certification report</certification>.
answerBudgetAssemblee.ombreTitle: What the accounts do not show
answerBudgetAssemblee.ombreDesc: Information that is missing, only aggregated or invisible on the balance sheet.
answerBudgetAssemblee.ombreParDepute: Nothing MP by MP. No expense spending is published per MP. Only the ethics officer sees the bank statements.
answerBudgetAssemblee.ombreStatistiques: No statistics on how day-to-day expenses are used. We know the cost of air tickets because the Assembly pays those invoices itself. The allowance, however, is paid into the MP's account: its use only shows on their statements, which only the ethics officer sees, and his audit method produces no statistics by type of spending.
answerBudgetAssemblee.ombreRecommandations: The Court's recommendations stay internal. We know there are {nb} of them and what topics they cover. The details are in a report handed to the Assembly's administration, which is not published with the accounts.
answerBudgetAssemblee.ombrePatrimoine: The Palais Bourbon is worth €1 on the balance sheet. Since it cannot be valued, it is recorded at a symbolic euro, like the Hôtel de Lassay. The reserves, for their part, are invested in a fund bought for {bilan} that is now worth {reelle}: the balance sheet keeps the purchase price, so about {gain} of gains do not show up.
answerBudgetAssemblee.ombreBail: A 99-year lease. On 10 October 2025, the Assembly signed a 99-year lease for a building on the Quai Anatole-France, starting in 2027. Its off-balance-sheet commitments, spending already signed but not yet paid, rise from {avant} to {apres}. The rent is not disclosed.
answerBudgetAssemblee.ombreRegistres: Declarations that rest on each MP. Stepping aside from a vote over a conflict of interest (recusal) is left entirely to the MP's judgement, and a gift only has to be declared above €150. The result: {deports} recusals over the whole parliamentary term, {cadeaux} gift declarations in 2025, {voyages} trips paid for by third parties, including {taiwan} at the invitation of the Taiwanese government and {qatar} of the State of Qatar.
answerBudgetAssemblee.ombreErreurs: Official documents that contradict each other. The Quaestors' report gives {caisse1} and then {caisse2} for the same subsidy, a forecast deficit of {prevu1} and then {prevu2}, a share of investment appropriations spent of {inv1} and then {inv2}. On the Court's recommendations, the committee writes that this year's {nb} are "four fewer" than last year's {reco2}; the Court itself counted {reco1} last year.
answerBudgetAssemblee.sectionAvenir: What lies ahead for the Assembly
answerBudgetAssemblee.avenirTitle: The choices of the coming years
answerBudgetAssemblee.avenirDesc: Based on the report on the 2025 accounts, published in 2026.
answerBudgetAssemblee.avenirReserves: Reserves running down. The prudential floor of {plancher} could be reached within three to five years. With a deficit of about {rythme} a year, close to the one planned for 2026 ({prevu}), the reserves would run out around {annee}.
answerBudgetAssemblee.avenirTravaux: Heavy building works. The Assembly eventually wants to give every MP a double office, and the law requires it to cut its offices' energy use by 40% by 2030. It will have to invest more than the {invest} a year of recent years.
answerBudgetAssemblee.avenirAccueil: A project paused after the prefect's opinion. The new visitor entrance to the Palais Bourbon, budgeted at {projet}, was put on hold by the Assembly's Bureau in February 2026: the prefect considered that digging under a courtyard and part of the Speaker's garden breached the district's heritage protection rules, and that the building permit risked being refused. {paye} had already been paid, and the architects could claim compensation if the project is abandoned. The special committee regrets that this money was committed "without any assurance that the project would be completed".
answerBudgetAssemblee.avenirPensions: Pensions frozen. Former MPs' pensions are not uprated in 2026, saving {min} to {max} a year.
answerBudgetAssemblee.enveloppeFrais: The office expense allowance: {avance} a month in mainland France and overseas departments since May 2025 ({avant} before), {pacifique} in the Pacific and {etranger} for MPs representing French citizens abroad (Bureau decree). It is paid in full every month into a dedicated bank account, whether the MP spends it or not, and covers the constituency office, a vehicle, communication or receptions, with no breakdown of its use. Whatever is not spent builds up and is returned at the end of the term; beyond what they have received, MPs pay out of their own pocket. The May increase covers telephone and accounting costs, moved onto the allowance.
answerBudgetAssemblee.enveloppeCollaborateurs: The assistants' allowance funds assistants' gross salaries, including the thirteenth month and meal bonus. It is not a strict ceiling: whatever the MP does not use in a month carries over to the following months, until the end of the parliamentary term. Employer contributions, payroll tax and the seniority bonus are not taken from it: the Assembly pays them on top, hence the gap with the real cost. Almost all MPs leave payroll to the Assembly: it pays the salaries directly, and the MP never receives this money.
answerBudgetAssemblee.enveloppeDirecte: No fixed amount. The Assembly itself pays for air and rail tickets between Paris and the constituency, and houses in Paris the MPs who need it. In 2025, it reimbursed rent for {loyers} MPs, paid for {nuits} hotel nights when the Assembly's Residence was full, and {residence} nights at the Residence. The amount varies from one MP to another.
answerBudgetAssemblee.dotationNote: Based on the <questeurs>Quaestors' report</questeurs>, the <commission>special committee's report</commission>, the <deontologue>ethics officer's report</deontologue>, the <arrete>Bureau decree on office expenses</arrete> and the <fiche>official fact sheet on MPs' material situation</fiche>.
answerBudgetAssemblee.fraisEquipement: of which phones and IT, approximately
answerBudgetAssemblee.fraisIntro: Three of the twelve spending categories directly concern MPs: "MPs themselves", which pays their salary, "MPs' assistants" and "MPs' office expenses". This section explains how that money reaches them: one salary and three envelopes.
answerBudgetAssemblee.enveloppeFraisLabel: A month in 2025: the official allowance in mainland France and overseas departments since May ({avant} before), plus the material allowance on average.
answerBudgetAssemblee.enveloppeCollabLabel: A month on average per MP in 2025: what the Assembly actually pays, contributions and taxes included.
answerBudgetAssemblee.enveloppeDirecteTitre: Envelope 3: travel and accommodation to sit
answerBudgetAssemblee.enveloppeDirecteLabel: A month on average per MP.
answerBudgetAssemblee.postesBarreLegende: Each colour is one item, from largest to smallest, repeated on its line below. The last four items, too small to see, share a grey. Hover over or tap a segment for its details.
answerBudgetAssemblee.materielNote: Breakdown of the material allowance rounded to the nearest hundred thousand euros in the <questeurs>Quaestors' report</questeurs>, which publishes no amount MP by MP.
answerBudgetAssemblee.effectifsDesc: As of 31 December 2025. They do not have the same employer: staff work for the institution, each assistant works for an MP.
answerBudgetAssemblee.effectifsDeputes: Elected to pass laws and scrutinise the Government. The Assembly has {sieges} seats: in 2025, two elections were annulled and three MPs were declared to have resigned by the Constitutional Council, leaving seats vacant. Their pay sits under the "MPs themselves" item.
answerBudgetAssemblee.effectifsFonctionnaires: Recruited through competitive exams, they organise sittings and committees, write the official records and maintain the buildings. There were {en2017} in 2017: in 2025, {departs} left, almost all on retirement, and {entrees} joined.
answerBudgetAssemblee.effectifsContractuels: Recruited for specialised or technical posts, or when a call for applications found no one. There are {hausse} more than five years ago, and they now make up {part} of the Assembly's {agents} staff. Of the {recrutements} recruited in 2025, mostly management assistants and reception staff, {remplacements} replaced a civil servant. On top of that, {cabinet} contract staff work in the Speaker's private office, counted separately.
answerBudgetAssemblee.effectifsCollaborateurs: They do not work for the Assembly but for an MP, who hires and dismisses them personally; the Assembly pays their salary. An assistant who works for several MPs has a contract with each of them: the report counts employment contracts, not people.
answerBudgetAssemblee.effectifsRenforts: Reinforcements. {gardes} Republican Guard gendarmes and Paris firefighters are seconded to the Assembly: they account for most of the {interim} in the "Temporary and seconded staff" sub-item. The Assembly also had {apprentis} apprentices at the end of 2025 and paid {stagiaires} interns during the year.
answerBudgetAssemblee.effectifsNote: Staff figures from the <questeurs>Quaestors' report</questeurs>, pp. 52-53, 77-79, 89 and 105.
answerBudgetAssemblee.resourcesAccueilNote: The deficit is also smaller than planned because spending came in {sousPrevision} below forecast. According to the <commission>special committee</commission>, half of that gap comes from pausing the visitor entrance project: {nonDepense} of the {budgete} planned for 2025 was not spent. This is not a deliberate saving, but spending suspended along with the project.
answerBudgetAssemblee.enveloppeFraisMaterielTexte: The material allowance: {moyenne} a month on average, on top of the office expense allowance. It covers mail, printing, taxis and equipment: the Assembly pays the invoices directly or reimburses the MP against receipts, so it knows the breakdown. No amount is published MP by MP: the average divides the {total} spent in 2025 by {sieges} seats and by 12 months.
answerBudgetAssemblee.fraisInvisible: Since 2026, a single allowance, checked afterwards by the ethics officer. In 2025, we knew that {materiel} had paid for mail, printing, taxis and equipment, because the Assembly checked and paid those invoices. Since 1 January 2026, the office expense allowance and the material allowance have been merged into a single allowance, paid every month into the MP's account: {dotation} for an MP elected in mainland France, up to {horsEurope} outside Europe. This spending now follows the office expense allowance rules: MPs pay it themselves from that account, with the same no-receipt tolerance, and the ethics officer only checks it afterwards. No breakdown is therefore published any more for any day-to-day expenses: {total} a year at 2025 levels. The Quaestors reply that the reform was not meant to save money, but to meet MPs' demand for simpler expense management. The special committee also notes that the merger made all of this spending subject to the ethics officer's audit.
answerBudgetAssemblee.enveloppeCollab2026: In 2026, the allowance rises to {credit} a month, including {transfert} taken from the former material allowance.
answerBudgetAssemblee.resumeRemuneration: Gross pay, unchanged since January 2024: the parliamentary allowance, the only money that goes to an MP with no particular office. Those who hold one receive an additional allowance, from {min} a month for a Bureau secretary to {max} for the Speaker.
answerBudgetAssemblee.resumeMoyens: Operating resources, which do not go to the MP: day-to-day expenses, assistants, travel and accommodation
answerBudgetAssemblee.detailMoyens: The {total} of resources in detail, envelope by envelope
answerBudgetAssemblee.ombreRetraites: {total} of pensions kept off the balance sheet. Pension rights already earned by former MPs ({deputes}) and former civil servants ({personnel}) are not recorded on the balance sheet as a liability: the Assembly chose to disclose them only in the notes to the financial statements, and no savings are set aside to pay them.
answerBudgetAssemblee.fraisControle: Receipts, yes; publication, no. Every expense paid from the office expense allowance needs a receipt, except up to {plafond} a week. MPs keep their receipts with their accountant, and each year send the ethics officer their bank statements and a table of their expenses by category (Bureau decree). The ethics officer audits every MP at least once per parliamentary term and can ask for the receipts at any time. The audit checks that each expense is allowed, but does not add up the tables: the ethics officer writes that the method does not provide statistical data on how the expenses break down. These tables are not public: in 2019, the Council of State ruled that the Assembly did not have to disclose MPs' expense statements.
answerBudgetAssemblee.chaineHorsTotal: Outside the total: the LCP-Assemblée nationale channel
answerBudgetAssemblee.chaineHorsTotalNote: Funded through a separate line of the State budget, it is counted neither in this item nor in the total.
answerBudgetAssemblee.methodologyLecture: Reading the documents: an AI helped write the scripts that read the official documents and split their amounts into items. No amount is produced by the AI itself: each line of the breakdown can be found at its page in the <csv>downloadable CSV</csv>.
answerBudgetAssemblee.historiqueLecture: When the solid line rises above the dotted one, the chamber spent more than it received: that deficit, in red, is usually drawn from its reserves.
