answerBudgetSenat.pageTitle: How much did the Senate cost in 2025, and where did the money go?
answerBudgetSenat.pageDescription: The Senate's 2025 budget explained simply: where the money comes from, what it pays for, how senators use their expenses, who checks and what stays out of sight.
answerBudgetSenat.shortAnswer: In {annee}, the Senate spent <hl>{depense}</hl>, including the Luxembourg Garden and Museum, about <hl>{parHabitant}</hl> per inhabitant over the year, or <hl>{parMois}</hl> a month. Its staff take up <hl>{personnel}</hl> of that spending, senators' assistants <hl>{collaborateurs}</hl> and pensions <hl>{retraites}</hl>. Senators' allowances alone account for <hl>{indemnites}</hl>. Its TV channel, Public Sénat, is not counted: the State funds it through a separate line of its budget, <hl>{chaine}</hl> in 2025, bringing the full cost to <hl>{complet}</hl>.
answerBudgetSenat.heroDesc: Spending actually paid during the year by the Senate's three budgets, according to its accounts certified by the Court of Audit.
answerBudgetSenat.heroExcedent: surplus: the Senate received more than it spent
answerBudgetSenat.conceptsTitle: What to know before reading the figures
answerBudgetSenat.conceptPerimetreTitle: Which budget are we talking about?
answerBudgetSenat.conceptPerimetreBody: The Senate's three budgets: its institutional mission ({senat}), the Luxembourg Garden ({jardin}) and the Luxembourg Museum ({musee}), which the report adds up as the "Senate budget". Not the State budget that senators vote on every autumn. Not counted here: the pension and social security funds, which have their own accounts, the refreshment bars, the National Assembly, and the Public Sénat TV channel, whose {publicSenat} allocation only passes through the Senate. The figures come from the <rapport>official report on the accounts</rapport>.
answerBudgetSenat.conceptCircuitTitle: Voted, paid, spent: three different figures
answerBudgetSenat.conceptCircuitBody: The initial budget planned {initial}, raised to {reparti} at the start of the year with carried-over works. The allocation paid by the State was {verse}, the same as in 2024: the Senate gave up a {hausse} increase to contribute to the budget effort. Spending actually paid came to {depense}. To compare two years, always compare the same one of the three.
answerBudgetSenat.conceptComptesTitle: Budget and accounts: two ways of counting
answerBudgetSenat.conceptComptesBody: The budget counts the money coming in and going out during the year: it shows a {excedent} surplus. The accounts, for their part, spread the cost of works over several years and count sales of reserve investments: {charges} of expenses and a {resultat} surplus. Both are correct. This page follows the budget, because it shows what was actually paid.
answerBudgetSenat.conceptCollaborateursBody: Assistants work for a senator, who hires them, sets their pay and dismisses them. An association, AGAS, draws up their contracts and pays their salaries with Senate money: {subventionAgas} in 2025. Staff, civil servants and contract workers, work for the institution itself. Headcounts for each are detailed in "Who works at the Senate".
answerBudgetSenat.conceptRenouvellementBody: Half the seats are up for election every three years, in September 2023 and then September 2026. In those years, outgoing senators' assistants are dismissed and newly elected senators receive their IT advance: the grant to AGAS reached {agas2023} in 2023. By contrast, 2025 comes before a renewal: support for former senators without a job is at its lowest, as in every year that precedes one.
answerBudgetSenat.resourcesTitle: How the {total} of resources break down
answerBudgetSenat.resourcesDesc: Almost everything comes from the State; the rest is own revenue. The Senate did not spend it all.
answerBudgetSenat.ressourcePropres: Own revenue: fees from the Garden, the Museum and restaurants, rentals, refunds, surplus from the social security funds
answerBudgetSenat.ressourceExcedent: Surplus: not spent, returned to reserves
answerBudgetSenat.resourcesPrelevementNote: At first, the budget planned the opposite: drawing {prevu} from reserves. That drawdown "ultimately proved unnecessary", according to the <rapport>report on the accounts</rapport>: running costs and works below forecasts, {reserve} of appropriations held back to cope with the freeze, and {caisses} of surplus from the social security funds paid back into the budget, revenue never planned in advance.
answerBudgetSenat.resourcesReserveNote: These reserves make up the special intervention reserve: {reserveBilan} on the balance sheet at the end of 2025, {reserveMarche} at market value. They are used in particular to pay for works the allocation does not cover.
answerBudgetSenat.sectionPostes: Where the money goes, item by item
answerBudgetSenat.postesIntro: Since 2023, the official report only publishes accounting chapters that mix several subjects. The "Travel, missions and receptions" chapter, for example, combines senators' air tickets ({avion}), committee missions and departmental receptions. Here, each chapter is split using the detailed tables of the same report, and each piece is filed by what it pays for. Open an item to see its details.
answerBudgetSenat.postesBarreLegende: Each colour is one item, from largest to smallest, repeated on its line below. The last five items, too small to see, share a grey. Hover over or tap a segment for its details.
answerBudgetSenat.retraitesCaisses: Former senators received {pensionsSenateurs} in pensions ({pensionnes} pensioners), against {cotisationsSenateurs} in contributions, employer share included. For staff, {pensionsPersonnel} in pensions against {cotisationsPersonnel} in contributions. The two funds were therefore {deficits} short over the year. That shortfall is paid by the income and sales of their investments, outside the budget.
answerBudgetSenat.retraitesPlacements: The two funds held {marche} of investments at market value at the end of 2025. Measured against pensions already promised, they cover {couvSenateurs} for former senators and {couvPersonnel} for staff, according to the <rapport>report on the accounts</rapport>.
answerBudgetSenat.retraitesComparaison: Careful with comparisons: the National Assembly's budget pays a balancing grant to its funds every year, which counts as spending. At the Senate, the funds' deficit is paid by their investments and does not appear in the budget. Comparing the two budgets as they stand therefore flatters the Senate.
answerBudgetSenat.groupesListeTitre: 2025 grant to each group, in thousands of euros
answerBudgetSenat.groupesNote: Table from the notes to the accounts. Each group receives a fixed share, a share per member and a share that grows with its size. The groups publish their <groupes>certified accounts</groupes>.
answerBudgetSenat.jardinNote: The Garden receives its own share of the State allocation, {dotation}, and collected {concessions} in fees from its concessions, up with the reopening of the tennis courts. The Museum's fee, {redevance}, did not cover the replacement of its fire safety system. Pensions for Garden staff, {versRetraites}, are counted under "Pensions".
answerBudgetSenat.collaborateursNote: On top of the grant, the Senate provides the association with {agents} of its own staff ({coutAgents} a year) and premises ({locaux}). Leave not yet taken by assistants at the end of 2025 amounts to {conges}, which the grant will pay.
answerBudgetSenat.effectifsDesc: At 31 December 2025, except assistants. They do not have the same employer: staff depend on the institution, each assistant depends on a senator.
answerBudgetSenat.effectifsSenateurs: Elected for six years by local councillors, with half renewed every three years. They vote on laws and scrutinise the Government. Their pay is under "Senators themselves".
answerBudgetSenat.effectifsFonctionnaires: Recruited through competitive exams, civil servants organise sittings and committees and maintain the Palace. The report counts budgeted positions, meaning posts rather than people: there were {texte2024} a year earlier according to its text, {annexe2024} according to the notes to the accounts.
answerBudgetSenat.effectifsContractuels: Recruited for specialised or temporary posts, including the private office of the President of the Senate. There were {en2024} at the end of 2024.
answerBudgetSenat.effectifsCollaborateurs: At 13 September 2026, the date of the <agas>public list</agas>: the Senate publishes no figure for the end of 2025. An assistant working for two senators has two contracts: that makes {personnes} people. Each senator may employ five at most.
answerBudgetSenat.effectifsRetraites: And retirees. The budget also contributes to the pensions of {senateurs} former senators and {personnel} former Senate staff.
answerBudgetSenat.effectifsNote: Staff figures from the <rapport>report on the accounts</rapport>, pp. 58-59 and 186.
answerBudgetSenat.fraisIntro: Three of the thirteen spending items concern senators directly: "Senators themselves", which pays their salary, "Senators' assistants" and "Senators' office expenses". This section explains how that money reaches them: an allowance and three blocks of resources.
answerBudgetSenat.dotationTitle: What each senator receives, and what the Senate pays for them
answerBudgetSenat.dotationDesc: Monthly amounts in 2025. The resources that come with the office fund the senator's work and do not go into their pocket. Only the general advance has a fixed amount: for the rest, the page gives the average, 2025 spending divided by {sieges} seats and by 12 months.
answerBudgetSenat.resumeRemuneration: Gross allowance, unchanged since January 2024: the only money that goes to a senator with no particular office. Those who hold one receive an additional allowance, from {fonctionMin} a month for a Bureau secretary to {fonctionMax} for the President of the Senate.
answerBudgetSenat.resumeMoyens: Operating resources, which do not go to the senator: office expenses, assistants, travel, telephone and postage
answerBudgetSenat.remunerationDetail: Basic allowance {base}, residence allowance {residence} and office allowance {fonction}. After contributions, including pension, {nette} net remains before tax.
answerBudgetSenat.detailMoyens: The {total} of resources, block by block
answerBudgetSenat.blocFraisLabel: Per month in 2025: the general advance at its official amount, plus the specific advances on average.
answerBudgetSenat.blocFraisAvanceTexte: The general advance: {avance} a month ({avant} before 2024), plus {outreMer} for senators from overseas territories and {etranger} for those representing French citizens abroad (Quaestors' order). Paid into a dedicated account, it covers the local office, travel or communication, and every expense must be backed by a receipt online. Senators justified {depense} in 2025. Whatever is not justified is deducted from the next advance, except up to {report}, left available for the following year.
answerBudgetSenat.blocFraisSpecifiquesTexte: The specific advances: up to {hebergement} a month for accommodation in Paris, except for senators from Paris and those with an office-bedroom at the Senate, {representation} a month for certain positions, and {informatique} every three years for IT equipment. They cost {total} in 2025, the average shown for {sieges} seats.
answerBudgetSenat.fraisSansJustificatif: Up to {plafond} a year without an invoice. Part of the advance can be justified by a simple sworn statement, with no third-party document: {mensuel} a month on average, according to the Quaestors' circular. And at the end of 2025, the Senate recorded {creances} to recover, mostly advances paid during the year and not spent.
answerBudgetSenat.blocCollabLabel: Per month on average per senator in 2025: what the team really costs, contributions included.
answerBudgetSenat.blocCollabTexte: The allowance only pays gross salaries, for {max} assistants at most. It is strictly monthly: what is not used in a month cannot be carried over. Employer contributions, the thirteenth month, seniority pay, training and severance are paid on top, about half the association's budget according to the <rapport>report</rapport>. The senator never handles this money: AGAS pays the salaries.
answerBudgetSenat.blocDirecteLabel: Per month on average per senator.
answerBudgetSenat.blocDirecteTexte: No money is paid to the senator. The Senate itself pays for up to {passages} flights a year between their department and Paris, rail travel across the national network, taxis and Paris-region transport up to {taxis} a year ({taxisMax} at most depending on the office held), telephone up to {telephone} a year, and part of the postage. In all, {total} in 2025.
answerBudgetSenat.dotationNote: Based on the <rapport>report on the accounts</rapport>, the Senate factsheets on the <indemnite>parliamentary allowance</indemnite> and <moyens>resources available to senators</moyens>, the <arreteQuesture>Quaestors' order on office expenses</arreteQuesture> and the <circulaire>Quaestors' circular</circulaire>.
answerBudgetSenat.reglesTitle: Allowed or refused: what the Ethics Committee says
answerBudgetSenat.reglesDesc: Cases decided by the Committee, without names, as in its report.
answerBudgetSenat.regleSecheLinge: Advised against: a tumble dryer. A senator who owns their local office wanted to buy one with their advance. The Committee found it was not essential to running the office.
answerBudgetSenat.regleSport: Refused: a gym. A fitness centre membership cannot be paid for by the advance: everyday living expenses have no link with the mandate.
answerBudgetSenat.regleTrottinette: Refused: a vehicle for an assistant, even an e-scooter. The senator can, however, pay them a sustainable mobility allowance for commuting.
answerBudgetSenat.regleRolandGarros: Refused: Roland-Garros. An invitation from the French Tennis Federation to matches at the tournament could not be accepted: being invited as a senator is not enough to create a link with the mandate.
answerBudgetSenat.regleMicroOndes: Accepted: a microwave oven. For an office-bedroom with no kitchen area, so the senator can eat on site on sitting nights.
answerBudgetSenat.regleIA: Accepted: an artificial intelligence subscription. A chatbot to draft texts or organise trips, provided no personal or sensitive data is shared with it.
answerBudgetSenat.reglesNote: Based on the <deontologie>activity report of the Parliamentary Ethics Committee</deontologie> published in April 2026.
answerBudgetSenat.sectionControle: Who checks, and with what loopholes
answerBudgetSenat.controleDesc: From voting the budget to checking each senator's expenses.
answerBudgetSenat.controleDecision: Who decides. The budget is prepared by the Quaestors, senators elected by their colleagues, after a debate in the Senate's Bureau. A committee shared by both chambers, chaired by a judge from the Court of Audit, sets what the State pays them.
answerBudgetSenat.controleCommission: The special committee. {membres} senators, who cannot sit on the Bureau, examine the accounts, can carry out on-site and document checks, and discharge the Quaestors in a public report.
answerBudgetSenat.controleCour: The Court of Audit. It has certified the accounts since an agreement signed in 2013. For 2025, it finds them lawful and fair, with no reservation, and {nb} recommendations against {avant} a year earlier.
answerBudgetSenat.controleComite: The Ethics Committee. {membres} senators from all groups check the office expenses of all their colleagues every year, on anonymised files, with two firms of independent chartered accountants, around twenty people. These roles are unpaid.
answerBudgetSenat.controleTaux: of expenses verified, on average per senator
answerBudgetSenat.controleMethode: Checks are done by sampling: {approfondis} senators had an in-depth check and {transversaux} a lighter cross-cutting check, across {justificatifs} receipts. The most scrutinised senator had {max} of their expenses verified. The review of 2025 spending has not yet been published.
answerBudgetSenat.faillesTitle: Loopholes in the checks, with examples
answerBudgetSenat.faillesDesc: Pointed out in the official texts and reports themselves.
answerBudgetSenat.failleEntreSoi: A committee made up of senators. The Ethics Committee is made up of {membres} senators. At the National Assembly, checking expenses falls to an ethics officer who is not an MP.
answerBudgetSenat.failleMontants: No repaid amount is published. The Committee's report describes its method and anonymous cases, but says neither how many senators had to repay, nor how much. The Bureau only received an assessment: "the very large majority of senators scrupulously complied with the rules".
answerBudgetSenat.failleDirectes: {total} outside the Committee's checks. Flights, trains, taxis, telephone and postage paid directly by the Senate "are not subject to checks" by the Committee, under the Bureau's order.
answerBudgetSenat.failleSecret: Nobody else sees the receipts. The Committee is "the only third party with access to their details", and "no one may" consult summaries drawn from senators' declarations, the same order says.
answerBudgetSenat.failleCour: The Court relies on a letter. On office expenses, its certification report cites a letter signed by the chair of the Ethics Committee and the accountants, and no review of the documents, whose details the order reserves for the Committee.
answerBudgetSenat.failleQuesture: The scope of the Court's audit under discussion. In 2025, the special committee asked the Court to respect the Senate's autonomy "scrupulously" (report on the 2024 accounts), and a Quaestor told the Bureau that "it is not for the Court of Audit either to give an opinion on the use of the Senate's resources or to take part in communicating on its financial and accounting management". A year later, the committee highlighted "the continued reduction in the number of recommendations made and in their very subject".
answerBudgetSenat.faillesNote: Based on the <arreteBureau>Bureau's order on office expenses</arreteBureau>, the <deontologie>Ethics Committee's report</deontologie>, the <certification>certification report</certification> and the <bureau>minutes of the Bureau</bureau>.
answerBudgetSenat.ombreTitle: What the accounts do not show
answerBudgetSenat.ombreDesc: Information that is missing, aggregated or invisible on the balance sheet.
answerBudgetSenat.ombreParSenateur: Nothing senator by senator. No expense spending is published per senator: the rules reserve the details of receipts for the Ethics Committee alone.
answerBudgetSenat.ombrePatrimoine: The Luxembourg Palace is worth €1 on the balance sheet. The Palace, the Petit Luxembourg and the Garden are recorded at a symbolic euro, like the artworks present when the accounts were opened: only works carried out since then have a value.
answerBudgetSenat.ombrePlusValues: {latentes} of uncounted gains. The pension funds' investments were bought for {achat} and are worth {marche} at market value, including {interets} of interest receivable. The balance sheet keeps them at purchase price, less provisions, and the gains are only mentioned in the notes.
answerBudgetSenat.ombreRetraites: {total} of pensions off the balance sheet. No provision is recorded for the pensions and health costs already promised to former senators and staff. This amount fell by {baisse} in a year ({avant} at the end of 2024), not through savings but because of a calculation setting: the interest rate used to estimate these commitments rose, for senators, from {taux2024} to {taux2025}.
answerBudgetSenat.ombreCapitalInvestissement: About {montant} already promised to funds. The Senate's funds and reserve have committed to paying this sum into private equity funds, which invest in unlisted companies. The commitment only appears in the notes.
answerBudgetSenat.ombreRecommandations: The Court's recommendations stay internal. Their number, {nb}, and their themes are known. Their details are in a report given to the Senate's administration, which is not published.
answerBudgetSenat.ombreRegistres: Declarations that rely on each senator. Senators declare themselves when they step back from a vote over a conflict of interest (a recusal): the public register lists {nbDeports} in 2025. The list of gifts and invitations worth over €150 records {nbCadeaux} gifts and {deplacements} trips paid for by third parties received in 2025.
answerBudgetSenat.ombreErreurs: A report that contradicts itself. Air tickets cost {avion1} in one table and {avion2} in the text, the Paris metro {ratp1} then {ratp2}. The grant to groups is {groupes1} in the accounts, but their table adds up to {groupes2}. The reserve is worth {reserve1} on the balance sheet and {reserve2} in the commentary.
answerBudgetSenat.sectionAvenir: What lies ahead for the Senate
answerBudgetSenat.avenirDesc: Based on budget documents published in 2025 and 2026.
answerBudgetSenat.avenirReserve: A shrinking reserve. If the allocation stayed frozen, the Senate's reserve would fall from {fin2026} at the end of 2026 to {fin2027} at the end of 2027, then {fin2028} at the end of 2028: "less than one month of spending", whereas the Senate's autonomy requires keeping at least {mois} months, according to the finance committee report. This projection dates from November 2025, when the budget still planned to draw {prevu2025} from reserves in 2025: the year ended in surplus, and the basis of the calculation is not published.
answerBudgetSenat.avenirTravaux: Works picking up again. Investment would rise to {inv2026} in 2026, {inv2027} in 2027 and {inv2028} in 2028: roofs and timber frames of the Petit Luxembourg, heating and air conditioning, the Palace's chilled water. For 2026, the budget already plans to draw {prelevement} from reserves.
answerBudgetSenat.avenirDotation: An increase requested for 2027. The Bureau requested {dotation}, 2% more, for {depenses} of spending, Garden and Museum included, and plans "at this stage" no further increase.
answerBudgetSenat.avenirAutonomie: Autonomy in question. A prolonged freeze of the allocation "would risk undermining the Senate's budgetary autonomy as early as {annee}", the lead Quaestor warned in May 2026. Budget documents also announce a review, from 2027, of how heritage renovation is funded and of the State's share in it.
answerBudgetSenat.avenirNote: Based on the <plf2026>special report on public authorities</plf2026> of the 2026 finance bill and the <bureau>minutes of the Bureau</bureau> of 28 May and 2 July 2026.
answerBudgetSenat.historiqueDesc: Actual spending, and surplus or deficit of the three budgets, each year. Over six years, spending rose by {hausse}, and surpluses and deficits nearly cancel out: a cumulative surplus of {cumul}. The State allocation, frozen from 2012 to 2021, was raised from 2022 to 2024.
answerBudgetSenat.methodologyPerimetre: Scope: spending actually paid in 2025 by the Senate's three budgets, the institutional mission, the Luxembourg Garden and the Luxembourg Museum. The figures come from the <rapport>special committee's report on the 2025 accounts</rapport>, the <certification>Court of Audit's certification report</certification>, factsheets and orders published by the Senate and the <deontologie>Ethics Committee's report</deontologie>. The pension and social security funds have their own accounts: only what the budget pays them is counted. The cost per inhabitant divides spending by the population at 1 January 2026, 69.1 million people according to <insee>INSEE's demographic review</insee>.
answerBudgetSenat.methodologyDecoupage: Breakdown: the Senate's execution table only publishes accounting chapters. Each is split using the detailed tables of the same report, and the last piece takes the remainder so the chapter adds up to the euro; the Garden and the Museum, published account by account, are filed as they are. The check matches each destination of the summary table (running costs, parliamentary charges, staff) to within €1. Two amounts are derived rather than read: the institutional mission's contribution to the staff pension fund ({cotisation} received by the fund, minus {jardin} published for the Garden), and {reste} that the summary table assigns to staff without details, taken from travel. The full mapping, with the page for each piece, can be <csv>downloaded as CSV</csv>.
answerBudgetSenat.methodologyArrondis: Rounding: the lines of the breakdown add up to {lignes}, {ecart} less than the official total of {officiel}, amounts being rounded to the euro line by line. Each item's share is calculated on the sum of the lines and rounded to one decimal place.
answerBudgetSenat.methodologyLimites: Limits: salaries are not broken down by department, so the real cost of IT or buildings exceeds their item. The amounts the report publishes for committees and international activities are net of revenue: the "Parliamentary activities" item is built from accounting chapters and does not match them exactly.

personnel.desc: The {fonctionnaires} civil servants and {contractuels} contract staff who keep the institution running, presented below in "Who works at the Senate". The employer contribution paid to their pension fund is taken out and counted under "Pensions". Training, recruitment exams, staff canteens and the transport levy, filed elsewhere by the report, are added in.

collaborateurs.desc: Assistants work for a senator, who hires and dismisses them: the senator remains their employer. Their payroll goes through AGAS (the association for the management of senators' assistants), which receives a grant from the Senate. It pays the gross salaries drawn from each senator's allowance ({credit} gross a month), about half of the total, plus employer contributions, the thirteenth month and seniority pay, training, employee savings and retirement plans, health and welfare insurance, severance pay, and the association's own costs: statutory auditor, assistants' travel, occupational health, staff welfare. The report does not publish the share of each of these costs.

fraisMandat.desc: The general office expense advance, the three specific advances (Paris accommodation, IT, hospitality) and what the Senate pays directly: air and rail tickets, taxis, telephone and postage. For the advances, the amount counted is what senators backed with receipts, not the sum paid out. Details in "Senators and their expenses".

retraites.desc: What the budget pays to the Senate's two pension funds, the former senators' fund ({caisseSenateurs}) and the staff fund ({caissePersonnel}): the employer contribution, pension supplements for children and retirees' social security. The Garden contributes {versRetraites}, taken out of its own item.

senateurs.desc: The allowances of the {sieges} senators, their social security, their training, the subsidy to the senators' restaurant, and back-to-work support, the equivalent of unemployment benefit for former senators. A senator who is not re-elected and earns less than the basic allowance ({base} gross a month) receives the difference between their income, local offices included, and a ceiling that falls every quarter, for four years at most and never beyond age 64. The allowance is taxable and paid by the Senate's budget: no unemployment contribution is deducted from senators' allowance.

batiments.desc: The Luxembourg Palace, the Petit Luxembourg and the nearby office buildings: upkeep and maintenance, technical equipment including a new CCTV system, energy, works, rent and cleaning. Investment in 2025 was the lowest since 2016: the renovation of the buildings at 26 and 36 rue de Vaugirard, €61.1 million in total, is finished.

groupes.desc: A monthly grant to each of the eight political groups and to the administrative body of non-attached senators, which employ their own staff.

jardinMusee.desc: Two separate Senate budgets. The Luxembourg Garden, a public park open to all: gardeners and staff, upkeep, restoration of the railings and purchase of the merry-go-round in 2025. The Luxembourg Museum, run by the national museums agency (RMN). The National Assembly has no equivalent.

fonctionnement.desc: Vehicles, supplies, insurance, lawyers' and experts' fees, departmental mail and receptions, printing of parliamentary papers, and the grant to the Republican Guard, which provides security at the Palace.

communication.desc: Filming of sittings and meetings, their broadcasting, the website and the multimedia newsroom, and the chamber's audiovisual equipment.

informatique.desc: Maintenance of software and of the electronic voting system, computers, servers and phones, equipment rental and internet lines. Not counted here: the salaries of the Senate's IT staff, included in staff, and senators' IT advance, included in their office expenses.

activite.desc: Missions by committees, delegations and friendship groups, dues to the international assemblies the Senate belongs to, the travel and receptions of the President of the Senate, and the share of offices run jointly with the National Assembly.

patrimoine.desc: Subscriptions, documentation and audiovisual archives, restoration of artworks, historic furniture and old books, including the Library's decor.

meta.title: Connect an AI assistant to LoiClair
meta.description: LoiClair's MCP server: query French parliamentary data from an AI assistant, in French or in English.

mcp.titre: Connect an AI assistant to LoiClair
mcp.chapo: LoiClair joins many sources that nothing else connects: the National Assembly, the Senate, Légifrance, Wikidata, the National Directory of Elected Officials, the Constitutional Council, the High Authority for Transparency in Public Life, and the press. This server opens that work to your assistant, so it can answer questions about French laws and lawmakers without leaving your conversation.

adresse.aide: In Claude, ChatGPT or any compatible client, add a connector and paste this address. No account and no key are required: access is free and read-only.

outils.titre: What your assistant will be able to do
outils.chapo: Ten read-only tools. Every answer carries a link to LoiClair, in French and in English: the page of the member or of the file for profiles and searches, the method article for figures and votes.
outils.catalogueFactsDesc: The eighteen “Facts” articles, with their question and link. This is the map: it shows an assistant what the site can answer.
outils.chercherEluDesc: By name, department, parliamentary group, chamber, held local offices or voting attendance. Filters combine freely.
outils.ficheEluDesc: Identity, group, constituency, local offices, declared interests and activity score, including why someone may be excluded from the ranking.
outils.votesEluDesc: Their position on recent recorded votes. The scope is stated explicitly: named breakdowns are not published for every vote.
outils.chercherLoiDesc: By words in the title, topic, or stage of progress.
outils.ficheLoiDesc: Its stage, who introduced it, its amendments, its enactment and the state of its implementing decrees.
outils.trouverTexteDesc: By tabling number or title, with a link to the official document.
outils.detailScrutinDesc: The tally of a recorded vote and each group's majority position.
outils.chiffresClesDesc: Enactment rates, implementation of laws, delays, amendments, attendance, held local offices, and both chambers' budgets.
outils.actualiteDesc: Stages cleared over a week or a month: tablings, floor votes, joint committees, enactments and implementing decrees.

limites.chapo: Some data stays on the site, and that is deliberate.
limites.resumesIADesc: Only their link is passed on. Generated text should be read with the warnings of the page that carries it; taken out of that context, it would read as a source.
limites.debatsDesc: Several hundred thousand floor interventions are stored. Passing them along would flood the answer without clarifying anything, while their own page puts them in context.
limites.centilesTitre: The inner workings of the activity score
limites.centilesDesc: The relative positions behind the score stay internal: outside their cohort they say nothing about a person, yet would read as facts.
limites.agregationsDesc: A gift's value, a trip's length and a number of company shares share one field. Adding them up would produce a meaningless figure.

attribution.texte: The data is free to reuse, provided LoiClair is credited. Official sources remain governed by their own open licences. The LoiClair name and logos are not granted: you may reuse the data, not publish a service under that identity.

choixModeleIA.pageMetaDesc: How LoiClair chooses its AI models, task by task: comparative tests on real texts, results and method.
choixModeleIA.intro: LoiClair currently uses {n, plural, one {one AI model} other {# AI models}}, each chosen for specific tasks, most often by a test we ran ourselves: the “Who writes what” block shows which does what. {modeleMammouth}, by OpenAI, is called through Mammouth, a French company that gives access to models from several providers; {modeleAnthropic} is called directly from Anthropic. For each task, we look for a model that is both good and cheap: LoiClair is free, and every call has a cost. The less it costs, the more we can offer each reader, with the widest possible usage limit.
choixModeleIA.evalAnswer: We tested {n} models on real legislative texts. {modele} scores <hl>{score}/10</hl> for <hl>{cout}</hl> per 1,000 summaries. The best model tested, {meilleur}, is only {ecart} point better, for a price {ratio} times higher.
choixModeleIA.evalDate: Measured on {date}, over {resumes} graded summaries, with the same prompt for every model. The prompt may have changed since, to improve the summaries of the chosen model.
choixModeleIA.evalChartHowTo: Each logo is a model, marked with its provider's logo and numbered as in the table. The higher it sits, the better its summaries; the further right, the more it costs. The price scale is logarithmic: each gridline multiplies the price by 10. The line joins the quality-price frontier: the models that no other model beats on both quality and price. The model chosen is circled. The shaded area at the top left holds the good summaries at a low price: that is where the choice is made.
choixModeleIA.evalChartAria: Scatter plot: each model's score out of 10 against its cost per 1,000 summaries.
choixModeleIA.cardAttitreDesc: If another one does better for a reasonable price, we switch.
choixModeleIA.evalLegende: Score: weighted average of the five criteria. Instructions: share of the prompt's measurable rules that were followed (lengths, number of entries, stories in the third person). Draw spread: average difference in score for the same text between two generations, measured for the finalists only; the smaller it is, the more consistent the model. In bold: the models on the quality-price frontier. In colour: the best value in each column.
choixModeleIA.sectionSuivant: What if a better model comes along?
choixModeleIA.suivantBody: LoiClair is not tied to any AI. The tasks that have a benchmark keep it to judge the next model. If we switch the summary model, the summaries of laws, debates and Constitutional Council decisions are rewritten with it.

lienInstructions.desc: What the AI writes and the exact instructions it receives

choixModeleIA.evalGraves: It also makes very few serious errors, the kind that would mislead a reader about what the text does: <hl>{graves}</hl> per 10 summaries, against up to {pire} for {nomPire}.
choixModeleIA.ficheIntro: Each dossier has a short card: a 100 to 150 word summary, read as is in the newsletter and indexed by the site's search, and one to three themes used by the filters. This task has its own benchmark, which pits {retenu}, by Anthropic, against {compare}.
choixModeleIA.ficheMethode: The instructions were rewritten in {versions} versions on a first set of 20 dossiers. Then both models wrote, with the same final instructions, the cards of 20 other dossiers that no version had seen. {juge}, from a third family, compared blind the {paires} pairs of cards that had a summary, without knowing which model wrote which, on accuracy, completeness, neutrality, clarity and choice of themes.
choixModeleIA.ficheResultat: <hl>{retenu} was preferred {gagne} times, {compare} {perdu} times</hl>, with {egal} tie.
choixModeleIA.ficheChoix: LoiClair is free: to keep it that way, the team looks for the highest-quality solutions, in line with LoiClair's neutrality principles, while keeping costs low. {retenu} costs about {ratio} times more per card ({coutRetenu} versus {coutCompare} per 1,000 cards), but its calls use API credits that Anthropic includes in the Claude Code subscription, the tool the site is built with. Since that subscription is paid for anyway, these credits are a bonus: using them costs nothing extra. LoiClair is not sponsored by Anthropic.
choixModeleIA.ficheLimites: Small sample and a single judge: this result says the two models are on a par for this task, not that one clearly beats the other. Measured on {date}. The scripts, cards and judgments are published in <lien>scripts/banc-fiches-courtes</lien>.
choixModeleIA.ficheTableLegende: Average scores out of 10 given by the judge over {paires} pairs of cards, with the same instructions for both models. “Preferred” counts the pairs its card won; {egal} pair ended in a tie.
choixModeleIA.concerneIntro: The <lien>What affects me</lien> page says, for each article of law and each adopted amendment, which citizen situations it directly affects (employee, tenant, retiree…), and quotes the passage that supports it. For this sorting, we pitted {retenu}, by Anthropic, against {compare}, and had independent AIs from other families settle between them.
choixModeleIA.concerneMethode: The benchmark gathers {total} real articles and amendments. Each link shown is reviewed blind by three AIs from other families, {juges}, which say whether the situation is really affected; the majority decides. Before trusting them, a team member settled {cas} cases where they disagreed: each time, they sided with the majority.
choixModeleIA.concerneBoucle: The instructions were then improved by a recursive loop, run by Claude, the AI the site is built with. At each round, it reads the errors flagged by the judges, rewrites the instructions to fix one family of errors (a measure that applies to everyone, a situation wrongly attributed to the reader, an effect that is only indirect), has {reglage} items sorted again, twice to smooth out chance, and keeps the new version only if the share of correct links goes up without the model missing more situations. These rounds were graded by a cheaper jury.
choixModeleIA.concerneResultat: In the final test, {retenu} and {compare} sorted, with the same final instructions, a new set of articles and amendments that no round had seen, graded again by the three independent AIs. <hl>{retenu} keeps an edge on every criterion</hl>:
choixModeleIA.concerneTableLegende: On the {test} test items, by majority of the three judges. Correct: share of the links shown that the judges rate correct. If “certain”, if “likely”: the same share, by the degree of certainty the model gives itself. Situations found: share of the situations the judges say are affected that the model shows. Faithful sentences: share of explanations faithful to the text.
choixModeleIA.concerneChoix: {retenu} costs barely more ({coutRetenu} versus {coutCompare} per 1,000 texts). Its price stays low because the sorting runs in batches, every day, which Anthropic's API bills at half price, whereas {compare} was called directly. Its calls also use the same API credits as the short card, which cost nothing extra. At equal price it would be kept anyway: it does better on every criterion.
choixModeleIA.concerneLimites: The final test covers only {test} items, and the three judges, themselves AIs, agree with one another only about four times out of five. Measured on {date}. The scripts, the instructions tried, the sortings and the judgments are published in <lien>scripts/banc-ce-qui-me-concerne</lien>.
choixModeleIA.cardBancsDesc: The main tasks each have their own benchmark: models compared on real texts, most often graded blind by other AIs.
choixModeleIA.cardModelesTitle: {n, plural, one {# model in use} other {# models in use}}
choixModeleIA.quiTacheAutres: Debate and Constitutional Council decision summaries, newsletter
choixModeleIA.evalMethode: {n} real texts taken from LoiClair's database (laws, consolidated versions and decrees, from {min} to {max} characters), {fr} summarised in French and {en} in English. Each model received the instructions in production on that date, with the same format and the same temperature; the finalists summarised each text twice. {jury} AI graders, often more powerful than the models tested, scored the summaries blind, never grading a model from their own family, on five criteria: accuracy weighs {exactitude}% of the score, neutrality {neutralite}%, completeness, clarity and examples {autres}% each. The choice is made on the quality-price frontier, not on a simple ratio, which would let a nearly free but poor model win.
choixModeleIA.evalLimitesCourt: The benchmark is small ({n} short or medium texts) and its graders are themselves AIs: it separates clearly better or worse models, not two models 0.2 points apart. Texts over 500,000 characters were not tested. GPT-6 Luna at medium reasoning does barely better than the low setting, for a higher price: the low setting was kept. The scripts are published in <lien>scripts/banc-modeles</lien>, with the <grille>grading rubric</grille> that was used; redoing the measurement costs about $7.
choixModeleIA.quiTacheTitres: English dossier, law and vote titles
choixModeleIA.titresTitle: English dossier, law and vote titles: {modele}
choixModeleIA.titresIntro: On the English version of the site, the official title of each dossier is translated by the AI, as is that of the published laws cited by the pages on how laws are applied and that of votes. It is shown in place of the French title; on a dossier page, with the AI badge and the official title underneath. The task is short and repetitive: translate faithfully, with the parliamentary vocabulary used on the rest of the site.
choixModeleIA.titresMethode: The instructions were tuned on 30 titles chosen to cover every type of text and the hard cases (acronyms, budget, overseas territories, very long titles, titles starting with a lower-case letter), read by the team next to the French title. They were then checked on 90 randomly drawn titles never seen during tuning, read by Claude, the AI the site is developed with. The same instructions were then tried on 30 titles of published laws (“LOI n° … du …”), with no change needed. On vote titles (“sur l'ensemble de la proposition de loi…”), they sometimes dropped the leading article (“whole of the bill”): three instructions were added (keep that article, translate the preliminary motion to reject, leave political group names in French), then checked on 29 vote titles, on the 40 from a run where the article had disappeared, and on the 12 motions to reject. Finally, all 4,553 translated titles were read by Claude: a few mistranslations (“dénoncer un accord” rendered as “denounce”, to criticise, instead of “terminate”, to end it), infinitives turned into “-ing” forms, and the same term rendered several ways. A rule on false friends, rules of form and some fifteen vocabulary entries were added, checked on 97 faulty titles, and every title was translated again.
choixModeleIA.titresChoix: {modele}, already in use for the short card, gave good translations from the first tries. Only the reasoning setting was compared. At “low”, about one title in eight broke an instruction, for instance by adding a type of text the title does not name; at “medium”, two or three in 80, on points of style. “Medium” was kept: it costs three times as much, which is worth it given the quality improvements.
choixModeleIA.titresLimites: No model other than {modele} was tried, and the translations were not graded blind by other AIs: they were read. A translation is still a translation: under a dossier's title, the official French title is always shown, and it alone is authoritative. The scripts are published in <lien>scripts/banc-titres-en</lien>.

definitions.futur_parent: Person expecting a child (pregnancy, adoption under way) or planning to have one.
definitions.jeune: Young adult aged 18 to 25, studying or not, working or not.
definitions.senior: Person aged 55 or over, working or not.
definitions.epargnant: Person who saves or invests (savings accounts, life insurance, savings plans, shares, crypto-assets).
definitions.patrimoine_ifi: Household liable for the real estate wealth tax (IFI).
definitions.emprunteur: Person repaying a mortgage or consumer loan.
definitions.allocataire: Person receiving the RSA, a housing benefit (APL, ALF, ALS), the activity bonus or free supplementary health cover (C2S). The disabled adult allowance is not included.
definitions.heritier_donateur: Person who passes on or receives assets, by gift or inheritance.
definitions.particulier_employeur: Person who employs a nanny, home help or domestic worker at home.
definitions.handicap: Person with a disability, recognised by the MDPH or not, receiving the AAH or PCH or not.
definitions.malade_chronique: Person with a long-term illness (recognised as such or not) that requires regular care.
definitions.aidant: Person who regularly helps a sick, disabled or older relative without doing so professionally, or who acts as their legal guardian or curator.
definitions.age_dependant: Older person losing autonomy, at home or in a care home (EHPAD), receiving the APA or not.
definitions.automobiliste: Person who owns or uses a car, motorbike or van, electric or not.
definitions.cycliste: Person who gets around by bike, e-bike or e-scooter.
definitions.usager_transports: Person who travels by train, coach, bus, metro, tram or plane.
definitions.etranger_ue: National of another European Union country living in France.
definitions.etranger_hors_ue: Person from a non-EU country living in France: residence permit holder, asylum seeker or refugee.
definitions.animal: Person who has a pet or a horse.
definitions.chasseur_pecheur: Person who hunts, fishes or practises sport shooting as a hobby.
definitions.fumeur: Person who smokes tobacco or uses an e-cigarette.
definitions.joueur: Person who bets on sports, plays poker, the lottery or online gambling games.
definitions.elu_local: Municipal, intercommunal, departmental or regional elected official (mayor, deputy mayor, councillor).
definitions.benevole: Volunteer or volunteer manager of an association, or civic service volunteer.
definitions.pompier_volontaire: Volunteer firefighter, or reservist of the armed forces, police or gendarmerie.
definitions.syndique: Member of the works council (CSE), union representative or union member.
definitions.ancien_combattant: Veteran, repatriate, harki, or member of their family.
